articles.headline: UK Inflation Rises to 2.9% in July, Fueling Interest Rate Hike Concerns
body: The UK's Consumer Prices Index (CPI) rose to 2.9% in the year to July, an increase from June's figure of 2.6%. This uptick in inflation, announced by the Office for National Statistics (ONS), is expected to strengthen arguments for the Bank of England to raise interest rates before the end of the year.

The increase is primarily attributed to rising energy bills, following a 13% increase in the price cap on July 1, 2026. While falling transport costs partially offset this rise, the ongoing conflict in the Middle East continues to create significant uncertainty in economic forecasts, leading to volatile energy prices.

The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee, which has kept interest rates unchanged at 3.75% since December, will announce its next decision on September 17. Market commentators suggest a rate hike is expected in September, with another potentially following in February, as the Bank aims to bring inflation back to its 2% target.

articles.headline: FOMC Minutes Reveal Elevated Inflation Concerns and Higher Rate Expectations
body: Minutes from the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting revealed that headline inflation remains above targeted levels in many foreign economies, largely due to increases in retail energy and food prices stemming from the conflict in the Middle East.
Both the market-implied expected path of the federal funds rate and nominal Treasury yields have moved up, reflecting FOMC communications perceived as more restrictive than anticipated.

While total inflation is expected to decline in the second half of the year, with core inflation projected to slow modestly, some participants noted that underlying inflation, even excluding energy and tariff-affected items, appeared elevated.

articles.headline: FOMC Minutes Reveal Inflation Concerns Tied to Middle East Conflict and AI Demand
body: Minutes from the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on July 28-29, 2026, indicate that total consumer price inflation was 4.1 percent in May, with core PCE price inflation at 3.4 percent.

Staff attributed these elevated inflation levels to factors including past tariff increases, higher energy and input costs stemming from the conflict in the Middle East, and a surge in demand related to the AI buildout.

While total inflation is expected to decline in the second half of the year as gasoline prices move lower and core inflation slows, the effects of tariffs and the Middle East conflict are projected to wane, with inflation reaching approximately 2 percent in 2028.

body: The United States International Trade Commission (USITC) announced on August 19, 2026, its affirmative injury determinations in antidumping and countervailing duty investigations concerning hardwood and decorative plywood from China, Indonesia, and Vietnam.

The USITC found that these imports, which the U.S. Department of Commerce determined are subsidized and sold in the United States at less than fair value, are causing injury to the domestic industry. As a result, Commerce will issue antidumping and countervailing duty orders on imports of this product from the three countries.

However, the USITC also found that imports of softwood structural plywood from China, Indonesia, and Vietnam were negligible and voted to terminate those investigations. This decision highlights the ongoing efforts by the U.S. to address unfair trade practices and protect domestic industries.

articles.headline: Iran's Parliament Approves Plan to Combat 'Foreign Infiltration' Amidst Public Alarm
body: Iran's hardline-dominated parliament has approved the broad outlines of a plan aimed at combatting foreign "infiltration," with a significant focus on academia, media, and the cultural sector. Proponents argue the plan complements existing national security laws and bolsters wartime security.

The envisioned legislation, which has been released in an updated 33-article version, has raised alarm among the public, experts, and even elements within the government, who fear it will further curtail personal freedoms.

Majid Ansari, Deputy for Legal Affairs for President Masoud Pezeshkian, stated the government is in "explicit opposition" to the plan, warning it would impose "serious restrictions" on scientific work, obstruct academic access to international colleagues, damage Iran's international image, and accelerate brain drain.

articles.headline: FOMC Minutes Highlight Middle East Conflict's Impact on Global Inflation and Oil Prices
body: Minutes from the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on July 28-29, 2026, revealed that developments in financial markets were significantly influenced by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. Oil prices ended the intermeeting period higher following an escalation of tensions in the region.

The conflict contributed to headline inflation remaining above targeted levels in many foreign economies, primarily due to increases in retail energy and food prices. Staff analysis attributed higher energy and input costs, along with past tariff increases and the surge in AI-related demand, to elevated total and core PCE price inflation in May.

Looking ahead, total inflation is expected to decline in the second half of the year as retail gasoline prices are forecast to move lower and core inflation slows modestly. Inflation is projected to step down further next year as the effects of tariffs and the Middle East conflict wane, aiming for approximately 2 percent in 2028.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates ICC Officials and Venezuelan Entity, Issues New General License
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting officials of the International Criminal Court (ICC) and a Venezuela-related entity. Specifically, Tomoko Akane of Japan, the ICC President, and Abdoulaye Seye of Senegal, an ICC senior trial lawyer, have been added to the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List.

These designations stem from their alleged involvement in efforts by the ICC to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute officials whose governments have not consented to ICC jurisdiction. The U.S. Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, characterized the ICC as a 'corrupt and fatally politicized supranational court.'

In a related action, OFAC also designated Bluwaves Properties Limited, a British Virgin Islands-based entity, for its ties to Venezuela's oil industry. Concurrently, OFAC issued International Criminal Court-related General License 12, authorizing the wind down of transactions involving certain blocked persons.

articles.headline: Global Government Borrowing Costs Hit Multi-Year Highs Amid Inflation Fears
body: Government borrowing costs across France, Germany, and Japan have reached multi-year highs, driven by investor concerns that the Middle East crisis will sustain high inflation. The yield on 30-year French bonds rose to its highest level since September 2008, while Germany's equivalent hit its highest since 2011.

In Tokyo, the 10-year Japanese government bond yield surged to a three-decade high, reaching 2.93% before a slight dip following weaker-than-expected GDP data. This rise in bond yields reflects traders seeking higher returns on government debt due to fears that central banks will continue to tighten monetary policy to control inflation.

Oil and gas prices are also on the rise, with Brent crude trading at approximately $89.49 per barrel, following reduced shipping activity through the Strait of Hormuz and concerns about a potential ceasefire in the region.

articles.headline: U.S. Annual Inflation Slows to 3.4% in July, Core Inflation Eases
body: U.S. annual inflation continued its downward trend, slowing to 3.4% in July from 3.5% in June, aligning with market expectations.
Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, also eased to 2.5% in July, marking its slowest pace since March 2021.

This sustained deceleration in inflation reinforces expectations that the Federal Reserve will keep interest rates unchanged at its next meeting, following its decision in July to hold rates at 3.5%-3.75%.

articles.headline: U.S. Gas Prices Hit Record Highs for August Amid Stalled Iran Talks and Refining Shortages
body: U.S. gas prices have reached their highest ever recorded for August, with the national average at $4.06 per gallon on Monday, $0.05 higher than last week and $1 more expensive than a year ago. In California and Hawaii, averages hit approximately $5.50 a gallon. This surge is primarily driven by a critical global shortage of refining capacity, with 7.5 million barrels daily lost worldwide.

Energy prices have been elevated since the US-Israel war with Iran began at the end of February, leading to the blockage of the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway for a fifth of global oil. Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, reached $112 a barrel in March, a high not seen since 2022, and while prices have since come down closer to $85 a barrel, they are still about 30% higher than a year ago.

Peace talks between the U.S. and Iran have stalled, and Donald Trump has issued fresh threats against Oman, further exacerbating market anxieties. The Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed to commercial shipping, with only about 10 vessels transiting daily compared to 88 pre-conflict. This ongoing geopolitical tension, coupled with infrastructure destruction in the Middle East and Russia, severely limits fuel production and depletes domestic inventories.

articles.headline: Central Banks Grapple with Inflation Amidst Middle East Conflict and Energy Price Volatility
body: Central banks in the U.S., UK, and Eurozone are facing a complex challenge as they navigate persistent inflation fueled by elevated oil prices and geopolitical tensions in the Middle East.
The U.S. Federal Reserve, the Bank of England, and the European Central Bank have largely kept interest rates on hold, but the prospect of further tightening remains if inflation accelerates.

Despite a temporary easing of tensions with Iran in June, which led to a dip in energy prices and a slight cooling of inflation, renewed conflict has pushed oil prices back up, threatening to reignite inflationary pressures.

articles.headline: Central Banks Face Dilemma as Inflation Rises Amidst Slowing Growth and Middle East Crisis
body: Central banks, including the U.S. Federal Reserve, the Bank of England, and the European Central Bank, are in a challenging position as the Middle East crisis continues into its sixth month. Elevated oil prices are fueling inflationary pressures while simultaneously threatening to impede economic growth.

U.S. inflation edged lower to 3.4% last month, down from 3.5% in June and 4.2% in May, largely due to easing petrol prices following a U.S. memorandum of understanding with Iran. However, the price of Brent crude has since risen to approximately $90 per barrel, which is expected to drive up energy and transport costs across the U.S. in the latter half of the year, potentially pushing inflation back towards 4%.

Despite a majority of Fed policy committee members voting last month to keep the benchmark interest rate unchanged at 3.50%-3.75%, a growing minority argues that tighter policy is necessary given that inflation has remained above target since February 2021. Financial markets anticipate at least one, and possibly two, quarter-point increases by mid-next year, potentially raising the Fed's target rate to 4-4.25%.

articles.headline: Central Banks Grapple with Inflation Amidst Slowing Growth and Middle East Crisis
body: Central banks, including the US Federal Reserve, the Bank of England, and the European Central Bank, are facing a difficult dilemma as they confront rising inflation alongside threats of slowing economic growth. The ongoing Middle East crisis, now in its sixth month, continues to keep oil prices elevated, exacerbating inflationary pressures.

US inflation edged lower to 3.4% last month, down from 3.5% in June, partly due to easing petrol prices following a US memorandum of understanding with Iran. However, the price of Brent crude has since risen to about $90 per barrel, suggesting inflation could climb back towards 4%, double the Fed's target.

Many analysts have applauded the Fed's new boss, Kevin Warsh, for instigating an all-embracing review of its operations. Despite this, financial markets predict the Bank of England will raise rates this year, possibly from as early as its next meeting in September, with rates potentially reaching 4.25% by late 2027.

The latest threats come as the two-month window to negotiate peace with Iran expired on Monday with no end to the conflict in sight. Trump's unpredictable and often outrageous approach to diplomacy has reportedly upset U.S. partners and failed to achieve the breakthrough he promised to end the war.

Oman is not a party to the war, and the various conflicts in the Middle East continue to escalate. This development highlights the volatile geopolitical landscape in the region and the challenges in achieving a peaceful resolution.

articles.headline: UN Warns of Dangerously Overlooked Land Degradation and Desertification
body: The United Nations is highlighting a dangerously overlooked environmental crisis: the degradation of land and the alarming spread of desertification across the globe. This issue is intensifying due to rising temperatures, droughts, and deforestation, impacting what the UN describes as our 'most vital infrastructure.'

As heatwaves become deadlier and fires and disasters ravage cities, the phenomenon of fertile land becoming unproductive and desert-like is accelerating. This environmental challenge poses significant threats to food security, biodiversity, and human livelihoods worldwide.

The UN is urging greater attention and action to push back against desertification, emphasizing the critical need for land restoration efforts to protect ecosystems and ensure sustainable development for future generations.

articles.headline: Iranians Face 'Limited Options' as War with US Devastates Economy
body: Millions of Iranians are struggling to make ends meet as a months-long war with the United States and a naval blockade of Iranian ports devastate the country's economy. Food inflation has soared to over 128% year-on-year, with prices for oils and fats, milk, cheese, eggs, meat, and poultry seeing increases of 145% to 261%.

Job losses have occurred across most industries in 2026, and youth unemployment reached 23.4% in the spring, a 3.7% increase year-on-year. The economic woes are compounded by systemic issues of corruption and mismanagement, alongside decades of U.S. and United Nations sanctions.

Despite the severe economic impact, the Iranian economy is reportedly far from collapse after more than five months of conflict. U.S. President Donald Trump has vowed to hit Iran hard economically, with the Treasury Secretary indicating 'never before seen' measures.

The U.S. Central Command has reported redirecting 55 vessels linked to Iran since the blockade was reinstated. Meanwhile, Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has appointed new military leaders to replace those killed during initial Israeli and U.S. airstrikes, including Ali Abdollahi as chief of staff, Kioumars Heydari as deputy commander, and Hossein Taeb as Basij commander.

Such visits by Japanese officials frequently draw criticism from neighboring countries, particularly those that suffered under Japanese occupation during World War II. The shrine includes convicted war criminals among those commemorated, making it a flashpoint for diplomatic tensions in the region.
The incident is expected to further strain diplomatic relations between Japan and its East Asian neighbors, potentially impacting regional cooperation on various issues.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi clarified that the Islamabad MoU marked an 'end of the war, not a ceasefire,' asserting that the U.S. violated the deal, leading to a resumption of fighting and negating any 60-day ceasefire extension.

Meanwhile, at least 11 people have been killed in Israeli attacks across southern Lebanon, marking the deadliest day since a ceasefire went into effect in June. Israeli authorities reported that three of its soldiers, including an officer, were wounded in an attack attributed to Hezbollah.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: UN Security Council Committee Amends ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions List
body: On August 14, 2026, the Security Council Committee concerning ISIL (Da'esh), Al-Qaida and associated individuals, groups, undertakings and entities enacted amendments to four entries on its Sanctions List.

These amendments, which include strikethrough and underline changes, pertain to individuals and entities subject to the assets freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo set out in Security Council resolution 2734 (2024).

The updates ensure the accuracy and effectiveness of the sanctions list, which is adopted under Chapter VII of the Charter of the United Nations. Singapore, for example, gives domestic effect to these UN lists, meaning the updates directly impact obligations for financial institutions and other regulated businesses in the country.

This increase reflects investor concerns over persistent inflation and the nation's rising national debt, prompting demands for a heavier premium on long-duration U.S. debt.
The bond market's reaction suggests worries that policymakers will maintain high interest rates for an extended period, impacting the Treasury Department's efforts to fund a growing deficit.

articles.headline: U.S. Long-Term Borrowing Costs Reach 25-Year High Amid Inflation Fears
body: U.S. long-term borrowing costs have risen to a 25-year high, with an auction of 30-year U.S. Treasury bonds incurring a yield of 5.216%, the highest since 2001. This indicates that investors are demanding a significant premium for long-duration U.S. debt due to concerns over persistent inflation and the country's rising national debt.

The increased yield suggests investor worries that inflation will remain high, prompting policymakers to maintain elevated interest rates for an extended period. This development could impact future government borrowing and overall market stability.

Adding to market concerns, U.S. retail spending fell by 0.6% month-on-month in July, suggesting consumers are feeling the squeeze from inflation. This includes drops in spending at online retailers and motor vehicle dealers.

articles.headline: Euro Area Records €8.6 Billion Trade Surplus in June 2026
body: The euro area recorded a trade in goods surplus of €8.6 billion with the rest of the world in June 2026, an improvement compared to the €4.8 billion surplus in June 2025. This follows a deficit of €9.0 billion in May 2026.
Euro area exports of goods to the rest of the world increased by 14.4% to €272.5 billion in June 2026 compared to the previous year, while imports rose by 13.1% to €264.0 billion.

The improvement in the trade balance was primarily driven by a higher surplus in chemicals and related products, as well as surpluses in other manufactured goods and food and drink, despite a larger energy deficit.

articles.headline: US Long-Term Borrowing Costs Reach 25-Year High Amid Economic Uncertainty
body: US long-term borrowing costs have surged to a 25-year high, with the sale of 30-year bonds reflecting the highest borrowing costs since 2001. This development signals growing investor concerns about inflation and the future trajectory of interest rates.

The rise in borrowing costs could impact government spending, corporate investments, and consumer lending, potentially slowing economic growth. Analysts are closely watching how the Federal Reserve will respond to these market dynamics.
This comes as global economic growth faces headwinds from supply-chain disruptions in the Middle East, new tariffs, and soaring semiconductor prices driven by AI infrastructure investments.

articles.headline: Gas and Diesel Prices on Track for Most Expensive August Ever Amid Refining Shortage
body: Americans are facing the most expensive August ever at the fuel pump, with national average prices for regular gas at $4.07 per gallon and diesel at $5.40 per gallon, setting new daily records.

This surge is primarily driven by a critical global shortage of refining capacity, with an estimated 7.5 million barrels daily lost worldwide. Infrastructure destruction in the Middle East and Russia, where nearly 40% of capacity is gone, severely limits fuel production.

Experts warn that even falling crude prices will not significantly lower fuel costs without restored refining capacity. Upcoming refinery maintenance could further exacerbate the situation, ensuring elevated prices and sustained inflationary pressure.

articles.headline: BIS Reaches Administrative Enforcement Settlement with Plexon, Inc.
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced an administrative enforcement settlement with Plexon, Inc. on August 14, 2026. This settlement is part of BIS's ongoing efforts to enforce the Export Administration Regulations (EAR).

BIS investigations are a serious enforcement risk in international trade, often extending beyond administrative penalties to criminal investigations, export bans, and personal liability for executives and employees. Enforcement risk is particularly high in matters involving dual-use technologies, semiconductors, and advanced manufacturing.

This action underscores BIS's commitment to advancing U.S. national security, foreign policy, and economic objectives by ensuring an effective export control and treaty compliance system. Companies are reminded of the strict liability nature of many EAR violations, where intent is not required for enforcement.

articles.headline: BIS Imposes Export Restrictions on Black Mass and Tungsten Waste, Citing National Defense Criticality
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has published a temporary final rule effectively prohibiting the export of black mass and tungsten waste and scrap without prior BIS authorization. This rule, taking effect on August 27, 2026, and expiring one year later, is a direct response to a Presidential Determination finding these recoverable critical minerals and materials (CMMs) scarce and essential to national defense.

Beginning August 27, U.S. persons involved in the sale of covered CMMs must allocate 100 percent of monthly sales to U.S. persons. Sales to non-U.S. persons are prohibited unless BIS grants a specific adjustment or exception.

BIS is actively seeking public comments on whether additional sales requirements are necessary to promote national defense, as well as feedback on the framework of the temporary Defense Production Act (DPAS) regulatory provisions. This action highlights a growing focus on securing domestic supply chains for critical minerals.
articles.source: Holland & Knight / Bureau of Industry and Security

articles.headline: U.S. Inflation Cools to 3.4% in July, Easing Pressure on Federal Reserve
body: The annual inflation rate in the United States slowed for the second consecutive month in July 2026, reaching 3.4%, down from 3.5% in June.

This cooling trend, which aligns with economists' expectations, is primarily attributed to a decline in gasoline prices and other energy costs, offering some relief to consumers and potentially influencing the Federal Reserve's upcoming interest rate decisions.
Despite the overall easing, energy prices remain elevated compared to pre-war levels, with gasoline up 24.6% and fuel oil up 39.1% from a year prior, largely due to the ongoing conflict in Iran.
articles.source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics / Reuters / CBS News

articles.headline: Federal Reserve Weighs September Rate Hike Amid Cooling Inflation and Weak Jobs Report
body: The Federal Reserve is currently assessing whether to raise interest rates at its September meeting, following July's inflation data showing a slight cooling to 3.4% and a surprisingly weak jobs report last week.

While some economists believe the benign inflation data, coupled with the weak employment figures, provides solid grounds for the Fed to keep policy unchanged, others, including some bank presidents, are amplifying calls for rate hikes, arguing that inflation is not moving towards the Fed's 2% target.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has indicated that while interest rates could be part of the solution, they would not be used 'in isolation,' and emphasized that decisions would not be based on single monthly reports.
articles.source: The Guardian / CBS News / Argus Media

articles.headline: U.S. Wholesale Inflation Slows in July as Gas and Food Costs Fall
body: Wholesale inflation in the United States slowed in July, with the Labor Department's producer price index (PPI) rising 4.7% from a year ago, down from 5.5% in June. On a monthly basis, wholesale prices were unchanged from June to July.

Excluding volatile food and energy categories, core wholesale inflation dropped to 4.2% in July compared to a year earlier, a decrease from 4.7% in June. This cooling in wholesale prices suggests a potential easing of consumer inflation in the coming months.

However, gas prices, which had fallen in early July, rose later in the month and into early August, posing a risk for August inflation figures. The Federal Reserve is closely monitoring these trends as it considers future interest rate decisions.

articles.headline: Wholesale Price Inflation Slows in July as Gas and Food Costs Decline
body: Wholesale inflation in the U.S. slowed in July, with the Labor Department's producer price index rising 4.7% from a year ago, down from 5.5% in June.

On a monthly basis, wholesale prices were unchanged from June to July, after a 0.1% decrease the previous month. Excluding volatile food and energy categories, core wholesale inflation dropped to 4.2% in July, down from 4.7% in June.

This cooling in wholesale prices provides the Federal Reserve with more flexibility to potentially avoid a rate hike in September, as officials debate whether to raise interest rates or maintain current levels in hopes that inflation continues to decline.

articles.headline: U.S. Consumer Price Inflation Cools to 3.4% in July, Core Inflation at 2.5%
body: U.S. consumer prices cooled slightly in July, with the annualized inflation rate dipping to 3.4%, though prices remain elevated compared to pre-Iran war levels.
Core inflation, which excludes volatile energy and food prices, increased slightly to 2.5% year-over-year and rose a modest 0.2% since last month.

The energy index declined slightly in July, with gasoline falling nearly 3% over the last month, but still sitting about 15% higher than the year before. Brent crude prices dipped in June following a brief peace agreement between the U.S. and Iran, but rose again when the deal collapsed in July.
articles.source: The Guardian / Fisher Investments / U.S. Congress Joint Economic Committee

articles.headline: U.S. Trade on Track to Surpass $6 Trillion in 2026, Driven by Tech and Critical Minerals
body: U.S. trade is projected to exceed $6 trillion for the first time in 2026, a significant milestone that would follow the $5 trillion mark achieved just four years prior. This forecast is based on historical growth patterns, with the first half of 2026 already reaching $2.98 trillion.

Key exports fueling this growth since 2022 include gold, which has surged over 422% due to global economic concerns, and silver, experiencing a remarkable 1,539% increase, driven by demand in solar, AI, and electric vehicles. Civilian aircraft and parts, computers, and computer parts are also major contributors, with AI investments largely attributing to the tech sector's rise.

Globally, goods trade reached an estimated $13.7 trillion in the first half of 2026, a 12.5% increase from the same period in 2025, with services trade growing by 10.5%. However, a significant portion of this growth reflects higher prices rather than increased trade volumes, influenced by disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and concerns over energy supplies.

articles.headline: U.S. Diplomat Condemns Israeli Settler Siege of West Bank Homes as 'Act of Terror'

articles.headline: Iran Warns U.S. Risks 'Bigger Miscalculation' Over Strait of Hormuz Amid Escalating Tensions

The Strait of Hormuz is a vital chokepoint for global oil shipments, and any disruption there has significant implications for international energy markets. The U.S. has asserted its control over the Strait, with President Donald Trump stating, 'We totally control the Strait of Hormuz.'
The ongoing standoff highlights the precarious security situation in the region and the potential for miscalculation to lead to broader conflict, impacting global trade and stability.

These amendments, specified with strikethrough and underline, are for individuals and entities subject to the assets freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo set out in paragraph 1 of Security Council resolution 2734 (2024).
The changes were adopted under Chapter VII of the Charter of the United Nations, reflecting ongoing efforts to combat terrorism and its financing.

articles.headline: BIS Streamlines Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued a final rule effective August 13, 2026, to streamline export controls for drone exports.

This rule shifts focus away from widely available, commercial capabilities and tailors controls to Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) with capabilities that adversaries could use to pose a national security threat to the United States.
By doing so, BIS aims to allocate licensing and enforcement resources more effectively where they matter most for national security.

articles.headline: BIS Eases Export Controls on Certain Drones and Related Technologies
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has announced a final rule easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR), effective August 13, 2026.

This rule eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls and increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to 3 hours. Conforming changes remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours.

While easing some controls, BIS maintains military end-use and end-user controls on these lower endurance drones and associated software and technology, and clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use. This action follows Executive Order 14307, 'Unleashing American Drone Dominance,' issued on June 6, 2025.
articles.source: Federal Register / Bureau of Industry and Security

articles.headline: BIS Restricts Export of Critical Minerals: Black Mass and Tungsten Waste Require Licenses
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has published a temporary final rule restricting the export of black mass and tungsten waste and scrap without a license, effective August 27, 2026.
Black mass, defined as shredded lithium-ion battery scrap containing cathode and anode materials, and tungsten waste and scrap are now subject to these restrictions.

This measure aims to address an 'inadequate supply' of these critical minerals, which BIS states threatens national defense and security. U.S. persons engaged in the sale of these materials must allocate 100 percent of sales to U.S. persons unless a license is obtained from BIS.
articles.source: Federal Register / Thompson Hines SmarTrade / Holland & Knight

articles.headline: BIS Eases Export Controls on Certain Drones and Related Components
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has issued a final rule easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR), effective August 13, 2026.

This rule eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls and increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to 3 hours.

Conforming changes remove national security controls on software and technology associated with lower endurance UAVs, while maintaining military end-use and end-user controls. The rule also clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain military-designed UAVs and removes national security controls on specific parts and components that do not provide significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: BIS Eases Export Controls on Commercial Drones, Streamlining Regulations
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has published a final rule easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones), related software, and parts under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). This rule, effective August 13, 2026, aims to reduce licensing burdens for many commercial drone manufacturers and exporters.

Key changes include eliminating wind-gust tolerance as a control parameter and increasing the national security control threshold for certain UAVs from 30 minutes of endurance to three hours. Conforming changes also remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than three hours.

While easing controls on lower-endurance drones, BIS maintains military end-use and end-user controls on these systems and associated software and technology, and clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use. This regulatory shift allows BIS to focus licensing and enforcement resources on higher-endurance systems, missile-relevant platforms, and military-specific UAV capabilities.

articles.headline: BIS Amends EAR to Streamline Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) promulgated a final rule, 'Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports,' effective August 13, 2026. This rule amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to ease and update certain civilian, dual-use, and military export controls on Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) and related components, accessories, technology, and software.

The changes are intended to align UAV export controls with current commercial drone technology, particularly for items with foreign availability that were previously treated as sensitive but are now globally obtainable. This aims to support the competitiveness of the U.S. drone industrial base and facilitate exports to foreign partners.

Concurrently, the EAR maintains controls on UAVs, Remotely Piloted Vehicles (RPVs), and related items that could provide adversaries with military, intelligence, or missile-related capabilities, ensuring national security remains a priority.

articles.headline: Rice Lake Weighing Systems Settles with OFAC for Iran Sanctions Violations by Italian Subsidiary
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a $60,764 settlement with Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc., a Wisconsin-based manufacturer of weighing equipment. The settlement resolves potential civil liability for eight apparent violations of Iran sanctions by Rice Lake's Italian subsidiary, Dini Argeo S.r.l. (Dini).

Between July 2019 and November 2021, Dini exported weighing equipment to a distributor in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), knowing that these goods would be reexported to an end-user in Iran. OFAC determined that these apparent violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and non-egregious.

This case highlights the risks U.S. companies face from their global subsidiaries, particularly concerning sanctions programs like Iran's, which require foreign firms owned or controlled by U.S. persons to comply to nearly the same extent as their U.S. parent. OFAC emphasizes the importance of effective, risk-based controls and comprehensive understanding of sanctions requirements by all relevant personnel within foreign subsidiaries.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Export Compliance Daily

body: The Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation (OFSI) has amended and extended General Licence INT/2025/8031092 (Continuation of Business of Lukoil International Entities) and General Licence INT/2025/7895596 (Continuation of Business of Lukoil Bulgaria Entities). These licenses permit the continuation of certain business operations involving Lukoil International GmbH and its subsidiaries, and specified Bulgarian subsidiaries of PJSC Lukoil, despite Russia asset-freeze restrictions.

The amended General Licenses introduce a new one-off notification requirement: entities relying on either license must notify OFSI and provide current contact details within 14 days of first use on or after August 12, 2026, or within 14 days of that date for existing users. The Lukoil International license has been extended until February 26, 2027, while the Lukoil Bulgaria license expires on October 29, 2026.

articles.headline: Federal Reserve and ECB Face Pressure to Hold or Hike Rates Amid Inflation Concerns
body: Market experts are warning that developed central banks, including the U.S. Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank (ECB), are likely to maintain or even increase interest rates in the coming months to keep inflation in check.
This outlook represents a sharp reversal from the beginning of the year, when markets were pricing in rate cuts.

Geopolitical developments, particularly the ongoing conflict in the Middle East and its impact on the Strait of Hormuz, are contributing to elevated energy prices, which in turn influence growth, inflation, and monetary policy expectations across regions.

articles.headline: Oil Prices Remain Elevated Amid Middle East Tensions and Iran War

Despite a slight dip in U.S. inflation data, the conflict over the Strait of Hormuz and access to oil is expected to keep energy prices high in the coming weeks and months.
Increased domestic production and the expansion of renewable capacity have contributed to an energy surplus, but geopolitical factors continue to exert upward pressure on prices.

articles.headline: U.S. Inflation Cools to 3.4% in July as Gas Prices Decline
body: U.S. inflation slowed in July, with the Consumer Price Index (CPI) rising 3.4% from a year ago, a slight decrease from the 3.5% recorded in June. This modest decline was primarily driven by falling gasoline prices.

Excluding volatile food and energy categories, core inflation also eased to 2.5% year-over-year in July, down from 2.6% in June. This figure matches a post-pandemic low seen earlier in the year, before the Iran war.

On a monthly basis, consumer prices rose just 0.1% from June to July, while core prices increased by 0.2%. Despite the cooling, overall price increases remain above the Federal Reserve's 2% target, and elevated oil prices in late July and August suggest potential acceleration in overall inflation next month.
articles.source: Bureau of Labor Statistics / BNN Bloomberg / Morningstar

articles.headline: Brent Crude Prices Surge for Sixth Straight Session Amid Geopolitical Tensions
body: Brent crude prices have risen for a sixth consecutive session, marking the longest streak since late April, as geopolitical flashpoints continue to influence global markets.
Houthi attacks on vessels in the Red Sea, including Saudi tankers, have disrupted shipping lanes and pushed Brent crude above $100, intensifying inflation risks for central banks.
This sustained increase in energy costs is adding pressure on central banks to contain energy-driven inflation, impacting their policy decisions.

articles.headline: Global Oil Prices Remain Elevated Despite Cooling Inflation, EIA Forecasts Future Decline
body: Global oil prices, particularly Brent crude, have remained near levels from the first week of August, averaging around $85 per barrel in the third quarter of 2026, despite a slight cooling in overall inflation.
The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) attributes these elevated prices to reduced oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, which has further lowered global oil inventories.
However, the EIA forecasts a gradual decline in Brent crude prices to an average of $69 per barrel in 2027, as inventories are expected to rebuild with most production recovering by early next year.
articles.source: U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) / WBAL Radio

articles.headline: U.S. Consumer Price Index Rises 3.4% Annually in July, Energy Prices Decline
body: The U.S. Consumer Price Index (CPI) for All Urban Consumers increased by 0.1 percent on a seasonally adjusted basis in July, following a 0.4 percent decrease in June. Over the last 12 months, the all-items index rose 3.4 percent before seasonal adjustment.

The index for all items less food and energy rose 2.5 percent over the past year, while the shelter index increased 3.2 percent. Energy prices, however, declined by 1.48 percent from June to July, with gasoline falling nearly 3% over the last month.

Despite the slight cooling in July, consumer prices remain elevated compared to pre-war levels with Iran. The Federal Reserve is weighing this data as it considers whether to increase interest rates in its upcoming September meeting.
articles.source: Bureau of Labor Statistics / The Guardian / Crux Investor

articles.headline: U.S. Inflation Slows to 3.4% in July, Energy Costs Threaten August Rebound
body: The annual inflation rate in the United States decreased to 3.4% in July 2026, down from 3.5% in June, aligning with expectations. This marks the second consecutive month of slowing inflation, moving further below the 2023 high of 4.2% reached in May.

The slowdown was largely attributed to a cooling in energy prices, with gasoline falling 2.9% month-over-month and fuel oil dropping 1.7%. However, this relief may be temporary, as gasoline prices are already rebounding in August, reaching an average of $4.03 per gallon, up from $3.87 a month ago.

Rising crude oil prices and stronger refining margins are driving this reversal, posing upside risks to August inflation and complicating the Federal Reserve's path to its 2% target. The energy index, despite a monthly decline, still increased 14.7% for the 12 months ending July.
articles.source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics / Trading Economics

articles.headline: U.S. Consumer Price Index Shows Modest Increases in July
body: The Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) in the United States increased 3.4 percent over the last 12 months ending July 2026, a slight decrease from the 3.5 percent rise observed in the 12 months ending June. The index for all items less food and energy rose 2.5 percent over the year.

For the month of July, the all items index was unchanged prior to seasonal adjustment. The food index saw a 0.1 percent increase in July, following a 0.2 percent rise in June, while the index for food at home decreased by 0.1 percent over the month.

Notable increases over the last year include airline fares (+25.5 percent), medical care (+1.7 percent), recreation (+2.6 percent), and household furnishings and operations (+2.2 percent). The shelter index increased 3.2 percent over the past year.

articles.headline: Worsening Drought and Record Heat Grip Europe, Fueling Wildfires and Low River Flows
body: A prolonged period of poor rainfall combined with recurrent and severe heatwaves is exacerbating drought conditions across Europe, with forecasts indicating warmer and drier weather into September. Drought has significantly deteriorated in July and August, pushing Europe's four major rivers—the Loire, Po, Rhine, and Danube—to record low levels.

The sequence of extreme heatwaves, intensified by global warming, has had a compounding effect, turning dry conditions into fuel for devastating wildfires in France and Spain in July. By August 5, 2026, the total burnt area in the EU had already surpassed that of the same period in 2025.

Water resources, crops, energy systems, river transport, tourism, and ecosystems are all under increasing pressure. Forecasts point to a continued risk of heatwaves throughout August and into September, with low to extremely low river discharge levels expected across many catchments in France, the Alpine region, and Eastern Europe.

articles.headline: Cholera Spreads Rapidly Across West and Central Africa, Affecting Millions of Children
body: Cholera is spreading rapidly across West and Central Africa, with active outbreaks now reported in six countries and millions of children at increasing risk, according to UNICEF. The outbreaks are concentrated along two major transmission corridors: the Lake Chad Basin and the Congo River Basin.

Nigeria has the largest outbreak in the region, with over 50,000 cumulative cases and 338 deaths recorded since January 1, largely driven by a major outbreak in Borno state. The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has recorded the highest death toll, with nearly 700 deaths from more than 30,400 cases.

Seasonal rains, flooding, population displacement, and cross-border transmission are accelerating the spread of the waterborne disease. Children are disproportionately affected, with those under 10 accounting for 44% of reported cases in the Central African Republic (CAR) and nearly two-thirds of infections among children under 15 in Chad.

articles.headline: New EU Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation Enters into Application
body: New European Union rules on packaging, established by the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR), have begun to apply on a phased basis from August 12, 2026. This regulation aims to reduce waste, increase recycling, and enhance the safety of food-contact packaging.

A key measure now in effect is a restriction on per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in food-contact packaging, prohibiting products containing PFAS above strict limits from being placed on the EU market. This is designed to reduce exposure to 'forever chemicals' that can accumulate in the environment and human body.

The PPWR also seeks to strengthen the Single Market for packaging and facilitate cross-border businesses through common rules, replacing fragmented national regulations. From 2028, a harmonized labeling system for packaging will apply across the EU to streamline waste sorting and improve recycling efficiency.

articles.headline: Youth Unemployment Rises Globally, ILO Report Finds
body: A new report by the UN's International Labour Organization (ILO) reveals that global youth unemployment is on the rise again after a post-pandemic improvement. The unemployment rate for individuals aged 15 to 24 ticked up to 12.4% in 2025, leaving 67 million young people jobless worldwide.

Factors contributing to this difficult labor market include slower global economic growth, geopolitical tensions, and the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on entry-level jobs. The report estimates that 6.1% of jobs held by young people are highly exposed to AI-related changes, particularly clerical and administrative roles.

The ILO recommends a human-centered approach to AI governance, increased investment in quality education, strengthened employment services, expanded social protection, and job creation initiatives to address this growing challenge.

articles.headline: FinCEN Permanently Eliminates Beneficial Ownership Reporting for US Companies and Persons
body: On August 11, 2026, the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) issued a final rule permanently eliminating the requirement for U.S. companies and U.S. persons to report beneficial ownership information (BOI) under the Corporate Transparency Act (CTA).

This final rule, which took effect upon its publication in the Federal Register on August 14, 2026, confirms the relief and clarifications contemplated by an interim rule issued in March 2025. FinCEN will also delete previously reported BOI submitted by U.S. persons from its beneficial ownership information database.

Under the Final Rule, only entities formed under the law of a foreign country that have registered to do business in any U.S. state or Tribal jurisdiction will qualify as 'reporting companies' subject to BOI obligations. This significant change exempts most U.S. domestic companies from further BOI filing, updates, or corrective submissions.
articles.source: FinCEN / Troutman Pepper Locke / Sidley Austin LLP

articles.headline: Commerce Department Cancels $7.8 Billion in Chip R&D Awards, Citing New Administration Priorities

The cancellations were attributed to a need to align with the Trump administration's current priorities.

These cancellations directly conflict with statutory requirements embedded in the FY21 National Defense Authorization Act, which mandated funding for programs like the National Semiconductor Technology Center and the National Advanced Packaging Manufacturing Program (NAPMP).

The GAO report recommends that the Secretary of Commerce ensure the Director of the CHIPS for America Research and Development Office either proceeds with existing NAPMP awards or develops an alternative implementation plan within one year from August 6, 2026.

The document specifically highlights the potential for a serious situation similar to Russia's aggression against Ukraine to occur in the Indo-Pacific region, particularly in East Asia.

The white paper identifies China as presenting 'the greatest strategic challenge,' citing Beijing's growing concordance with Moscow in joint exercises as an alarming trend. It also reiterates that the Japan-U.S. alliance remains the 'cornerstone' of its security.

Japan aims to strengthen its defense capability to take primary responsibility for dealing with invasions by fiscal year 2027, with support from its allies. The OCC's decision, communicated in a letter dated August 4, 2026, highlighted that the proposed President and CEO had limited knowledge of national banking laws and regulations, planned to be part-time, and intended to spend a majority of the year outside the United States.

While the denial does not prohibit a future de novo charter application, the OCC expects any subsequent application to satisfactorily address the reasons for this action and be consistent with statutory and regulatory factors for approval.

body: Iran is currently deliberating a new arrangement for the Strait of Hormuz, a critical global oil chokepoint, amidst uncertain prospects for negotiations with the United States. This comes as Iran issues new demands in its pursuit of a deal.
The discussions around the Strait of Hormuz are taking place against a backdrop of ongoing regional tensions and the broader implications of the Iran conflict on energy prices.
Recent reports indicate that Iran seeks to 'create grounds' for talks, while Israel has rejected a proposed 15-point plan for Gaza, further complicating the regional geopolitical landscape.

articles.headline: Israel Rejects Trump's 15-Point Plan for Gaza, Hamas Calls for Full Implementation
body: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected a 15-point plan for Gaza proposed by former U.S. President Donald Trump, stating that Israel will not withdraw forces from Gaza until Hamas is fully disarmed. This rejection comes amidst ongoing discussions about the future of the region.

In contrast, Hamas has called for the full implementation of Trump's proposed plan, highlighting the deep divisions and conflicting objectives among the parties involved. Palestinian politicians have expressed that Netanyahu's rejection is not a surprise.
The situation in Gaza remains critical, with reports of children still struggling with hunger following the 2025 famine and concerns about another emerging food emergency.

articles.headline: Middle East Tensions Escalate with Gaza Casualties and Houthi Attacks
body: Tensions in the Middle East remain high, with reports from Al Jazeera indicating that at least 300 children in Gaza have been killed in 300 days since a ceasefire agreement was supposedly implemented last October. This grim statistic was reported by the UN Children's Fund (UNICEF), highlighting the ongoing humanitarian crisis in the region.

Further escalating regional instability, Houthi attacks in Yemen have reportedly killed seven people, and a refinery in Saudi Arabia was targeted. These incidents underscore the continued conflict and its devastating impact on civilian populations and critical infrastructure.

In other regional news, Syria has announced a deal with Moscow regarding the future of Russian bases in the country, a development that could have significant implications for regional power dynamics. Meanwhile, Israel has reportedly rejected a 15-point peace plan for Gaza proposed by the Trump administration, further stoking tensions with the U.S.
articles.source: Al Jazeera / AP News / The Guardian

Meanwhile, Thailand is grappling with the aftermath of a tragic school shooting, where the death toll has risen to nine after a 12-year-old victim succumbed to their injuries. This incident has brought renewed attention to issues of gun violence and school safety in the region.
These events underscore the diverse challenges and developments occurring across the Asia Pacific, ranging from significant economic shifts to profound social tragedies.

articles.headline: US Pledges $1 Billion in Security Aid to Colombia for Drug Crackdown
body: The United States has pledged $1 billion in security aid to Colombia, as the new right-wing president of the South American nation has committed to a significant crackdown on drug trafficking. This aid package aims to bolster Colombia's efforts in combating illicit drug operations and strengthening its security forces.

The commitment of substantial U.S. assistance signals a renewed focus on anti-narcotics cooperation between the two countries under the new Colombian administration. The funds are expected to support various initiatives, including law enforcement operations, interdiction efforts, and alternative development programs.

This development highlights the ongoing challenges of drug production and trafficking in the region and the continued international efforts to address these complex issues through bilateral partnerships.

The ongoing conflict and the rejection of the peace proposal highlight the persistent challenges in achieving a lasting resolution in the region.

articles.headline: Yemen's Houthis Launch Drone Attack on Saudi Aramco Refinery
body: Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels have claimed responsibility for a drone attack on Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery.
This incident occurred just two days after Saudi Arabia signed a defense pact with Turkey and Pakistan, in response to growing regional instability.
The Houthis had previously declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea last month, citing a Saudi siege against them, an allegation denied by Riyadh.

articles.headline: Iran Outlines Six Conditions for Reopening Strait of Hormuz Amidst Ongoing Tensions
body: Iran has presented six conditions for the full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, as articulated by Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr. These conditions include an end to U.S. threats against Iran, a halt to military action against Iran and its regional allies, and the withdrawal of U.S. naval and air forces involved in the blockade.
Further demands include compensation for damages incurred during recent conflicts, the lifting of all U.S. sanctions on Iran, and the unconditional release of frozen Iranian assets.

This detailed list of demands comes amidst ongoing negotiations with Oman regarding a new mechanism for navigation through the vital waterway, with disagreements persisting over the extent of Iranian control and potential transit fees.

articles.headline: Israel Rejects Trump's Gaza Plan; Houthis Strike Saudi Aramco Refinery
body: Israel has formally rejected U.S. President Donald Trump's 'Board of Peace's 15-point plan for Gaza,' indicating a significant divergence in approaches to regional peace. The details of Israel's objections were not immediately made public.

In a separate development, Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels claimed responsibility for a strike on a Saudi Aramco refinery. This attack underscores the ongoing regional tensions and the Houthis' continued capacity to target critical infrastructure in Saudi Arabia.

These events highlight the volatile security situation in the Middle East, with ongoing conflicts and diplomatic disagreements shaping the geopolitical landscape. The rejection of the Gaza plan could further complicate efforts to achieve a lasting peace in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.

articles.headline: Fed Grapples with Persistent Inflation, Rate Hike Debate Intensifies
body: Five years of elevated inflation are testing the patience of U.S. Federal Reserve officials, leading to a deepening split within the committee regarding future interest rate policy. While the Fed held its benchmark rate steady in July, a significant minority of policymakers are advocating for rate hikes amidst persistent price pressures.

The debate is fueled by ambiguous economic data, including a surprise decline in July payrolls, which did little to clarify the inflation outlook. Some officials believe inflation may cool on its own, while others express concern that waiting too long could entrench price pressures.

Despite the Consumer Price Index falling below 3% in July for the first time in over three years, and the central bank's preferred measure of inflation at 3.3% excluding food and energy, the ongoing Middle East conflict and its impact on energy prices continue to contribute to inflationary risks.

articles.headline: Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey Forge NATO-Style Defense Pact Amid Regional Tensions
body: Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey have signed a mutual defense agreement in Mecca, establishing a NATO-style pact where an armed attack against one will be considered an attack against all three. This development signifies the institutional beginning of a new regional security architecture in the Sunni Muslim world.

The pact comes amidst heightened tensions in the Middle East, particularly with Iran. Iranian retaliatory strikes have exposed vulnerabilities in U.S. basing structures in the Gulf, leading to the repositioning of combat forces and potential closures of American bases.

Iran has also issued explicit warnings to Gulf states, threatening to strike their oil, power, and water plants unless they persuade the U.S. to cease strikes on Iran and seek a negotiated end to the conflict. This diplomatic push aims to deter further U.S. military action by highlighting the potential for severe economic disruption across the Gulf.

This pact stipulates that an armed attack against one nation will be considered an attack against all three.

The agreement comes as conflict in the Middle East has intensified, with attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, and an uncertain prospect for negotiations between the U.S. and Iran. The U.S.-Iran war has accelerated a transformation already underway, exposing the vulnerability of U.S. basing structures in the Gulf and forcing the repositioning of substantial combat forces. This new alliance aims to diminish Iranian power, which has been central to Tehran's regional strategy, particularly through strikes on Saudi Arabia from Iran, Iraqi Shia militias, and Houthis in Yemen.

This pact, which considers an armed attack against one as an attack against all three, brings together the most powerful and influential countries of the Sunni Muslim world.

This development suggests a move towards a post-American Middle East, where regional powers are taking greater responsibility for their own security. The pact could significantly alter the geopolitical landscape and influence future conflicts in the region.

articles.headline: Iran Grapples with Diverse Narratives on US-Israel Conflict After Missile Strike
body: Five months after a U.S.-made Tomahawk missile struck a primary school in Minab, southern Iran, killing 156 people including 120 children, the country is grappling with varied perspectives on the US-Israel war. While some Iranians believe the conflict has strengthened national unity, others contend it has deepened repression, with all mourning the significant loss of life.

The attack on February 28, which President Donald Trump urged Iranians to use to 'seize control of your destiny,' has instead reshaped Iran in unexpected ways. Minab has become a symbol of civilian suffering, with portraits of the deceased adorning walls and billboards across the city.

The ongoing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East continue to be a significant factor influencing global markets and energy prices, as evidenced by recent market downturns and concerns over the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.headline: Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkiye Forge New Regional Security Architecture in Mecca Pact
body: Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkiye have signed a joint defense agreement in Mecca, marking the institutional beginning of a new regional security architecture. This pact unites the three most powerful and influential countries of the Sunni Muslim world, establishing that an armed attack against one will be regarded as an attack against all three.

This development comes as the US-Iran war has accelerated a transformation in the Middle East, exposing the vulnerability of US basing structures in the Gulf and forcing the repositioning of combat forces. Several American bases are expected to close due to lost strategic utility.

The agreement gives political form to an architecture already being built, with Pakistani forces already deployed alongside Saudi forces and integrated into Saudi-led structures. This new balance of regional power is expected to force restraint on both Tehran and Israel.

This pact signifies a significant shift in the Middle East's security architecture, effectively extending a nuclear umbrella over the Gulf without direct U.S. involvement.

The agreement, which considers an armed attack against one as an attack against all, is seen as an attempt by regional powers to hedge against declining confidence in unilateral U.S. deterrence, particularly in the wake of the Iran war. Pakistan's implicit nuclear extension to Riyadh is a particularly consequential aspect of this new alliance.

This development is expected to sideline Iran's containment narrative and potentially erode American leverage in basing and arms sales in the region. The pact brings together the three most powerful and influential countries of the Sunni Muslim world, marking the institutional beginning of a new regional security framework.

Titan Exchange is accused of holding tens of millions of dollars on behalf of Shahr Bank and is linked to a financier previously sanctioned for aiding a separate shipping and sanctions-evasion network. Several Iranian nationals were also designated, including Saeed Ghasempour, a Shahr Bank employee who reportedly coordinated currency conversions with Russia's VTB Bank, and staff members of Iran-based Farab Soroush Afagh Qeshm, who managed invoices and payments for the scheme.

Additionally, a cluster of shell companies in Hong Kong, Singapore, and Dubai, used to funnel payments through intermediary accounts, were also designated. body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has taken action against multiple networks across several countries, including two digital asset exchanges, for enabling Iran's 'rahbar' banking system to move hundreds of millions of dollars. This action targets cryptocurrency platforms, corporate networks, and an online gambling enterprise that OFAC states helped move and conceal illicit proceeds for the benefit of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and other terrorist groups.

Among the designated entities are Republic of Georgia-based SHPS Shelbit (Shelbit), which operates the Shelbit Exchange, and its operator Siavash Kayvanpour. Digital currency addresses belonging to the IRGC have sent and received millions in digital assets from Shelbit Exchange. The action also targets Iranian nationals Shima Sharifi and Peivand Mohammad, employees of FSAQ, who coordinate invoices and payments for sanctions evasion, and Amir Hendi, an IT specialist providing critical infrastructure support to Titan Exchange.

Additionally, OFAC issued an amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) to clarify that foreign financial institutions and other non-U.S. persons may face sanctions exposure for dealing with Iranian digital asset exchanges designated under Executive Order 13902, including Nobitex, Wallex, Bitpin, Ramzinex, and Aban Tether.

articles.headline: Trump Imposes 15% Tariff on Polysilicon to Challenge China's Dominance
body: President Donald Trump has ordered a new 15% tariff on imported products made of polysilicon, a critical ingredient in microchip manufacturing primarily produced by China. This tariff, set to take effect on December 4, aims to bolster US chip and solar panel supply chains and enhance competitiveness with Beijing in artificial intelligence and energy sectors.

The executive order, signed on Thursday, also establishes a series of price floors for polysilicon and related products, including minimum import prices of $21 per kilogram for polysilicon and $0.22 per watt for solar cells. This move is intended to create a 'protected domestic market' for US producers, shielding them from global distortions and perceived dumping by Chinese rivals.

China's foreign affairs ministry has criticized the new measures, accusing the US of 'overstretching the concept of national security' and 'abusing state power to go after Chinese businesses.' This action follows a Commerce Department national security investigation into polysilicon imports and adds to escalating trade tensions between the two economic superpowers.
articles.source: The Guardian / South China Morning Post / Reuters

This action, based on a Section 232 investigation by the Secretary of Commerce, aims to revitalize the domestic polysilicon industry, which has seen America's share of global production capacity decline significantly.
The administration cites national security concerns, emphasizing that a secure domestic supply of polysilicon is essential for producing semiconductors and supporting AI and solar power initiatives.

articles.headline: Russia Imports Fuel from South Korea Amid Ukrainian Strikes on Refineries
body: Russia has begun importing petroleum products from South Korea, with nearly 30,000 metric tons of fuel shipped in late July, as Ukrainian drone strikes continue to impact Russian energy infrastructure. This marks a significant shift for Russia, typically a net exporter of diesel.

At least two tankers loaded with petroleum products, including diesel and potentially jet fuel, departed from the container port of Ulsan, South Korea, bound for Russia's Far East. One vessel has already arrived in Russia but has not yet unloaded its cargo.

The increased demand for fuel imports follows a series of Ukrainian attacks that pushed Russian refinery processing down to its lowest level since May 2002 in July. Moscow has extended restrictions on diesel exports and a gasoline export ban through January 2027 to manage domestic supply.

articles.headline: Iran's Grip on Strait of Hormuz Becomes Potent Economic Weapon Amid US Blockade
body: Iran has transformed its ability to restrict commercial passage through the Strait of Hormuz into a potent economic weapon amidst the ongoing conflict with the United States and Israel. Following the collapse of the June 17 Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) and the reinstatement of a U.S. blockade on July 14, Iran has targeted commercial shipping and Gulf States.

Data from IMF PortWatch indicates a drastic reduction in transit volume through the strait, with an average of only about four ships per day passing through in the seven days ending August 2, compared to approximately 90 during the corresponding week of 2025. Estimated transit volume fell from 3.5 million to about 143,000 metric tonnes per day.

The security situation in the Strait of Hormuz remains highly volatile, with Iran's Yemeni Houthi partners threatening to expand the maritime conflict in the Red Sea. These developments highlight the significant impact of geopolitical tensions on global shipping and energy markets.

The agreement, which has been under discussion for a considerable period, has been expedited by recent regional developments. Riyadh seeks to strengthen its security ties as the ongoing conflict has emboldened Iran and its Houthi allies in Yemen, leading to attacks on Saudi Arabia.

U.S. President Donald Trump expressed expectations for the war with Iran to end 'pretty soon,' stating that Tehran cannot 'go on much longer.' articles.headline: Pacific Ministers Fail to Agree on Joint Response to China's Missile Launch
body: Pacific Island foreign ministers, meeting in Suva, Fiji, on August 7, 2026, failed to reach a consensus on a joint response to China's missile launch in July. This lack of a unified statement underscores existing divisions among Pacific Island governments on how to confront growing strategic competition in the region.

China's test-firing of a missile into the Pacific alarmed regional powers, including New Zealand, whose foreign minister expressed support for a joint response. However, two members, identified as Nauru and Kiribati, reportedly refused to sign on to the statement.

China has been expanding its influence in the Pacific through infrastructure financing, diplomatic outreach, and security cooperation, prompting concern among traditional partners like Australia and New Zealand. Despite calls for unity and a commitment to an 'Ocean of Peace' declaration, the divisions highlight the complexities of regional geopolitics.

articles.headline: Childhood Ebola Deaths Rise in DR Congo; New Vaccine Shows Promise
body: Childhood deaths from Ebola are on the rise in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), as efforts advance towards enhanced treatment and the world's first vaccine for the Bundibugyo species of Ebola. The World Health Organization (WHO) reported on Tuesday that deaths and cases are increasing in the largest ever outbreak on record in the DRC.

An advisory group met on July 31 to review new data on the Ervebo vaccine, examining preliminary animal study data that showed some cross-protection against Bundibugyo virus disease, particularly against death. The group found no safety concerns for its use in vaccinating contacts of confirmed cases.
While results from the new vaccine trial may be months away, the prioritization of Ervebo for use in affected areas offers a glimmer of hope in combating the escalating crisis.

articles.headline: US Officials Indicate Progress Towards Hormuz Deal with Iran Amidst New Sanctions
body: U.S. officials have indicated significant progress towards a deal with Tehran regarding the Strait of Hormuz, with a potential agreement expected as early as this weekend. This development comes even as the United States imposed fresh sanctions targeting Iran's financial networks.

The U.S. Treasury's latest sanctions targeted currency exchange houses, shell companies, and financial facilitators accused of helping Iran move hundreds of millions of dollars through the international financial system. The State Department stated these measures aim to cut financial lifelines sustaining Iran's ruling elite.

Despite the new sanctions, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent suggested that a 30- to 60-day ceasefire agreement with Iran could be reached 'shortly,' potentially reopening the Strait of Hormuz and leading to a decrease in energy prices.

articles.headline: Mecca Joint Defence Agreement Signed, Signaling New Regional Security Architecture
body: Saudi Arabia, Turkiye, and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement on August 7, 2026, committing each country to treat an armed attack against one as an attack against all. This pact marks the institutional beginning of a new regional security architecture.
The agreement brings together three of the most powerful and influential countries in the Sunni Muslim world, a development accelerated by the ongoing U.S.-Iran war.

Analysts suggest that the pact is a step towards a post-American Middle East, as Iranian retaliatory strikes have exposed vulnerabilities in the U.S. basing structure in the Gulf, leading to a repositioning of combat forces and potential closure of some American bases.

articles.headline: BIS Imposes Temporary Export Controls on Lithium Battery Black Mass and Tungsten Waste
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued a temporary final rule on August 5, 2026, imposing export controls on certain recycled battery materials, specifically black mass and tungsten waste and scrap.

This action, effective August 27, 2026, and lasting for one year, requires U.S. persons engaged in the sale of these materials to allocate 100% of monthly sales to U.S. persons, unless an adjustment or exception is obtained from BIS.

The measure aims to secure the domestic supply chain for critical minerals, following a presidential determination authorizing BIS to institute export restrictions on recoverable critical minerals and materials deemed essential for national defense and security.

articles.headline: Bipartisan Push to Extend and Expand Semiconductor Manufacturing Tax Credit
body: Senate Finance Committee leadership is advocating for an extension of the Advanced Manufacturing Investment Credit (Section 48D), a crucial tax credit for semiconductor manufacturing facilities set to expire at the end of 2026.

Amid bipartisan and industry efforts, Senate Finance Committee Chair Mike Crapo (R-ID) and Ranking Member Ron Wyden (D-OR) released a joint statement reaffirming their support for the credit, highlighting its role in strengthening domestic semiconductor supply chains, creating jobs, and advancing national security.

The credit, originally established under the 2022 CHIPS and Science Act, provides a 25% credit for qualified property, which was increased to 35% for property placed in service after December 31, 2025, but its sunset date remains a concern.

articles.headline: Senate Finance Committee Leaders Call for Extension and Expansion of Semiconductor Manufacturing Tax Credit
body: Senate Finance Committee Chair Mike Crapo (R-ID) and Ranking Member Ron Wyden (D-OR) have issued a joint statement reaffirming their support for the Section 48D Advanced Manufacturing Investment Credit (AMIC) and calling for its extension.

The AMIC, established under the 2022 CHIPS and Science Act, provides a 25% credit for qualified semiconductor manufacturing facilities, which was increased to 35% for property placed in service after December 31, 2025.

Under current law, facilities must begin construction by December 31, 2026, to qualify, and there is bipartisan and industry effort to extend the credit and expand its availability to upstream materials used in semiconductor production.

articles.headline: Bipartisan Push for Extension and Expansion of Semiconductor Manufacturing Tax Credit
body: Senate Finance Committee leadership, including Chairman Mike Crapo (R-ID) and Ranking Member Ron Wyden (D-OR), have called for an extension of the Advanced Manufacturing Investment Credit (AMIC) for semiconductor manufacturing facilities. The credit, currently available through 2026, is a critical tool for strengthening domestic semiconductor supply chains and creating jobs.

The AMIC, established under the 2022 CHIPS and Science Act and increased to 35% last year, has spurred significant investments across the United States. However, the 'One Big Beautiful Bill Act' failed to address the credit's December 31, 2026, sunset.

Bipartisan, bicameral bills introduced this congressional session also advocate for enhancing the credit, reflecting broad support for its role in advancing national security interests. This push comes as the federal government recently announced $874 million in incentives for seven chip companies.

articles.headline: BIS Restricts Exportation of Black Mass and Tungsten Waste and Scrap Without License
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has published a temporary final rule restricting the exportation of black mass and tungsten waste and scrap without a license. Effective August 27, 2026, U.S. persons engaged in the sale of these materials must allocate 100% of monthly sales to U.S. persons, unless an adjustment or exception is obtained from BIS.

This action is taken pursuant to Section 101 of the Defense Production Act of 1950 and a Presidential Determination on Recoverable Critical Minerals and Materials, aiming to address the scarcity of these critical materials for national defense. Black mass is defined as shredded lithium-ion battery scrap containing cathode and anode materials, while tungsten waste and scrap are also covered.

BIS is accepting public comments until November 4, 2026, on whether additional sales requirements are necessary to promote national defense, including potential restrictions on other critical minerals. The rule applies for one year unless revoked.
articles.source: Federal Register / Sandler, Travis & Rosenberg, P.A.

This tariff, effective December 4, aims to bolster U.S. chip and solar panel supply chains and enhance competitiveness in artificial intelligence and energy sectors.

The executive order, signed on Thursday evening, emphasizes ensuring the commercial viability of U.S. production of polysilicon and its derivatives to meet economic and national security requirements. Polysilicon is an ultra-pure form of silicon vital for semiconductors, AI processing power, data centers, and solar power generation.
