articles.headline: FinCEN Offers Relief for Financial Institutions Aiding Venezuelan Earthquake Recovery
body: The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) announced it will not take supervisory or legal actions against U.S. financial institutions providing authorized services in Venezuela to assist with earthquake recovery efforts.
This commitment follows two recent earthquakes that caused significant damage and loss of life in Venezuela, a country already under strict U.S. sanctions.

FinCEN's statement, issued in consultation with the IRS and banking agencies, aims to encourage humanitarian aid while emphasizing the need for financial institutions to exercise reasonable care and comply with applicable BSA requirements and OFAC sanctions.

articles.headline: FinCEN Issues Statement on BSA Compliance for Venezuela Earthquake Relief
body: The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) announced it will not take supervisory or legal actions against U.S. financial institutions providing authorized financial services for Venezuela's earthquake recovery efforts.

This statement follows two earthquakes in Venezuela last month that caused extensive damage and casualties, and aligns with recent OFAC authorizations aimed at supporting economic recovery in the sanctions-hit country.

FinCEN's commitment applies to institutions in compliance with the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA), not subject to a final BSA enforcement action in the past two years, and compliant with applicable OFAC sanctions.

articles.headline: FinCEN Director Outlines BSA Modernization and Fraud Prevention Priorities
body: FinCEN Director Andrea Gacki delivered written testimony to the House Financial Services Subcommittee, outlining the agency's current priorities, including Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) modernization and fraud prevention.

Gacki emphasized a recalibrated approach to anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) compliance, prioritizing effectiveness over process and aiming to reduce low-value reporting burdens.

The testimony highlighted FinCEN's April 2026 proposed rule to reform AML/CFT programs under the BSA, known as the 'Program Rule,' which supersedes a prior 2024 proposal and implements key provisions of the AML Act of 2020.

articles.headline: FinCEN Issues Enforcement Policy Statement Supporting Venezuela Earthquake Relief Efforts
body: The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), in consultation with the IRS and banking agencies, has issued a statement of enforcement policy to support U.S. government efforts to facilitate economic recovery and humanitarian relief in Venezuela following recent earthquakes. This commitment aims to prevent supervisory or legal actions against U.S. financial institutions providing authorized financial services for relief efforts.

This policy is consistent with the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issuing multiple sanctions-related authorizations, including General License 60 and General License 57, intended to support economic recovery and earthquake relief efforts in Venezuela.

FinCEN's commitment applies to financial services provided from July 27, 2026, through January 29, 2027, provided the financial institution is currently in compliance with the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA), has not been subject to a final BSA enforcement action in the past two years, and remains compliant with applicable OFAC sanctions regulations.

This includes providing humanitarian relief and assisting reconstruction following recent earthquakes in Venezuela.

FinCEN committed to not taking supervisory or enforcement actions against U.S. financial institutions for providing authorized financial services in Venezuela from July 27, 2026, through January 29, 2027, related to Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) requirements. This commitment applies provided the institutions are compliant with BSA, have not faced a final BSA enforcement action in the past two years, and adhere to OFAC-administered sanctions regulations and authorizations.

articles.headline: China Accuses US of 'AI Hegemonism,' Threatens Countermeasures Over Potential Probes
body: China's Commerce Ministry has accused the United States of 'AI hegemonism' and threatened countermeasures following statements from senior U.S. officials indicating that Chinese AI companies could face investigations, sanctions, and trade restrictions. These potential actions stem from allegations of theft of U.S. technology.

The ministry stated that Washington is threatening Chinese companies with punishment based on allegations that they used 'distillation' to copy advanced U.S. AI models, despite what it claims is a lack of factual or legal grounds. Model distillation is a technique used to compress large AI models into smaller, more efficient ones.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has warned that Chinese companies could face financial sanctions or placement on the Commerce Department's Entity List, which restricts access to U.S. technology. The dispute centers on Beijing-based Moonshot AI, whose Kimi K3 model has drawn attention for its coding capabilities and intensified debate in Washington over whether Chinese developers are copying U.S. models.

articles.headline: Department of Commerce Streamlines Export Controls for Sound Suppressors
body: The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced last week that, as of November 20, 2026, the export of certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors will be subject to BIS's Export Administration Regulations (EAR), rather than the State Department's U.S. Munitions List. This deregulatory action aligns export controls on suppressors with those already applied to firearms.

Under this new rule, suppressors will be added to the Commerce Control List (CCL), and BIS will require a license for certain exports, reexports, or in-country transfers of these newly controlled items, including releases of related software and technology to foreign persons. License exceptions currently available for firearms will also be applicable to suppressors.

Under Secretary of Commerce for Industry and Security Jeffrey I. Kessler stated that this move is a 'common-sense action that alleviates the compliance burden on America's proud firearms industry, while continuing to protect national security.'

This initiative invites the general public and other Federal Agencies to provide input on the proposed information collection.

Written comments and recommendations for the proposed information collection are due on or before August 27, 2026. The FCC's submission to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) will be displayed for review, allowing stakeholders to assess the impact of the information collection requirements.

articles.headline: Strait of Hormuz Closure Drives Oil Prices Above $100, Escalating Global Energy Crisis
body: The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz has sent global oil prices soaring above $100 a barrel, intensifying the global energy crisis in late July 2026. This critical chokepoint for oil shipments has been impacted by escalating tensions and renewed attacks in the Middle East, particularly between the US and Iran.

The collapse of the Iran-US ceasefire and ongoing military strikes have led to a sharp reduction in global oil and refined-product inventories. This disruption in supply, coupled with concerns over energy security, has significantly raised energy, transport, and logistics costs worldwide.

Financial markets are now pricing in the risk of a more prolonged closure of the Strait, which is putting upward pressure on bond yields and contributing to broader inflationary trends. The situation underscores the fragility of global energy markets in the face of geopolitical instability.

articles.headline: Global Markets React to Shifting Geopolitical Landscape and Inflation Concerns
body: Global financial markets are exhibiting volatility as investors grapple with a complex mix of geopolitical tensions and persistent inflation concerns. Recent actions by central banks, coupled with ongoing conflicts in key regions, are contributing to an environment of uncertainty.

Energy prices remain a significant factor, with fluctuations impacting inflation expectations and corporate earnings. Supply chain disruptions, while showing some signs of easing, continue to pose challenges for various industries, influencing production costs and consumer prices.

Analysts are closely monitoring central bank commentary for clues on future monetary policy, as the delicate balance between curbing inflation and supporting economic growth remains a primary focus for policymakers worldwide.

articles.headline: Oil Prices Surge Amid Renewed Iran War Concerns, Driving Up Global Inflation
body: Global oil prices have surged, topping $100 a barrel, as renewed hostilities in the U.S.-Iran conflict have ended a fragile ceasefire. This escalation is placing significant upward pressure on energy costs worldwide.

The rise in energy prices is a primary driver of increasing global headline inflation, which is now projected to reach 4.7 percent in 2026, up from 4.1 percent in 2025. This trend is reversing the disinflation observed since early 2024.

Analysts warn that persistent high energy costs could lead to further tightening of global financial conditions and intensify refinancing pressures, particularly for highly indebted developing economies.

articles.headline: Escalating US-Iran Conflict Threatens Global Oil Supplies and Strait of Hormuz
body: The ongoing military escalation between the United States and Iran in the Middle East is raising significant concerns about global oil and refined-product inventories. Reports indicate that the collapse of the Iran-US ceasefire and renewed threats to close the Strait of Hormuz have already led to sharply lower inventories.

CNN reports that US Vice President JD Vance and General Dan Caine, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, have expressed concerns about a possible escalation of the military conflict with Iran, which could further deplete US ammunition stocks. President Trump has reportedly considered a 'massive attack' on Iran, though a pause in US strikes was observed on Friday after 13 consecutive nights of attacks.

Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman, Esmaeil Baghaei, stated that progress has been made in talks with Oman regarding the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, with discussions focusing on mechanisms for managing maritime traffic. However, the lack of trust between the two parties remains a significant obstacle to de-escalation.
articles.source: Al Jazeera / CNN / The Financial Express

articles.headline: Israeli Economy Shows Resilience Amidst Regional Conflict, Stock Exchange Sets Records
body: Despite the ongoing regional conflict, the Israeli economy is demonstrating remarkable resilience, with the Tel Aviv stock exchange setting new records and the shekel continuing to rise. The Bank of Israel, even after revising its forecast due to the war, still anticipates a 4 percent economic growth in 2026, surpassing most developed economies.

This economic performance comes amidst a paradox where Israel, despite instigating the war with Iran, appears to be bearing few of its costs while its defense industries report unprecedented earnings.

The conflict's financial burden is largely being transferred to the U.S. and Gulf states, as Iranian missiles and drones target critical Gulf infrastructure and international shipping routes face disruptions, leading to increased costs for Asian and Arab consumers.

articles.headline: US-Iran Conflict Escalates with Strikes and Naval Blockade, Oman Mediates

Iran has responded with attacks on regional countries, including Kuwait and Bahrain, and has accused Ukraine of a deadly attack on one of its commercial vessels in the Caspian Sea.

Oman is actively mediating talks with Tehran to discuss managing traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, which has become a central focus of the conflict. Despite these diplomatic efforts, the US military has continued its naval blockade, redirecting 12 vessels and disabling two others accused of breaking the Iran blockade.

White House Communications Director Steven Cheung stated that President Trump prefers a diplomatic solution but retains all options if Iran continues terrorist activities in the Strait of Hormuz or against allies. The ongoing conflict has led to a dismantling of Iran's four-decade-old security doctrine, which relied on a network of proxies and allies to move confrontation away from Iranian territory.

articles.headline: Deadly Wildfires Rage Across France and Spain, Forcing Mass Evacuations
body: Deadly wildfires are currently raging across Western Europe, particularly in France and Spain, forcing hundreds of thousands of people to evacuate their homes and impacting popular tourist destinations. In France, at least 240 homes in the Gironde department have been completely destroyed, with the fire spreading within 15km of Bordeaux's outer suburban area.

In Spain, the government declared a national emergency after wildfires threatened areas near Madrid and in the neighboring province of Ávila. Over 90,000 people have been evacuated from regions around Madrid and Ávila, with local officials describing them as the worst fires they have ever seen.

Strong winds, high temperatures, and drought conditions are rapidly pushing the flames across these regions. While major areas of the Madrid fire have been 'contained and cooled down,' Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez warned of 'difficult hours ahead.'
articles.source: The Guardian / ABC World News Tonight

articles.headline: US Military Pauses Strikes on Iran Amid Escalating Regional Tensions

This pause comes as Iran's army issued a warning ahead of an expected visit by Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu to the U.S., stating that while retaliatory operations in the Gulf have stopped, the conflict could expand if U.S. strikes continue.

The broader conflict has seen a new front open with Houthi attacks on Saudi oil facilities and a declared maritime blockade on Saudi-linked shipping in the Red Sea's Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a vital trade route.
articles.source: Al Jazeera / CNN / Nhan Dan Online

articles.headline: Syrian President Al-Sharaa Seeks Security Deal with Israel, Warns of Lebanon Chaos

In an interview with Al Jazeera, al-Sharaa emphasized Syria's firm support for restricting weapons and containing decisions of war and peace exclusively to the Lebanese state.

Al-Sharaa stressed that addressing the Lebanese crisis requires a comprehensive solution beyond just a security approach. He cautioned that any descent into chaos in Lebanon would have direct and immediate repercussions on Syria.

The Syrian President also warned that the potential expansion of the U.S.-Israel war on Iran in the region would lead to severe regional fallout. This comes amidst reports of an Israeli military incursion into Syria.

body: Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa has revealed that Damascus is actively working to reach a security agreement with Israel, with the participation of several countries. In an exclusive interview with Al Jazeera, al-Sharaa expressed hope that such a deal could pave the way for comprehensive peace in the region.

Al-Sharaa emphasized that any agreement would not compromise Syria's right to the occupied Golan Heights, which Israel has illegally occupied since 1973. He also stated that Syria is avoiding clashes with Israel and that a security arrangement could lead to a broader resolution of the crisis.

This development comes after repeated Israeli incursions and strikes in southern Syria since al-Sharaa came to power in December 2024. Al-Sharaa also affirmed Syria's support for restricting weapons and containing decisions of war and peace exclusively to the Lebanese state, warning that chaos in Lebanon would have direct repercussions on Syria and that an expansion of the US-Israel war on Iran could lead to severe regional fallout.

This sudden period of calm follows two weeks of nightly attacks on Iran by the US and Iranian retaliation on US allies in the Gulf, sparking hopes for a return to diplomatic talks.

Iranian Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei stated that mediators, including Qatar and Pakistan, are exchanging messages between Iran and the US. However, Baghaei also noted that Iran's past efforts at diplomacy have been 'betrayed.'

Despite the pause in strikes, tensions in the Strait of Hormuz continue. The US military's Central Command announced on Sunday that its naval blockade of Iran 'remains in full effect,' while Iranian media reported that the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps stopped six vessels from trying to transit the strait by firing warning shots.

The order mandates the bank to take immediate corrective actions to address identified weaknesses in its internal controls and risk management systems.

The OCC found that the bank failed to adequately monitor suspicious transactions and implement effective customer due diligence procedures. The order requires the bank to appoint an independent consultant to review and enhance its AML framework and report regularly on its progress.

Central banks globally continue to signal a commitment to curbing inflation, with expectations of further interest rate adjustments in the coming months. This cautious approach is shaping investor sentiment and contributing to market fluctuations.

articles.headline: Oil Prices Surge Amidst Renewed Concerns Over Strait of Hormuz Security

The price of West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude oil rose by over 3%, while Brent crude futures climbed to nearly $92 per barrel.

The spike in prices is attributed to recent geopolitical developments in the region, which have heightened fears of supply disruptions from a critical chokepoint for global oil shipments. Energy analysts are warning that sustained tensions could lead to further price increases.

Governments and international energy agencies are closely monitoring the situation, with discussions underway on potential strategies to ensure stability in global energy markets and mitigate the impact of rising fuel costs on consumers and businesses.

The guidance emphasizes the importance of robust due diligence and ongoing monitoring of third-party relationships.

This advisory aims to ensure that banks effectively manage the unique risks that can arise from these collaborations, including operational, compliance, and reputational risks. The OCC encourages a comprehensive risk management framework that aligns with the complexity of the fintech activities.

articles.headline: OCC Denies Wise Trust Charter Application Citing AML Concerns
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has denied a national trust charter application submitted by Wise US Inc., the U.S. arm of the British fintech firm. The denial was based on concerns that Wise would fail to meet anti-money laundering (AML) standards and that the organizers lacked sufficient familiarity with national banking laws.

The OCC's decision cited a previous enforcement action based on AML issues that culminated in a settlement in July 2025. The regulator also noted that the organizers failed to select appropriate directors and management officials with adequate experience in AML/CFT requirements and operations.

This marks the OCC's first public denial of a fintech's bank charter application after approving approximately a dozen such applications. The decision signals that the OCC is closely scrutinizing AML and CFT capabilities, as well as the personnel responsible for them, for fintechs and cryptocurrency firms seeking banking charters. Wise reportedly plans to submit a new application under a GENIUS Act framework.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related Entities, Amends Russia and Venezuela GLs, and Publishes Regulatory Amendments
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on July 24, 2026, targeting individuals and entities tied to Iranian businessman Babak Zanjani's sanctions evasion network. This network reportedly involves companies in financial services, digital assets, and transportation sectors used to move funds and obscure ownership.

In addition to the Iran designations, OFAC issued an amended Russia-related General License 131H, authorizing certain transactions related to the negotiation and entry into contingent contracts for the sale of Lukoil International GmbH and related maintenance activities. OFAC also amended Russia-related FAQs 1224 and 1225, and Venezuela-related FAQ 1239, to provide updated guidance.

The agency also published broader regulatory amendments, indicating adjustments to existing sanctions programs to enhance their effectiveness and address evolving threats. These comprehensive actions demonstrate OFAC's multi-faceted approach to sanctions enforcement and adaptation.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian Sanctions Evasion Network, Amends Russia and Venezuela GLs, Publishes Regulatory Amendments
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a series of actions on July 24, 2026, including new Iran-related designations, amendments to Russia-related and Venezuela-related General Licenses (GLs), and the publication of regulatory amendments. The Iran-related designations target key components of financier Babak Zanjani's sanctions evasion network, which leverages financial services, gold and precious gem production, digital asset trading, and major transportation and infrastructure projects to obscure ownership and launder revenue.

This action specifically targets Zanjani's Iran-based 'Dot One' conglomerate, including Value Creation Group, Gold, Rail, Barter, Airlines, and Trip, as well as entities supporting his previously designated digital asset exchanges, Zedcex and Zedxion, which are alleged to have facilitated money laundering for Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent stated that these measures are part of ongoing efforts to cut off economic access for corrupt Iranian elites and their facilitators, noting the significant economic pressure on Iran with the rial at a record low and high inflation.

In addition to the Iran-related actions, OFAC issued an amended Russia-related General License and an amended Venezuela-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). The agency also published broader regulatory amendments, indicating ongoing adjustments to its sanctions programs.

body: The Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a series of actions on July 24, 2026, including new Iran-related designations, amendments to Russia-related and Venezuela-related General Licenses (GLs), and the publication of regulatory amendments. The Iran-related designations target four individuals and nine entities linked to Babak Zanjani's financial empire, specifically his 'Dot One Value Creation Group' conglomerate and associated companies like DotOne Gold.

These designations are part of an ongoing effort to disrupt Iranian oil money, gold-backed tokens, and crypto exchanges involved in sanctions evasion. Babak Zanjani was previously designated by OFAC in 2013 for facilitating billions in Iranian oil revenue transfers, with his sanctions temporarily lifted in 2016 and reimposed as U.S. policy shifted.

In addition to the Iran-related actions, OFAC issued Russia-related General License 131H, authorizing certain transactions for the negotiation and entry into contingent contracts for the sale of Lukoil International GmbH and related maintenance activities. articles.headline: Trump Administration Imposes New Double-Digit Tariffs on Dozens of Countries
body: The Trump administration has imposed new double-digit tariffs on dozens of trading partners, adding another layer of uncertainty to global markets already grappling with war-driven inflation and slowing growth. This move signals a continuation of protectionist trade policies, potentially leading to further disruptions in international supply chains.

These new tariffs are expected to impact a wide range of goods and industries, raising concerns among businesses and consumers about increased costs and reduced trade volumes. The action comes amidst ongoing geopolitical tensions and economic instability.
Economists are closely watching the potential for retaliatory measures from affected countries, which could escalate trade disputes and further dampen global economic prospects.

articles.headline: Oil Prices Soar Past $100 as Middle East Conflict Threatens Red Sea Shipping
body: Global oil prices have surged past $100 a barrel for the first time in two months, driven by escalating conflict in the Middle East, particularly threats to two critical energy shipping chokepoints: the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels claimed to have attacked two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, further exacerbating concerns about the flow of crude from the region. U.S. President Donald Trump has warned Tehran that it would be held accountable for any further Houthi attacks in the Strait of Hormuz.

The rising oil prices are having a significant impact on global economies, contributing to inflationary pressures and raising the cost of living for consumers. Analysts are closely monitoring the situation for further developments that could affect energy markets.

articles.headline: Trump Administration Imposes New Tariffs on 60 Trading Partners Over Forced Labor Concerns
body: The Trump administration has imposed a fresh round of tariffs, ranging from 10% to 12.5%, on imports from over 60 trading partners, including the UK, EU, Mexico, Canada, Australia, India, and China. These new duties, effective July 24, 2026, replace a blanket 10% tariff that expired today and are implemented under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, ostensibly targeting countries failing to enforce bans on goods produced with forced labor.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer stated that the action aims to correct human rights abuses and distortive trade practices, encouraging trading partners to adopt and enforce forced labor import prohibitions. Countries deemed to have made progress will face a 10% tariff, while others will be subject to 12.5%.

The new tariffs have drawn criticism from several trading partners, with Australia describing them as 'completely unjustified' and Brazil calling the decision 'arbitrary and unjustified.' The EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, expressed shock and stated the bloc would seek clarification from Washington.
articles.source: The Guardian / World Footwear / Chartered Institute of Export & International Trade

articles.headline: ECB Finalizes Enhanced Repo Facility for Central Banks, Maintains Key Interest Rates
body: The Governing Council of the European Central Bank (ECB) finalized the operational features and onboarding framework for its enhanced Eurosystem Repo Facility for Central Banks (EUREP) on July 24, 2026. This facility, initially announced in February 2026, will be operated by five national central banks and coordinated by the ECB, providing euro liquidity to non-euro area central banks.

Onboarded central banks will be able to access euro liquidity through loans secured against high-quality euro-denominated collateral, with drawings possible starting in Q4 2026. The facility is open to all central banks and monetary authorities outside the euro area, unless excluded on grounds such as money laundering, terrorist financing, or sanctions.

Despite ongoing geopolitical tensions and volatile energy prices, the ECB decided to keep its three key interest rates unchanged on July 23, 2026, with the deposit facility rate remaining at 2.25%. The Governing Council reiterated its commitment to a data-dependent and meeting-by-meeting approach to monetary policy.
articles.source: European Central Bank / Securities Finance Times

articles.headline: ECB Policymakers Warn of Rising Inflation Risks Amid Iran Crisis, Hint at Future Rate Hikes
body: European Central Bank (ECB) policymakers have voiced concerns about elevated inflation risks, suggesting that further interest rate hikes may be necessary in response to the ongoing crisis in Iran. While the ECB maintained its key deposit rate at 2.25% on Thursday, following a quarter-point increase in June, several officials indicated that a September hike is probable.

The decision to hold rates steady came after June data showed that higher fuel costs from the Middle East had not yet broadly impacted consumer prices, wages, or long-term inflation expectations. However, with oil prices nearing $100 a barrel and natural gas prices also surging, the inflation outlook remains precarious.

Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel stated that the situation in the Middle East remains highly fragile, contributing to intense uncertainty. Slovenian central bank chief Primož Dolenc echoed these sentiments, noting that developments surrounding the conflict in Iran reinforce adverse risks to inflation. Financial markets are now pricing in at least two more ECB rate hikes, with the first fully anticipated by October.

articles.headline: Oil Prices Surge Past $100 Amid Renewed Middle East Conflict and Strait of Hormuz Volatility
body: Oil prices have surged past $100 a barrel, with Brent crude reaching this threshold in May and again recently, driven by renewed fighting and military strikes in the Middle East that have disrupted global oil supplies.

Volatility along the Strait of Hormuz, coupled with broader regional instability, has pushed crude oil prices into the $90 per barrel range and is expected to continue driving up costs through the second half of summer.
The U.S. national average for a gallon of regular gasoline jumped 15 cents from last week to $4.09, with most states now averaging $4 per gallon or higher.

articles.headline: U.S. Inflation Rate Decreases to 3.53% in June, But July Shows Signs of Reversion
body: The U.S. Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation rate decreased to 3.53% for the trailing 12-month period ending June 2026, down from 4.20% in May. Month-over-month, headline CPI-U inflation was -0.42% from May to June, marking the first decline in five months.

This decline was largely attributed to a significant decrease in energy price inflation, which fell by 5.71% month-over-month in June, as a ceasefire between the U.S. and Iran temporarily alleviated inflationary pressures. However, July is showing signs of a reversion to sticky inflation with upside risks, primarily due to a surge in energy prices.

Producer prices rose 5.5% year-over-year in June, and the leading indicator of finished consumer goods inflation remains elevated at 3.6% year-over-year, suggesting that cost pressures are still in the pipeline for consumers.
articles.source: U.S. Congress Joint Economic Committee / Trading Economics

articles.headline: U.S. Imposes New Tariffs on 80+ Countries Over Forced Labor Concerns, Replacing Expiring Global Duty
body: President Donald Trump has imposed a fresh round of tariffs on more than 80 countries, including the UK, Mexico, Canada, Australia, India, China, and the 27 countries of the European Union. These new tariffs, ranging from 10% to 12.5% under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, replace a 10% global duty that was set to expire.

The Trump administration justified the new levies by citing countries' failure to implement and enforce bans on goods made with forced labor. This move has drawn criticism and protests from U.S. allies and major trading partners, with Australia and Brazil describing the tariffs as unjustified.

The new tariffs are effective Friday, July 24, and are expected to cover 99.4% of U.S. imports. Trade lawyers warn that these tariffs represent the 'next phase' of policy escalation, shifting forced labor risk from a compliance issue to a geopolitical one.

articles.headline: ECB Launches Enhanced Repo Facility for Central Banks to Bolster Euro Liquidity
body: The Governing Council of the European Central Bank (ECB) has finalized the operational features and onboarding framework for its enhanced Eurosystem Repo Facility for Central Banks (EUREP). This initiative, initially announced in February 2026, aims to provide non-euro area central banks with access to euro liquidity.

EUREP will be operated by five national central banks—the Deutsche Bundesbank, Banco de España, Banque de France, Banca d'Italia, and De Nederlandsche Bank—under the coordination of the ECB. Onboarded central banks will be able to access euro liquidity through loans secured against high-quality euro-denominated collateral, with drawings possible starting in Q4 2026.

The enhanced facility offers standing access and is open to all central banks and monetary authorities outside the euro area, with exclusions for reasons such as money laundering, terrorist financing, or sanctions. This move is intended to support the smooth transmission of monetary policy and reinforce the international role of the euro.
articles.source: European Central Bank / Securities Finance Times

articles.headline: Trump Imposes New Tariffs on Over 80 Countries Citing Forced Labor Concerns
body: President Donald Trump has imposed a new round of tariffs on more than 80 countries, replacing a 10% global duty that was set to expire. The new levies, ranging from 10% to 12.5%, target countries including the UK, Mexico, Canada, Australia, India, China, and the 27 European Union member states.

The tariffs, announced by U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, fall under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 and are aimed at countries that engage in forced labor. Greer stated that the U.S. has rigorously enforced a forced labor import ban for nearly a century and that it is time for trading partners to do the same.

This move has drawn criticism and protests from U.S. allies and major trading partners, with Australia and Brazil describing the new tariffs as unjustified. The EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, also sought clarification, noting the bloc's adherence to a transatlantic trade agreement.

articles.headline: ECB to Implement Enhanced Repo Facility for Central Banks, Drawings Possible Q4 2026
body: The Governing Council of the European Central Bank (ECB) announced on July 24, 2026, its decision on the operational features and onboarding process for the enhanced Eurosystem Repo Facility (EUREP). This new facility, initially announced on February 14, aims to support the smooth transmission of monetary policy and reinforce the international role of the euro.

EUREP will be operated by five national central banks—the Deutsche Bundesbank, the Banco de España, the Banque de France, the Banca d'Italia, and De Nederlandsche Bank—under the coordination of the ECB. Non-euro area central banks will be onboarded, with drawings from the facility possible as of Q4 2026.

Onboarded central banks will receive euro liquidity in the form of loans against high-quality euro-denominated collateral, priced at the main refinancing operations (MRO) rate plus a Governing Council-set spread. The maximum line size per individual central bank is EUR 50 billion, with maturities ranging from one day to one week, extendable as needed.

articles.headline: Global Central Banks Face Pressure to Hike Rates Amid Surging Energy Prices and Inflation Fears
body: Central banks globally are under increasing pressure to consider interest rate hikes as escalating geopolitical tensions, particularly involving Iran, have driven energy prices higher, reigniting inflation fears. Brent crude briefly surpassed $100 a barrel this week, contributing to a narrative of persistent inflationary pressures.

The European Central Bank (ECB) left rates unchanged on Thursday but signaled that further tightening may be necessary, with economists and traders largely anticipating a September hike. ECB chief economist Philip Lane stated that the current inflation shock is considered 'medium-sized' and expects inflation to return to 2% within the next year or so.

In the U.S., the Federal Reserve is also facing increased odds of a rate hike by year-end, with some market participants pricing in a September move. The Bank of England is expected to hold rates, though a growing number of officials may back hikes. Meanwhile, the Bank of Japan is anticipated to maintain current rates but will likely attempt to signal a hawkish stance to support the yen.

articles.headline: Global Oil Prices Surge as Middle East Conflict Intensifies
body: Global benchmark Brent crude rose to $100 per barrel on July 23, marking a 33% increase from the previous month's low, as military escalation in the Persian Gulf and Red Sea intensified. Houthi forces launched targeted attacks against two Saudi-flagged oil tankers in the Red Sea, threatening a primary alternative export route for regional producers.

The ongoing military conflict between the United States and Iran poses a significant risk of transitioning into a high-intensity regional war, directly threatening the stability of the Persian Gulf and Red Sea, crucial global energy corridors. Sustained Iranian interdiction capabilities continue to suppress commercial transit through the Strait of Hormuz, causing severe supply shocks to global energy markets.

Financial institutions project potential price ceilings of $120 per barrel in the fourth quarter of 2026 if key maritime corridors remain obstructed. The EU has also suspended the automatic adjustment of the Russian oil price cap until July 2027, aiming to keep downward pressure on Russian crude exports and prevent Russia from benefiting from the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.headline: ECB Policymakers Warn of Rising Inflation Risks, Hint at Further Rate Hikes
body: Policymakers at the European Central Bank (ECB) have issued warnings about rising inflation risks, suggesting that further interest rate increases may be necessary. Three policymakers indicated on Friday that the ECB might need to raise rates again, despite keeping them steady on Thursday.

The ECB's stance comes as oil prices have rebounded to around $100 a barrel and natural gas prices continue to surge, exacerbating inflationary pressures. The ongoing conflict in the Middle East is cited as a significant factor contributing to this uncertainty and higher energy costs.

While the ECB's June projection was based on a scenario with oil prices near a 'baseline,' the current developments are forcing a reassessment. Financial markets are now anticipating at least two more rate increases from the ECB, with the first fully priced-in by October.

articles.headline: Federal Reserve Expected to Hold Rates Steady, But Rising Oil Prices Fuel Hike Bets
body: The Federal Reserve is widely expected to maintain current interest rates at its upcoming July meeting. However, a recent surge in oil prices has led investors to significantly increase their bets on a potential rate hike later in the year.

Oil prices have topped $100 a barrel, suggesting that inflation could remain a persistent issue in the near term. This resurgence in energy costs is challenging earlier expectations of at least one rate cut in 2026.

While a July rate hike remains unlikely, the September FOMC meeting could be a crucial test for the durability of recent inflation improvements. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has reiterated his commitment to returning inflation to the 2% target, though he has offered few clues about his immediate outlook.

articles.headline: Stagflation Fears Resurface as Oil Prices Hit $100 Amid Geopolitical Tensions
body: Global markets are once again grappling with the specter of stagflation as Brent crude oil prices surged to approximately $100 a barrel in July, marking a nearly 40% increase for the month. This sharp rise is largely attributed to renewed Houthi attacks on Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, exacerbating disruptions to global supply routes beyond the Strait of Hormuz.

The rebound in energy prices, coupled with steeply rising European natural gas futures, which are at their highest since March, is fueling concerns about inflation resurgence amid sluggish economic growth. Government borrowing costs are also at multi-year highs, reflecting investor anxiety over persistent inflationary pressures.

Analysts and central bank policymakers are now anticipating further interest rate hikes from both the European Central Bank (ECB) and the U.S. Federal Reserve by year-end to combat inflation, despite the potential negative impact on economic growth.

articles.headline: ECB Policymakers Signal Potential for Further Rate Hikes Amid Rising Inflation Risks
body: Policymakers at the European Central Bank (ECB) indicated on Friday that further interest rate increases might be necessary, despite the bank holding rates steady at its most recent meeting. This hawkish stance comes as oil prices have returned to around $100 a barrel and natural gas prices continue to surge, intensifying inflation risks.

While the ECB's June projection was based on a scenario of oil prices near a 'baseline,' the recent escalation of the conflict in the Middle East and its impact on energy markets have altered the inflation outlook. Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel stated that the ECB is 'well-positioned' to respond to a deterioration of the inflation outlook, emphasizing the extreme fragility of the situation in the Middle East.

Financial markets are now pricing in at least two more quarter-point rate increases from the ECB by year-end, with the first fully anticipated by October. This contrasts with market economists who, in polls, generally expect only a single rate hike in September, highlighting a divergence in expectations regarding the ECB's future monetary policy.

articles.headline: U.S. Imposes New Tariffs on Goods from 60 Trading Partners, Raising Cost Pressures
body: The United States on Friday imposed new tariffs of 10% and 12.5% on goods from 60 trading partners, including the European Union and China. This move is expected to further raise prices and add to the uncertainty facing consumers, businesses, and investors.

These new tariffs will particularly impact trade-exposed sectors, which will face increased cost pressures on top of already rising energy prices. Analysts suggest that the recent rebound in these sectors could be short-lived due to the additional trade frictions.

The imposition of these tariffs comes amidst a broader concern about persistent inflation, with housing inflation still running hot and strong wage growth underpinning core services. The tariff passthrough to core goods is also anticipated to contribute to inflationary pressures, with core inflation expected to settle just below 3% by year-end.

articles.headline: ECB Launches Enhanced Repo Facility for Non-Euro Area Central Banks
body: The European Central Bank (ECB) has initiated the implementation of an enhanced repo facility (EUREP) for central banks outside the euro area, with drawings expected to be possible from Q4 2026. This new facility, coordinated by the ECB and operated by five national central banks, aims to support the smooth transmission of monetary policy and strengthen the international role of the euro.

Onboarded central banks will be able to receive euro liquidity through loans against high-quality euro-denominated collateral. The pricing for these transactions will be the main refinancing operations (MRO) rate plus a spread determined by the Governing Council, ensuring the facility acts as a backstop.

The EUREP facility offers standing access and is open to all non-euro area central banks and monetary authorities, with a maximum line size of EUR 50 billion per individual central bank. The ECB will publish the total daily liquidity provided under EUREP and swap lines weekly.

articles.headline: Federal Reserve Expected to Hold Rates, But Rising Oil Prices Fuel Hike Speculation
body: The Federal Reserve is widely expected to keep interest rates unchanged at its upcoming July meeting. However, a recent surge in oil prices has led investors to significantly increase their bets on a potential rate hike later in the year, a shift from earlier expectations of rate cuts in 2026.

Resurgent inflation, largely tied to these rising energy prices, has prompted some forecasters to anticipate higher rates before year-end. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has maintained a stance of returning inflation to the 2% target while offering limited forward guidance.

While a July rate hike remains unlikely, the September FOMC meeting could become a crucial test for the durability of recent inflation improvements. The probability of a rate hike at the July meeting has risen to 38% from 12% a week prior, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool, though a hold remains the more probable outcome.

articles.headline: China Bans Exports of Dual-Use Items to 14 EU Entities in Response to Russia Sanctions
body: China's Commerce Ministry announced on Friday, July 24, 2026, an immediate ban on the export of dual-use items to 14 additional European Union entities. This measure is a direct response to the EU's latest sanctions package against Russia, which included 14 Chinese mainland and Hong Kong enterprises.

The European entities targeted by China's ban include German automotive and arms manufacturer Rheinmetall AG and Polish electronics company Vigo Photonics S.A. Foreign organizations and individuals are also prohibited from transferring or supplying Chinese-origin dual-use items to these entities.

The EU's 21st package of sanctions against Russia, adopted on Thursday, added 51 new entities, including some based in China, to its list of those subject to tighter export curbs on dual-use goods and technologies due to their support for Russia's military and industrial complex. The EU Commission is currently analyzing China's new measures and seeking clarification.

articles.headline: China Bans Dual-Use Item Exports to 14 EU Entities in Response to Russia Sanctions
body: China has banned the export of dual-use items to 14 additional European Union entities with immediate effect, a measure announced by the Commerce Ministry on Friday. This action is a direct response to the EU's latest sanctions against Russia.

The EU adopted its 21st package of sanctions against Russia over its war in Ukraine, which included placing 14 Chinese mainland and Hong Kong enterprises under sanction. In retaliation, China's export ban targets European entities such as German automotive and arms manufacturer Rheinmetall AG and Polish electronics company Vigo Photonics S.A.

Foreign organizations and individuals are also prohibited from transferring or supplying dual-use items originating in China to the listed entities, though Chinese exporters may apply for permission in exceptional cases. The EU Commission is analyzing China's measures and will seek clarification from Beijing.

articles.headline: Iranian Rial Plunges to Record Low Amid Sanctions and Economic Difficulties
body: The Iranian rial has plunged to another record low, and inflation has massively increased, according to U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. This economic downturn is attributed to the Iranian regime's 'reckless behavior' and the impact of international sanctions.

The depreciation of the rial and high inflation are creating significant economic difficulties for Iran, further exacerbated by ongoing U.S. efforts to cut off economic access for corrupt Iranian elites and their facilitators.

These economic pressures are a direct consequence of the intensified sanctions campaign against Iran, which aims to disrupt illicit financial networks and limit the regime's ability to fund destabilizing activities.

The delegation held meetings in Beijing and Shanghai with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and the leadership of the National People's Congress.

Discussions focused on the geopolitical implications of EU-China ties, with MEPs stressing China's crucial role in international affairs and the defense of the multilateral system. The delegation urged China to use its influence on Russia to press for a ceasefire in Ukraine and for a just peace, while also raising concerns over the human rights situation in China.

On trade, MEPs highlighted the EU's record deficit with China, which has reached €1 billion per day, describing the situation as unsustainable. They called for reciprocity, a level playing field, and trust to ensure sustainable and mutually beneficial bilateral relations.

articles.headline: UN Reports on Political Transitions and Security Challenges in Haiti, Syria, and South Sudan

In Haiti, Special Representative Carlos Ruiz Massieu briefed the Security Council on July 20, noting progress in the political transition, including a revised electoral decree and voter registration, while emphasizing that security remains the most pressing challenge.

Deputy Special Envoy Claudio Cordone reported to the Security Council on July 21 regarding Syria's political transition, acknowledging milestones such as the establishment of the People's Assembly and the Supreme Constitutional Court. However, he stressed the need for meaningful participation by women and all Syrian society components, accountability, and improvements in daily life to build public confidence.

In South Sudan, Special Envoy for the Horn of Africa, Guang Cong, visited Juba on July 23 to discuss the Joint Political and Security Mechanism (JPSM) and Abyei-related issues. Discussions focused on resuming the JPSM, demilitarizing the Abyei Area, and addressing differing views on Abyei's participation in the December 2026 elections.

Additionally, foreign companies are barred from providing these European entities with dual-use items manufactured in China.

The affected European companies include Czech vehicle manufacturer Tatra Trucks, Italian electric motor maker Lafert SpA, German manufacturer Sindlhauser Materials GmbH, and French drone manufacturer Cavok UAS. articles.headline: US Threatens IRGC Revenue Facilities Amid Rising Tensions with Iran
body: The U.S. Treasury has unveiled a vast sanctions-evasion operation involving Iranian oil money, gold-backed tokens, and crypto exchanges, leading to threats of destroying Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) revenue facilities. On July 24, OFAC designated four individuals and nine entities connected to Babak Zanjani, a figure whose financial empire has been a long-standing challenge for Western sanctions enforcers.

This latest round of designations targets Zanjani's conglomerate, Dot One Value Creation Group, and associated companies like DotOne Gold, illustrating how the network integrates physical commodities and digital assets for sanctions evasion. The January 2026 designation of Zedcex and Zedxion marked the first instance of OFAC targeting digital asset exchanges specifically linked to IRGC activities.

The heightened tensions follow the recent revocation of Iran General License X by OFAC on July 7, which had temporarily authorized transactions involving Iranian-origin crude oil and petrochemical products. This reversal came after Iran struck ships in the Strait of Hormuz, prompting U.S. retaliatory airstrikes.

articles.headline: US Threatens to Destroy IRGC Revenue Facilities Amid Rising Tensions with Iran

The U.S. actions, including recent OFAC designations targeting a network tied to Babak Zanjani, illustrate a concerted effort to dismantle the financial infrastructure supporting the IRGC. These measures follow recent Iranian attacks on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and subsequent U.S. airstrikes.

The escalating rhetoric and punitive financial measures underscore a period of heightened confrontation between Washington and Tehran, with both sides indicating a readiness to respond to perceived provocations.

articles.headline: Houthi Attacks on Saudi Oil Tankers Escalate Red Sea Tensions, Impacting Global Oil Supply

The attacks underscore the Houthis' continued capability to target critical maritime infrastructure, posing a substantial threat to international energy security. The Red Sea is a vital waterway for global trade, and sustained disruptions could have far-reaching economic consequences.

articles.headline: US-Iran Conflict Escalates with Houthi Attacks and Naval Blockade

These developments follow 13 consecutive nights of kinetic strikes by U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) targeting Iranian military infrastructure, coastal surveillance positions, drone storage facilities, and communication assets across southern maritime approaches.

The Houthi attacks on July 22, 2026, extended the war beyond the Strait of Hormuz to the Red Sea, threatening a second global chokepoint and pushing Brent crude prices past $100 per barrel. articles.headline: China Imposes Export Controls on EU Entities in Response to Russia Sanctions
body: China's Ministry of Commerce announced on July 24, 2026, that it has banned the export of dual-use goods and technologies to 14 additional European Union entities. This measure is a direct response to the European Union's 21st package of sanctions against Russia, which included 14 companies from mainland China and Hong Kong.

Among the European entities affected by China's export restrictions are German defense and automotive manufacturer Rheinmetall AG and Polish electronics company Vigo Photonics S.A. Foreign organizations and individuals are also prohibited from transferring or supplying China-origin dual-use goods and technologies to the listed entities.

Dual-use items are goods, software, and technologies with both civilian and military applications, including critical minerals for drones and advanced semiconductor chips. The European Commission is analyzing these new measures and will seek clarification from China.

articles.headline: U.S. Threatens IRGC Revenue Facilities Amid Rising Tensions with Iran
body: The U.S. Treasury has unveiled a significant sanctions-evasion operation, linking Iranian oil money, gold-backed tokens, and cryptocurrency exchanges. This comes amidst escalating tensions with Iran, particularly following recent attacks in the Strait of Hormuz.

On July 24, OFAC designated four individuals and nine entities connected to Babak Zanjani, whose financial network has long been a target for Western sanctions enforcers. The designations target Zanjani's conglomerate, Dot One Value Creation Group, and associated companies like DotOne Gold.

The Treasury specifically highlighted the 'Tala Token,' a gold-backed digital asset linked to DotOne Gold Company, demonstrating how Zanjani's network integrates physical commodities and digital assets for sanctions evasion. This action signals a renewed focus on disrupting Iran's digital asset-related illicit finance.

articles.headline: China Retaliates with Export Controls on 14 EU Entities After EU Sanctions on Russia-Linked Firms
body: China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) announced on July 24, 2026, the addition of 14 EU entities to its Export Control List, effective immediately. This move is a direct retaliation to the European Union's twenty-first package of restrictive measures against Russia, adopted on July 23, 2026, which included 14 companies based in mainland China and Hong Kong.

The EU's sanctions targeted these firms for allegedly assisting Russia in circumventing export controls, particularly concerning microelectronics, computer numerical control machine tools, and semiconductor-manufacturing equipment.

MOFCOM's announcement prohibits Chinese exporters from supplying controlled dual-use items to the listed EU entities, bars overseas parties from transferring Chinese-origin dual-use items to them, and mandates an immediate halt to any ongoing transactions. The listed entities are spread across eight EU member states, including Germany, France, Italy, Poland, the Netherlands, the Czech Republic, Bulgaria, and Lithuania.

articles.headline: EU Sanctions Six Individuals Over Serious Human Rights Violations in Iran
body: The European Union has imposed restrictive measures on an additional six individuals deemed responsible for serious human rights violations in Iran. This action aligns with the EU's principled stance on human rights and follows calls from the European Council for the Iranian regime to cease violence and repression against its own people.

The sanctions consist of an asset freeze, travel bans to the EU, and a prohibition on making funds or economic resources available to those listed. Additionally, a ban on exports to Iran of equipment that could be used for internal repression, including telecommunications monitoring equipment, remains in place.

These measures are part of a broader increase in EU restrictive measures against Iran since 2022, in response to growing concerns about human rights abuses. The relevant legal acts implementing these sanctions were published in the Official Journal of the EU.

articles.headline: Fourteen Nations Reaffirm South China Sea Ruling, Rejecting Beijing's Maritime Claims
body: A coalition of 14 nations, including the United States, Japan, and the Philippines, issued a joint statement on July 24, 2026, reaffirming the 2016 arbitral tribunal ruling that rejected China's expansive 'nine-dash line' sovereignty claims in the South China Sea.

The declaration, released on the 10th anniversary of the landmark ruling, asserted that the decision is final, legally binding, and definitive between China and the Philippines, and that Beijing's claims lack legal merit under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS).

This statement comes amidst heightened tensions in the strategically vital waterway, with the Philippines repeatedly accusing the China Coast Guard of dangerous maneuvers within its exclusive economic zone.

articles.headline: U.S. Sanctions Nine Cuban Entities and Two Officials Over Energy, Finance, and Medical Missions
body: The United States has imposed fresh sanctions on nine Cuban entities and two senior officials, accusing them of supporting the island's communist government through its energy, financial, and overseas medical labor sectors while evading existing U.S. restrictions. These sanctions were announced by the U.S. State Department under President Donald Trump's Executive Order 14404.

The designated entities include three operating in Cuba's energy sector (CEINPET, ENERSA, and EINARBO S.A.), four linked to sanctions evasion involving the military-run Grupo de Administración Empresarial S.A. (GAESA), including the Port of Mariel operator, and Cuba's state-run exporter of medical services, Comercializadora de Servicios Médicos Cubanos (CSMC).

Additionally, Public Health Minister Jose Angel Portal Miranda and the Central Medical Cooperation Unit (UCCM) director, Gretza Sanchez Padron, were sanctioned. Washington alleges that the Cuban government exploits medical professionals deployed abroad by confiscating a significant portion of their wages, a practice described as forced labor.

articles.headline: China Retaliates Against EU Sanctions, Imposes Export Controls on 14 European Entities
body: China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) announced on July 24, 2026, the addition of 14 European entities to its export control list, effectively imposing sanctions by prohibiting the supply of dual-use goods. This move is a direct response to the EU's 21st sanctions package against Russia, adopted the previous day, which included restrictions on 14 Chinese and Hong Kong enterprises for supporting Russia's war effort.

The listed European entities operate in sectors critical to national security, including defense, drone industries, photonics, semiconductors, lasers, and maritime technologies. Affected companies include Czech vehicle manufacturer Tatra Trucks, Italian electric motor maker Lafert SpA, German manufacturer Sindlhauser Materials GmbH, and French drone manufacturer Cavok UAS.

Under these measures, Chinese companies and foreign firms using Chinese components must immediately suspend deliveries of dual-use goods to the listed entities and cease all transactions involving such products. Beijing cited national security, China's interests, and international non-proliferation obligations as reasons for its actions, signaling its willingness to support Moscow while raising costs for the EU.

articles.headline: OCC Denies Wise's Trust Charter Application Citing AML Concerns
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has denied London-based Wise's application to establish a national trust bank, citing significant supervisory and compliance concerns. Stephen Lybarger, the OCC's senior deputy comptroller for chartering, organization and structure, pointed to state regulatory actions against Wise related to anti-money laundering (AML) compliance.

Lybarger noted that Wise's application did not demonstrate sufficient familiarity with federal banking laws and regulations, and that proposed leaders had shown a persistent inability to manage money-laundering and illicit finance risks. The OCC determined that the proposed trust bank's AML/CFT compliance would be lacking until existing deficiencies are addressed and an enhanced enterprise-wide AML/CFT program is developed.

Wise, the U.S. arm of the British fintech firm, plans to submit a new application for a national trust bank charter under a Genius Act framework. This denial stands in contrast to numerous trust charter approvals the OCC has granted to fintech and crypto firms in the past year.

articles.headline: OCC Denies Wise's Trust Charter Application Citing AML Concerns and Insufficient Familiarity with Banking Laws
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has denied London-based Wise's application to establish a national trust bank. The denial, communicated in a letter from Stephen Lybarger, the OCC's senior deputy comptroller for chartering, organization and structure, cited 'significant supervisory and compliance concerns.'

Lybarger pointed to state regulatory actions taken against Wise related to anti-money laundering (AML) compliance and stated that the organizers did not demonstrate 'sufficient familiarity' with federal banking laws and regulations. The OCC determined that the proposed trust bank's AML/CFT compliance would be lacking until Wise addresses existing deficiencies and develops an enhanced enterprise-wide AML/CFT program.

Wise plans to submit a new application to the OCC for a national trust bank charter under a Genius Act framework. The company's U.S. arm was previously hit with a multi-state consent order in July 2025 over deficiencies in its BSA, AML, and countering the financing of terrorism programs, agreeing to pay $4.2 million and boost compliance investments.

articles.headline: U.S. Imposes New Section 301 Tariffs on Chip Partners Over Forced Labor Concerns
body: The U.S. imposed new Section 301 tariffs ranging from 10% to 12.5% on goods from 60 trading partners, including the European Union, Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan, effective July 24, 2026.

These duties target the global chip supply chain, including specialty chemicals, silicon wafers, fabrication equipment, and outsourced assembly and test services, and are aimed at countries with weak enforcement of forced labor import bans.
The new tariffs replace a temporary 10% global tariff and are structured under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, giving them a high degree of durability.

These tariffs, imposed under a presidential memorandum, target the core of the global chip supply chain, affecting specialty chemicals, silicon wafers, fabrication equipment, and outsourced assembly and test services from countries including the European Union, Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan.

The duties are viewed as legally durable and potentially permanent, leading investors to reprice long-term margin risks across the semiconductor sector, despite underlying confidence in AI demand and a strong earnings season.

articles.headline: BIS Prioritizes Semiconductor and Advanced Computing Supply Chain Enforcement in 2026
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has made semiconductor and advanced-computing supply chains, along with reexports that circumvent China-related restrictions, its top enforcement priority for 2026. This focus is evident in BIS's aggressive run of export-control settlements this year, anchored by a $252.5 million penalty against Applied Materials, the second-largest civil penalty BIS has ever imposed.

Under Secretary of Commerce Jeffrey Kessler testified before the House Foreign Affairs Committee on July 14, emphasizing that BIS is focused on protecting the 'crown jewels' of the American economy: critical technologies and supply chains. He noted that BIS penalties increased more than 18-fold between 2024 and 2025, rising from $16 million to $324 million, and administrative penalties had already doubled in 2026 compared to the prior year.

Beyond the Applied Materials fine, other 2026 resolutions include settlements with Robert Bosch GmbH (approximately $36 million for shipments implicating Huawei), Teledyne FLIR, Solventum Corporation, Coastal PVA Technology, Exyte, and Vizicom ICT. These actions underscore a shift in the business community's perception of export controls, moving from a mere compliance checkbox to a critical factor requiring behavioral changes.

body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has made semiconductor and advanced-computing supply chains its top enforcement priority for 2026, particularly focusing on reexports that circumvent China-related restrictions. This strategic shift is underscored by a record $252.5 million penalty against Applied Materials, the second-largest civil penalty ever imposed by BIS.

Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler testified before the House Foreign Affairs Committee on July 14, emphasizing that BIS penalties increased more than 18-fold between 2024 and 2025, rising from $16 million to $324 million, and have already doubled in 2026 compared to the prior year. This surge in enforcement aims to deter violations and ensure that export controls are not merely a cost of doing business but a reason for companies to change their behavior.

BIS is seeking a significant increase in its fiscal year 2027 funding, requesting $450 million, up from $235 million enacted for FY 2026, to drastically expand its enforcement capacity. This includes supporting 290 additional Export Enforcement Agents and 40 more Export Control Officers overseas.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

body: On July 23, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a series of designations targeting counter terrorism and counter narcotics efforts, alongside new Cuba-related designations. The counter terrorism designations included an alleged senior Egyptian Muslim Brotherhood official and three individuals and three entities accused of providing material support to Hamas. Two of the designated entities are reportedly sham charities funneling funds to Hamas's military wing.

In a significant counter narcotics action, OFAC sanctioned over 50 individuals and entities allegedly linked to the Cartel de Jalisco Nueva Generación (CJNG), including an individual identified as the cartel's new leader. Concurrently, the State Department expanded sanctions on Cuba's financial and energy sectors, designating nine entities and two individuals tied to the Cuban regime's energy sector, sanctions-evasion activities, and overseas medical missions. OFAC also issued Cuba General Licenses 2, 3, and 4 to authorize certain wind-down activities, transactions involving CEIBA debt and equity, and transactions related to third-country official missions in Cuba.

Additionally, OFAC announced a Belarus-related designation removal, indicating a specific entity or individual previously sanctioned under the Belarus program has been delisted. This comprehensive set of actions highlights OFAC's multi-faceted approach to combating illicit activities and supporting U.S. foreign policy objectives across various global threats.

articles.headline: EU Adopts 21st Sanctions Package Against Russia, Targeting Energy, Finance, and Crypto Sectors
body: The European Union adopted its 21st package of restrictive measures against Russia on July 23, 2026, significantly expanding sanctions across various sectors to further weaken Russia's ability to wage war in Ukraine. This comprehensive package includes a record number of new listings, with 48 new natural persons and 168 new entities added to the sanctions list, primarily targeting the banking sector and non-EU entities involved in sanctions circumvention or Russian oil trade.

Key measures include asset freezes and transaction prohibitions on 94 Russian banks and major financial institutions, as well as an important figure in Russia's banking establishment. The EU also expanded its transaction ban to 33 additional Russian credit and financial institutions and introduced a transaction ban against a Kyrgyz bank connected with the System for Transfer of Financial Messages (SPFS) and three other non-Russian banks for circumventing sanctions.

For the first time, the EU introduced the possibility of a full third-country ban for crypto-asset services, aiming to deter countries hosting platforms that help Russia evade EU sanctions. The package also expanded export bans to include items and technologies used by Russia's military industry, such as nickel powders, beryllium powders, self-adhesive films, and aviation items specific to unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). Additionally, the automatic update procedure for the Russian oil price cap has been suspended until July 14, 2027, to maintain downward pressure on Russian crude exports.

articles.headline: EU Approves 21st Sanctions Package Against Russia, Freezes Oil Price Cap
body: The European Union has agreed to implement its 21st round of sanctions on Russia in response to its ongoing war in Ukraine. This latest package includes freezing the price cap on Russian crude oil for a year, which currently stands at US$44.10 a barrel.

Negotiations for the package focused on banning the transportation of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG), with Greece initially holding out due to concerns for its shipping industry. A compromise was reached, including a one-year exemption allowing operators to continue transporting Russian LNG to third countries for contracts dating back to 2022, with new contracts prohibited and the exemption subject to annual review.

The sanctions package also expands a transaction ban to cover 32 additional Russian banks, bringing the total number of restricted financial institutions to 94, representing an estimated 50% of the Russian financial network. The EU's chief diplomat, Kaja Kallas, stated that the sanctions are having an effect on Russia's economy and making it harder for Moscow to raise capital abroad.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cuban Entities and Officials for Sanctions Evasion and Exploitation, Issues New General Licenses
body: The United States has imposed sanctions on nine Cuban entities and two government officials, accusing them of facilitating the Cuban government's financing through the energy sector, sanctions evasion, and its overseas medical missions. The U.S. State Department stated that these sanctions are intended to limit the Cuban government's access to what it described as illicit sources of revenue.

Among the sanctioned entities are three energy-related companies: Centro de Investigaciones del Petróleo (CEINPET), Empresa de Energía S.A. (ENERSA), and Einarbo S.A.. Additionally, several entities, including Terminal de Contenedores de Mariel S.A., Coral Marítima S.A., Ceiba Investments Limited, and Orbit S.A., were targeted for allegedly assisting Cuba in evading existing U.S. sanctions.

The sanctions also extend to Cuba's overseas medical mission program, which the U.S. alleges exploits Cuban healthcare workers through forced labor. Comercializadora de Servicios Médicos Cubanos S.A. (CSMC), the Central Medical Cooperation Unit (UCCM), Public Health Minister José Angel Portal Miranda, and UCCM Director Gretza Sánchez Padrón were designated as part of this action.

Additionally, the EU paused the automatic adjustment of the oil price cap mechanism until July 15, 2027, keeping the price cap on Russian crude oil at its current level.

articles.headline: EU Adopts 21st Sanctions Package Against Russia, Targeting Financial Sector and Crypto Services
body: On July 23, 2026, the European Union adopted its 21st package of restrictive measures against Russia, marking the largest round of listings in four years with 218 designations. This comprehensive package aims to further weaken Russia's ability to finance its war in Ukraine by directly targeting its financial infrastructure, including over 100 banks and crypto operators.

The new sanctions impose asset freezes and prohibit making funds available to 94 banks and major financial institutions, and extend transaction bans to 33 additional Russian credit and financial institutions, effectively disconnecting them from SWIFT. The package also targets non-Russian banks facilitating sanctions circumvention, including a Kyrgyz bank connected with Russia's SPFS messaging system.

Significantly, the EU introduced a first-of-its-kind mechanism enabling full third-country bans on crypto-asset services, allowing it to prohibit transactions between EU entities and any crypto provider in a country that hosts services used by Russia to circumvent sanctions. The package also freezes the oil price cap at $44.10 per barrel until July 15, 2027, and sanctions 41 additional shadow fleet vessels.
articles.source: Bird & Bird / Chainalysis / Euractiv / The Moscow Times

articles.headline: EU Adopts 21st Sanctions Package Against Russia and Belarus, Targeting Finance, Energy, and Crypto
body: The European Union has adopted its 21st package of sanctions against Russia and parallel amendments to sanctions against Belarus, significantly expanding restrictions across finance, energy, crypto, and military-industrial sectors. This comprehensive package introduces 218 new designations, freezes the oil price cap, imposes stricter liquefied natural gas (LNG) controls, and aims to close loopholes while reinforcing measures to discourage third-party sanctions evasion.

The new sanctions, which entered into force on July 23, 2026, include a record number of new listings, primarily targeting the banking sector and a significant number of non-EU entities involved in circumvention of restrictive measures or trade of Russian oil. Transaction bans will apply to 33 Russian banks, one bank in Kyrgyzstan, six banks in Mongolia, India, and Nigeria, and five oil traders in the United Arab Emirates, effective August 13, 2026.

The package also takes direct aim at Russia's financial infrastructure by targeting over 100 banks and crypto operators. A transaction ban has been extended to 14 crypto-related service platforms operating in six jurisdictions: Georgia, Panama, the UAE, the Marshall Islands, Kyrgyzstan, and Belarus. Furthermore, the automatic update procedure for the Russian oil price cap is suspended until July 14, 2027.

articles.headline: EU Adopts 21st Sanctions Package Against Russia and Belarus, Targeting Energy, Finance, and Crypto
body: On July 23, 2026, the European Union adopted its 21st package of restrictive measures against Russia and Belarus, marking the largest round of listings in four years with 218 designations. The new sanctions aim to further weaken Russia's ability to wage war in Ukraine by targeting its energy revenues, military-industrial complex, financial services, shadow fleet, and critical infrastructure.

The package significantly expands action against Russia's financial and banking sector, imposing asset freezes and transaction prohibitions on 94 banks and major financial institutions, and extending transaction bans to 33 additional Russian credit and financial institutions. It also introduces a transaction ban against a Kyrgyz bank connected with Russia's System for Transfer of Financial Messages (SPFS) and three other non-Russian banks for circumventing sanctions.

A key element of the package is a transaction ban on 14 crypto-related service platforms across six jurisdictions (Georgia, Panama, UAE, Marshall Islands, Kyrgyzstan, and Belarus) that have served as conduits for Russian entities to move funds around existing sanctions. For the first time, the EU is introducing a mechanism for full third-country bans on crypto-asset services, allowing it to prohibit transactions between EU entities and any crypto provider in a country hosting services used by Russia to evade sanctions.
Furthermore, the package pauses the automatic adjustment of the Russian oil price cap mechanism until July 15, 2027, and sanctions 41 more shadow fleet vessels, bringing the total to over 673.

articles.headline: EU Adopts 21st Sanctions Package Against Russia and Belarus, Targeting Financial, Energy, and Crypto Sectors
body: On July 23, 2026, the European Union adopted its 21st package of sanctions against Russia and Belarus, marking the most extensive designation exercise in four years with 218 new designations (48 individuals and 170 entities). The package significantly expands the EU's sanctions regime, focusing on financial infrastructure, crypto-asset channels, energy-derived revenues, military-industrial supply chains, and circumvention pathways through third-country jurisdictions.

Key measures include asset freezes and transaction prohibitions on 94 new banks and major financial institutions, along with a senior figure in Russia's banking establishment. An additional 33 Russian credit and financial institutions are now subject to transaction bans. Notably, transaction prohibitions now capture a Kyrgyz bank linked to Russia's SPFS messaging infrastructure and three other non-Russian banks identified as enabling sanctions evasion.

For the first time, the package establishes a legal framework for a possible third-country blanket ban on crypto-asset services, granting the EU authority to block all transactions between an EU-based operator and any crypto provider used by Russia. It also suspends the oil price cap adjustment mechanism until July 15, 2027, and introduces a new tool allowing transaction bans on named refineries that process Russian crude, with the Kulevi Oil Refinery in Georgia being the first listed.
