articles.headline: UK Sanctions Russian Individuals and Entities for Cyber Attacks and Disinformation
body: The United Kingdom has imposed new sanctions on 24 individuals and entities linked to Russian state-sponsored cyber attacks, election interference, and the spread of anti-Ukraine narratives across Europe. This action, taken alongside EU allies, targets cybercriminal networks and senior GRU leadership figures.

Among those sanctioned are Vyacheslav Stafeyev, Ivan Senin, and Ivan Kasyanenko, identified for their roles in directing GRU cyber and hybrid threat operations. The UK aims to expose and disrupt those carrying out malign activities on behalf of the Russian state.

Additionally, the UK Sanctions List was updated on July 14, 2026, with a variation to the designation of Christodoulos Georgiou Vassiliades under the Russia (Sanctions) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019. Vassiliades is associated with Alisher Usmanov and Sberbank Investments Limited, a subsidiary of PJSC Sberbank, a Russian bank owned by the Russian Ministry of Finance.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Cyber and Cuba-Related Designations, Publishes New Cuba FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new cyber-related and Cuba designations, alongside the issuance of a new Cuba-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ 1262).

The Cuba designations include entities such as Grupo Empresarial del Comercio Exterior (GECOMEX) and Grupo Empresarial de Transporte Marítimo Portuario (GEMAR), designated pursuant to E.O. 14404. FAQ 1262 clarifies that non-U.S. persons, including foreign financial institutions, are not exposed to sanctions risk for winding down transactions with GECOMEX or GEMAR.

The cyber-related designations target malware and infrastructure providers supporting ransomware attacks against Americans. These actions aim to disrupt malicious cyber activities and further pressure the Cuban regime's sources of funding.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: EU Adds Individuals and Entities to Russia Sanctions Regimes
body: On July 13, 2026, the Council of the European Union added listings to two Russia restrictive-measures regimes, effective upon publication.

Regulation (EU) 2026/1708 amended Annex IV to Regulation (EU) 2024/1485 (human-rights measures), adding four individuals and five entities. Concurrently, Regulation (EU) 2026/1710 amended Annex I to Regulation (EU) 2024/2642 (destabilizing activities), adding nine individuals and four entities.
These new listings impose asset freezes and prohibit making funds or economic resources available to the newly sanctioned parties, with no phase-in period.

articles.headline: EU Proposes New Sanctions Regime Targeting Migrant Smuggling and Human Trafficking
body: The European Commission and the High Representative of the EU have proposed a new horizontal sanctions regime aimed at combating migrant smuggling, human trafficking, and other serious forms of organized crime.

This proposed framework would enable the EU to sanction individuals and entities involved in conduct originating outside the EU that poses a serious threat to the EU's values, security, or international security.
Under the proposed regime, listed individuals and entities would face asset freezes and a prohibition on making funds or economic resources available, with individuals also subject to travel bans.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Cyber-Related and Cuba Designations, Alongside New Cuba-Related FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new cyber-related designations and additional designations targeting entities in Cuba. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to counter malicious cyber activities and to maintain pressure on the Cuban government.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC also issued a new Cuba-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). This FAQ provides important clarifications regarding the scope of the Cuba sanctions program and aims to assist the public in understanding compliance requirements.

The designations and the new FAQ underscore the U.S. government's commitment to addressing threats in cyberspace and its continued policy towards Cuba, while also providing guidance for legitimate transactions and activities.

articles.headline: EU Sanctions Individuals and Entities for Human Rights Violations and Cyberattacks in Russia
body: The European Union has imposed sanctions on four individuals and five entities for human rights violations in Russia, specifically for their role in restricting freedom of expression, access to information, and freedom of association through new technologies.

Additionally, the Council sanctioned nine Russian individuals and four entities for their involvement in cyberattacks and malicious activities posing an external threat to EU member states. These actions underscore the EU's commitment to countering both internal repression and external cyber threats emanating from Russia.
These new listings are part of the EU's broader response to Russia's ongoing hybrid activities, including foreign information manipulation and interference against the EU and its partners.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Cyber-Related and Cuba Designations, Issues Cuba-Related FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new cyber-related designations on July 13, 2026, targeting individuals and entities allegedly enabling the malign activities of ransomware actors and other cybercriminals. Specifically, one individual and an entity were sanctioned for providing virtual private network (VPN) services to ransomware groups, while another individual was designated for selling tools to disguise ransomware and malware.
In a separate action, OFAC also imposed new designations related to Cuba. These designations are part of the ongoing U.S. policy to address concerns regarding the Cuban government.

To provide further clarity, OFAC issued a new Cuba-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). This FAQ aims to assist the public in understanding the scope of authorized activities and compliance requirements under the Cuba sanctions program.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber-Related and Cuba-Related Entities, Issues New FAQ
body: On July 13, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new cyber-related and Cuba designations. The cyber-related designations targeted two individuals and one entity for allegedly enabling the malign activities of ransomware actors and other cybercriminals, including those involved in ransomware attacks against Americans. One individual and the entity were sanctioned for providing virtual private network (VPN) services to ransomware groups, while the other individual was sanctioned for selling tools to disguise ransomware and malware.

In a coordinated action, the United Kingdom's Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office also sanctioned alleged cybercriminals. These actions underscore international efforts to combat cybercrime and its facilitators.

Additionally, OFAC issued a Cuba-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) 1262, clarifying that non-U.S. persons, including foreign financial institutions, generally will not be targeted for transactions ordinarily incident and necessary to the wind-down of dealings with designated Cuban entities like Grupo Empresarial del Comercio Exterior (GECOMEX) or Grupo Empresarial de Transporte Marítimo Portuario (GEMAR) through August 12, 2026. However, OFAC cautioned that transactions involving the return or transfer of assets to these entities could pose significant sanctions risk for non-U.S. persons.

articles.headline: EU Imposes New Sanctions on Russia for Human Rights Violations and Cyberattacks
body: On July 13, 2026, the European Union imposed new sanctions on Russia, targeting individuals and entities responsible for human rights violations and malicious cyber activities. These measures include four individuals and five entities involved in the continued use of new technologies to restrict freedom of expression, access to information, and freedom of association within Russia.

The sanctioned entities include companies responsible for developing and managing surveillance applications pre-installed on mobile devices sold in Russia, as well as those manufacturing hardware and software related to the System of Operative Investigative Measures (SORM), a surveillance system used to control internet and mobile communications.

Additionally, the EU Council designated nine individuals and four entities in response to Russian cyberattacks and other destabilizing activities directed against the EU, its Member States, and international partners. These listings were adopted under the EU's horizontal sanctions regime addressing cyberattacks.

articles.headline: EU Council Strengthens Sudan Sanctions Regime, Targets Gold Sector
body: The EU Council strengthened its restrictive measures against Sudan on July 13, 2026, by introducing new sectoral measures targeting the country's war economy. These measures expand the scope of the existing sanctions framework under Council Regulation (EU) 2023/2147.

The new restrictions specifically target the gold sector, identified by the EU Council as a key source of revenue sustaining the conflict in Sudan. This includes a prohibition on the purchase, import, or transfer of gold originating in Sudan when exported after July 15, 2026.
Additionally, a transitional period until January 16, 2027, has been introduced for the execution of certain contracts involving sodium cyanide concluded before July 15, 2026.
articles.source: Steptoe / Council of the European Union

These include four entities for their direct roles in carrying out, enabling, and financing the Cuban regime's violent repression, and six state-owned entities, such as Grupo Empresarial del Comercio Exterior (GECOMEX) and Grupo Empresarial de Transporte Marítimo Portuario (GEMAR), for funding the regime. articles.headline: UK Designates 10 Individuals Under Russia Sanctions Regime, Extends Brokerage General License
body: The UK's Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) has updated the UK Sanctions List with 10 new additions under the Russia sanctions regime. These individuals are now subject to asset freezes, travel bans, trust services sanctions, director disqualification sanctions, and internet services sanctions.

The designations are part of ongoing efforts to target individuals suspected of involvement in the destabilization of Ukraine. The internet services sanctions require social media services, internet access services, and application stores to take reasonable steps to prevent UK users from accessing content, sites, or applications provided by the designated individuals or entities.

Additionally, the Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation (OFSI) has published a one-year extension to General Licence INT/2025/6641960, known as the Brokerage General Licence. This license, which addresses non-designated third-party brokerage accounts held at designated brokerage firms under the UK's Russia and Belarus sanctions regimes, is now extended until July 16, 2027.

body: On July 13, 2026, the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) updated the UK Sanctions List with 10 new additions under The Russia (Sanctions) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019. articles.headline: Federal Reserve Governor Waller Expresses Concern Over Rising Core Inflation
body: Federal Reserve Governor Christopher J. Waller expressed concern over the elevated pace of core inflation in the U.S., which has steadily risen from 3 percent in December 2025 to 3.4 percent in May 2026. Waller highlighted that while headline inflation has been impacted by energy prices, the persistent rise in core inflation is more troubling.

Waller noted that earlier concerns about higher oil prices translating into broader inflation have diminished, but crude oil prices remain volatile, and farther-dated futures prices are still higher than before the Middle East conflict. He also pointed to AI-related demand as a potential source of inflationary pressure, citing large price increases in semiconductors, computer chips, servers, computers, and peripherals.

The Governor emphasized that the direction of core inflation has significant implications for monetary policy. He expects solid consumer spending growth to continue, supported by recently falling energy prices, and strong AI-related investment to persist in the near term.

articles.headline: Federal Reserve Governor Waller Expresses Concern Over Elevated Core Inflation
body: Federal Reserve Governor Christopher J. Waller expressed concern over the elevated pace of core inflation in the U.S. economy, noting that it has steadily risen from 3% in December 2025 to 3.4% in May. Waller highlighted that while headline PCE inflation, which includes energy prices, has been volatile, the persistent increase in core inflation is more troubling.

Waller indicated that the resilience of consumers, despite higher goods costs from tariffs and surging energy prices due to the Middle East conflict, has contributed to solid spending. However, he questioned whether core inflation will continue its upward trajectory or begin to decline towards the Fed's 2% target, with different implications for monetary policy.

Another potential source of inflationary pressure identified by Waller is the demand related to artificial intelligence, which is reflected in significant price increases for semiconductors, computer chips, servers, and other related goods.

articles.headline: Oil Prices Drop to $70 Amid Easing Strait of Hormuz Tensions, Inflationary Pressures Remain
body: Oil prices have recently fallen back to the $70 per barrel level, a development expected to help ease prices at the pump and other costs impacted by energy. This decline comes as tensions surrounding the Strait of Hormuz appear to be winding down, following a period of heightened conflict involving the U.S. and Iran.

Despite the drop in oil prices, inflationary pressures persist, with the May CPI reading increasing by 0.50% to an annualized rate of 4.20%. While the economic data may have cooled the need for further interest rate hikes this year, the Federal Reserve's ability to cut rates remains constrained by ongoing inflation.

articles.headline: U.S. Markets See Small-Cap Surge and AI-Driven Growth in First Half of 2026
body: The first half of 2026 saw the S&P 500 gain 9.6% (10.2% including dividends), crossing 7,600 for the first time, but the significant headline was the Russell 2000 index of smaller companies surging approximately 22%. International stocks also returned about 15%, while bonds saw barely positive returns due to rising yields.

Artificial intelligence continues to be the economy's biggest growth engine, with 2026's version being broader than last year's, including memory-chip makers, equipment suppliers, and power providers. First-quarter S&P 500 profits grew roughly 28% year over year on revenue growth near 12%, with about 85% of companies beating estimates.

Energy was among the strongest sectors after a June conflict involving the U.S., Israel, and Iran sent oil prices sharply higher. The U.S. economy grew at a 2.1% annualized pace in the first quarter, with unemployment at 4.2% in June and consistent job growth.
articles.source: Portus Wealth Advisors / Lake Ridge Bank

articles.headline: U.S. Consumer Spending Remains Resilient Despite Economic Headwinds
body: U.S. consumers have demonstrated remarkable resilience over the past several years, continuing to spend at a solid pace despite challenges such as high inflation, elevated interest rates, import tariffs, and increased energy prices from the Middle East conflict. This sustained spending is expected to continue, partly aided by the recent fall in oil prices from their April highs.

However, Federal Reserve Governor Christopher J. Waller expressed concern about the elevated pace of core inflation, which has steadily risen from 3% in December 2025 to 3.4% in May. While market-based measures of inflation compensation over the two- to five-year horizon have recently declined, Waller emphasized that anchored inflation expectations do not negate the need for central bank action in response to above-target inflation.

The upcoming June CPI data will be closely scrutinized, with headline inflation expected to moderate monthly, but core inflation is forecast to remain near 2.8–2.9% year-on-year, suggesting underlying price pressures are still firm enough to support the Federal Reserve's current policy stance.

articles.headline: China Expands Counter-Sanctions Toolkit, Raising Risks for Foreign Firms
body: China is actively expanding its counter-sanctions toolkit through new regulations and enforcement actions, creating increased risks for multinational companies operating within its jurisdiction. In April 2026, China's State Council introduced two new regulations aimed at broadening restrictions on foreign legal actions with extraterritorial effect in China and limiting information gathering on Chinese supply chains.

In May 2026, the Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) issued its first-ever blocking order under the 2021 Blocking Rules. This order prohibits the implementation of U.S. Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) designations against five Chinese 'teapot refineries' by any parties in China, directly challenging U.S. sanctions on entities allegedly purchasing Iranian crude oil.

These measures, alongside a draft law allowing Chinese prosecutors to bring cases against foreign organizations or individuals harming China's national interests, highlight Beijing's strategic response to foreign sanctions and export controls. Companies are now facing the complex challenge of complying with potentially conflicting legal obligations from both Chinese and foreign authorities.

articles.headline: Fed Governor Waller Expresses Concern Over Elevated Core Inflation
body: Federal Reserve Governor Christopher J. Waller stated on July 13, 2026, that while the U.S. economy remains solid, inflation and monetary policy are at a crossroads.
Waller expressed concern about the elevated pace of core inflation this year, which has steadily moved up to 3.4% in May, excluding the direct effects of consumer energy prices.

He highlighted that the direction core inflation takes will have significant implications for the future path of monetary policy, indicating that tomorrow's inflation data will be a key factor in determining appropriate policy actions.

articles.headline: EU Council Strengthens Sudan Sanctions Regime Targeting Gold Sector
body: The EU Council has strengthened its restrictive measures against Sudan by introducing new sectoral measures targeting the country's war economy. These measures expand the scope of the existing sanctions framework under Council Regulation (EU) 2023/2147.

The new restrictions specifically target the gold sector, which the EU Council identified as a key source of revenue sustaining the ongoing conflict in Sudan. The measures prohibit the purchase, import, or transfer of gold originating in Sudan when exported after July 15, 2026.

Additionally, the EU has banned the sale, supply, or transfer of certain goods to Sudan, and a transitional period until January 16, 2027, has been introduced for the execution of specific contracts involving sodium cyanide concluded before July 15, 2026.

articles.headline: EU Prepares Largest Russia Sanctions Expansion Amidst Escalating Conflict
body: The European Union is reportedly preparing its most significant expansion of sanctions against Russia since the onset of the Ukraine war. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas indicated that member states aim to approve 250 new sanctions listings targeting individuals and entities linked to Russia.

These proposed measures are part of Europe's ongoing response to Russia's recent attacks on civilians and its continued aggression in Ukraine. While negotiations for the broader 21st EU sanctions package are ongoing, several issues remain unresolved.

The discussions also encompassed the EU's Black Sea security strategy, freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, and cooperation with Gulf partners, highlighting the multifaceted nature of European foreign policy challenges.

articles.headline: U.S. Economy Shows Consumer Resilience Amidst Inflationary Pressures
body: A consistent feature of the U.S. economy over the past several years has been the resilience of consumers, who have continued spending at a solid pace despite high inflation, high interest rates, import tariffs, and higher energy prices.

Federal Reserve Governor Christopher J. Waller noted that the real side of the economy is in good shape, with solid consumer spending growth expected to continue, aided by recently falling energy prices from their April highs.

However, Waller also highlighted that inflation and monetary policy are at a crossroads, with core inflation steadily moving up this year, reaching 3.4 percent in May as measured by the 12-month personal consumption expenditures (PCE) rate. This elevated pace of core inflation remains a concern for the Federal Open Market Committee's (FOMC) 2 percent objective.

articles.headline: Federal Reserve Governor Waller Expresses Concern Over Elevated Core Inflation
body: Federal Reserve Governor Christopher J. Waller expressed concern over the elevated pace of core inflation in 2026, noting that it has steadily risen from 3 percent in December 2025 to 3.4 percent in May. Waller highlighted that while conventional wisdom suggests looking through one-time price increases, such as those from tariffs and oil price surges, the persistent rise in core inflation is a significant concern.

He emphasized that the direction core inflation takes has critical implications for monetary policy, as it is a good guide to future inflation. Waller also pointed to the inflationary impact of the boom in AI spending as another possible source of pressure, reflected in large price increases for semiconductors, computer chips, servers, and related equipment.

Despite these concerns, Waller noted the remarkable resilience of U.S. consumers, who have continued solid spending growth even amidst high inflation, interest rates, import tariffs, and energy price increases. He anticipates continued solid consumer spending, partly aided by recent declines in energy prices from their April highs.

body: The European Union is preparing what could be its largest expansion of sanctions against Russia since the start of the Ukraine war, with plans to approve 250 new sanctions listings.

These new measures will target individuals and entities linked to Russia, in response to Russia's recent attacks on civilians and its continued war in Ukraine. While negotiations continue over the broader 21st EU sanctions package, several issues remain unresolved.
The discussions also covered the EU's Black Sea security strategy, freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, and cooperation with Gulf partners.

articles.headline: Renewed Hostilities Threaten US-Iran Negotiations
body: Renewed hostilities in the Middle East have threatened to derail ongoing negotiations between the United States and Iran, following a mid-June Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) that anticipated a suspension of new sanctions designations.
President Trump stated on Truth Social that the ceasefire was no longer in effect after further hostilities, even as negotiations continue.
This escalation has led to a surge in oil prices and increased geopolitical risk, impacting global markets and central bank policy decisions.

articles.headline: U.S. Resumes Military Strikes on Iran and Reinstates Strait of Hormuz Blockade
body: President Donald Trump formally notified Congress on July 13, 2026, that the United States has resumed military strikes on Iran. This development marks a significant escalation in tensions in the Middle East.
On the same day, President Trump reinstated a blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, a critical chokepoint for global oil shipments.

Concurrently, the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) appears to have resumed its sanctions campaign against Iran, with expanded sanctions targeting illicit shipping networks.

articles.headline: OCC, FDIC, and NCUA Issue Guidance on Lending to Non-Work Authorized Borrowers
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), and National Credit Union Administration (NCUA) jointly issued guidance on July 13, 2026.

This interagency guidance reminds supervised financial institutions of their existing obligations regarding credit risk management, particularly concerning borrowers not legally authorized to work in the United States.
The guidance advises that such borrowers may present elevated credit risk due to potential uncertainties in income generation, employment continuity, and financial stability.

articles.headline: OCC Issues Guidance on Lending to Non-Work Authorized Borrowers
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), and National Credit Union Administration (NCUA) jointly issued guidance on July 13, 2026, reminding supervised financial institutions of their existing obligations regarding credit risk management for borrowers not legally authorized to work in the United States.

This interagency guidance follows a May 2026 Executive Order aimed at addressing perceived risks to the financial system from extending credit to the non-work authorized population. Regulators warn that such lending may present elevated credit risk due to uncertainties in income stability, employment, and financial sustainability.

Financial institutions are advised to incorporate these risks into their underwriting, account management, credit classification, allowance analysis, and compliance processes, while adhering to applicable consumer protection laws. The guidance also highlights potential portfolio concentration risks for institutions serving industries with significant immigrant workforces.
articles.source: OCC.gov / Consumer Financial Services Law Monitor

articles.headline: OCC Issues Interagency Guidance on Lending to Individuals Not Legally Authorized to Work in the United States
body: On July 13, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) issued interagency guidance concerning lending to individuals not legally authorized to work in the United States. This guidance aims to clarify regulatory expectations for banks engaging in such lending activities.

The interagency guidance provides a framework for financial institutions to assess and manage the risks associated with lending to this demographic, ensuring compliance with fair lending laws and other relevant regulations. It addresses issues such as identity verification and creditworthiness assessment.
This issuance reflects the OCC's commitment to promoting safe and sound banking practices while also addressing social and economic considerations related to financial inclusion.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

articles.headline: Agencies Issue Guidance on Lending to Individuals Not Legally Authorized to Work in the U.S.
body: Federal banking regulators, including the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), and National Credit Union Administration (NCUA), issued new interagency guidance on July 13, 2026. This guidance directs supervised financial institutions to scrutinize credit risk more closely when lending to individuals not legally authorized to work in the U.S.

The guidance follows a May 2026 Executive Order, 'Restoring Integrity to America's Financial System,' which aimed to address perceived risks to the financial system from extending credit to the non-work authorized population. Regulators warn that such lending may present heightened credit risk due to uncertainties in income stability, continued employment, and financial sustainability.

Institutions are reminded of their existing credit risk management obligations and must assess whether a borrower's income will remain stable throughout the loan's life. This coordinated regulatory focus signals that immigration status will be a significant factor in lending decisions.

articles.headline: Interagency Guidance Issued on Lending to Individuals Not Legally Authorized to Work in the U.S.
body: Federal banking regulators, including the OCC, FDIC, and NCUA, issued new interagency guidance on July 13, 2026, directing financial institutions to scrutinize credit risk when lending to individuals not legally authorized to work in the U.S.
This guidance follows a May 2026 Executive Order aimed at addressing perceived risks to the financial system from extending credit to this population.

The agencies emphasize that income stability and continued employment for non-work authorized borrowers are subject to greater uncertainty due to immigration enforcement activity, thus presenting heightened credit risk.

body: On July 13, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and other federal agencies issued interagency guidance concerning lending to individuals not legally authorized to work in the United States. This guidance aims to provide clarity and consistency for financial institutions on how to approach such lending practices.

The issuance of this guidance reflects a need to address the complexities surrounding financial services for various populations while ensuring compliance with existing laws and regulations. It is expected to help banks navigate potential risks and legal considerations.

This interagency effort highlights the ongoing commitment to fair and responsible banking practices, while also acknowledging the legal framework governing employment authorization in the United States.

articles.headline: OCC Issues Interagency Guidance on Lending to Non-Work Authorized Individuals
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), along with the FDIC and NCUA, has issued interagency guidance on lending to individuals not legally authorized to work in the United States. This guidance reminds supervised institutions of their existing credit risk management obligations as they apply to such borrowers.

The guidance follows a May 2026 Executive Order aimed at addressing perceived risks to the financial system from extending credit to the non-work authorized population. Regulators warn that lending to these borrowers may present heightened credit risk due to uncertainties regarding income stability, continued employment, and financial sustainability.
Financial institutions are advised to consider how uncertainties related to employment authorization may affect repayment capacity, collateral recovery, and other factors relevant to credit risk.

articles.headline: Agencies Issue Guidance on Lending to Non-Work Authorized Individuals
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), along with the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) and the National Credit Union Administration (NCUA), issued interagency guidance on July 13, 2026, regarding lending to individuals not legally authorized to work in the United States. This guidance reminds supervised financial institutions of their existing obligations concerning credit risk management in such cases.

The guidance follows a May 2026 Executive Order aimed at addressing perceived risks to the financial system from extending credit to the non-work authorized population. Regulators warn that lending to these individuals may present elevated credit risk due to uncertainties in income stability, employment, and financial sustainability, which are subject to immigration enforcement activity.

Financial institutions are advised to identify, measure, monitor, and control these risks through sound underwriting practices that assess a borrower's willingness and capacity to repay. The guidance also references the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's (CFPB) June 8, 2026, statement on ability to repay and immigration status, emphasizing creditor obligations under the Truth in Lending Act and the Equal Credit Opportunity Act.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency / National Credit Union Administration

articles.headline: Agencies Issue Interagency Guidance on Lending to Undocumented Individuals
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), along with other agencies, issued interagency guidance on lending to individuals not legally authorized to work in the United States on July 13, 2026. This guidance aims to clarify regulatory expectations for banks providing financial services to this population.

The guidance addresses the complexities and risks associated with lending to undocumented individuals, providing a framework for financial institutions to manage these risks while ensuring fair access to financial services. This is a significant development for banks operating in diverse communities.

This interagency effort seeks to promote consistency in regulatory approaches and to help financial institutions understand their obligations and opportunities in serving all segments of their communities, within the bounds of applicable laws and regulations.

articles.headline: OCC, FDIC, and NCUA Issue Joint Guidance on Lending to Undocumented Workers
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), in conjunction with the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) and the National Credit Union Administration (NCUA), issued joint guidance on July 13, 2026, regarding lending to individuals not legally authorized to work in the United States. This guidance implements an executive order from President Trump.

The guidance reminds financial institutions of their obligations concerning credit risk management, particularly for borrowers whose employment authorization may affect income stability, repayment capacity, and collateral recovery. It advises institutions to consider these uncertainties when lending to non-work authorized borrowers.

This follows earlier guidance from the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) and an advisory from the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), FDIC, OCC, and NCUA, in coordination with the IRS, warning financial institutions to be vigilant against potential illicit activity involving unlawful employment of undocumented immigrants.

body: The Department of Commerce's CHIPS Program Office announced a Direct Funding Agreement with Robert Bosch Semiconductor LLC for up to $225 million in incentives under the CHIPS and Science Act.

articles.headline: China Bans Helium Exports Amid Qatar Outage, Deepening Supply Squeeze
body: China has implemented a ban on helium exports, a move that is expected to deepen the global supply squeeze already exacerbated by an outage in Qatar.

This action by China, a significant player in the global helium market, could have widespread implications for industries reliant on the inert gas, including healthcare, aerospace, and electronics manufacturing. The ban highlights growing concerns over critical resource security and geopolitical leverage in trade.

articles.headline: South Korea's Market Enters Bear Territory
body: South Korea's stock market has officially entered a bear market, signaling a period of sustained decline for investors.

This downturn reflects broader economic concerns and could impact investor confidence in the region. Factors contributing to the bear market include global economic slowdowns, inflationary pressures, and geopolitical uncertainties.

articles.headline: IMF Warns of Global Economy in Crosscurrents of War and Technology
body: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) released its July 2026 World Economic Outlook Update, projecting global growth at 3.0 percent for 2026 and 3.4 percent for 2027. The report highlights that the global economy is navigating crosscurrents of ongoing conflicts, particularly in the Middle East, and the accelerating technology cycle driven by artificial intelligence.

The outlook is uneven, with energy importers and vulnerable economies facing headwinds from war-related shocks, while countries integrated into the global technology value chain are experiencing stronger activity. Global headline inflation is expected to increase from 4.1 percent in 2025 to 4.7 percent in 2026, primarily due to higher energy and food prices, before declining to 3.9 percent in 2027.

Risks to the outlook are more balanced than in April but remain tilted to the downside, with renewed Middle East conflict posing a significant threat to commodity price volatility, supply chains, and financial conditions.

articles.headline: Cuba's Power Grid Collapses Amid Diplomatic Tensions with U.S.
body: Cuba's entire power grid collapsed for the second time in less than a week, as diplomatic tensions with the U.S. continue.
This infrastructure failure occurred as Cuba reportedly disrupted the U.S. Ambassador's speech at the UN.
The grandson of former Cuban leader Castro is reportedly seeking talks with President Trump amidst the ongoing crisis.

articles.headline: New era for Gibraltar with removal of 118-year-old border controls with Spain
body: It is hoped that free movement between the UK territory and Spain will provide an economic boost.

articles.headline: Strait of Hormuz Remains Flashpoint as US-Iran Tensions Escalate
body: The Strait of Hormuz continues to be a central flashpoint in the Middle East as of July 2026, with Iran asserting control over sections of the waterway and tensions escalating with the United States. A senior U.S. official confirmed that safe passage through the strait is a precondition for any resumption of meaningful nuclear negotiations.

Despite a June 2026 memorandum of understanding aimed at securing a ceasefire, Iran has repeatedly attacked commercial vessels, prompting U.S. President Donald Trump to declare the ceasefire 'over' on July 8. This has led to renewed exchanges of strikes, widening the conflict from a maritime contest into a regional infrastructure crisis.

The renewed hostilities have injected fresh uncertainty into the global energy outlook, especially as global oil inventories are at dangerously low levels. The situation underscores the fragility of regional stability and the significant impact on international shipping and energy markets.
articles.source: Medium / KBA13 INSIGHT / Mackinder Forum / SABC News

articles.headline: U.S.-Iran Ceasefire Collapses Amid Renewed Hostilities and Nuclear Concerns
body: A U.S.-brokered ceasefire between Israel and Iran collapsed on July 10-11, 2026, with President Trump declaring it over, citing satellite imagery of Iranian nuclear reconstruction activity.
The renewed hostilities include reported U.S. strikes against Iranian military-related targets and Iranian retaliation against U.S. interests and regional partners.
This escalation follows a fragile truce and has intensified concerns about a wider Middle East conflict, impacting energy markets and regional stability.

articles.headline: India Deepens Indo-Pacific Partnerships Amidst Shifting Geopolitics
body: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi concluded a three-nation tour, deepening India's Indo-Pacific partnerships with Indonesia, Australia, and New Zealand.
The tour saw agreements on critical minerals, energy resilience, defense co-development, and technology supply chains, aiming to reduce dependence on China.

These efforts reflect a broader regional trend of countries strengthening ties and taking on a larger role in security and economic burdens amidst China's growing influence and evolving U.S. engagement.

articles.headline: Russian Forces Achieve Significant Territorial Gains in Ukraine
body: Russian forces achieved a net gain of 31 square miles of Ukrainian territory in the four-week period from June 9 to July 7, 2026, according to data from Ukraine's DeepState OSINT group. This represents a significant acceleration compared to the prior four-week period, in which Russia lost a net of one square mile.

This territorial gain is roughly the size of Manhattan Island, highlighting a shift in the dynamics of the conflict. The increased Russian offensive capacity was also demonstrated by a major missile-and-drone attack on Kyiv and other targets on the eve of the NATO summit in Ankara.

Ukraine has been running short of Patriot missiles, with Vladimir Zelensky repeatedly requesting more, but the U.S. has been burning through its stockpile intercepting Iranian missiles in the Middle East. This shortage contributed to Ukraine's inability to shoot down nearly 30 Russian ballistic missiles fired this week, which killed at least 50 people.

articles.headline: Terrorism in Africa Poses 'Greatest Uncertainty' to Global Threat Environment
body: Terrorism in Africa has been identified as 'the greatest uncertainty' in the global threat environment, according to CSIS's Global Terrorism Threat Assessment 2026. The African Union Transition Mission in Somalia (ATMIS) faces a funding crisis and mandate ambiguity, leaving it without the necessary resources to sustain operational tempo against the threat.

Western nations are pursuing an 'over-the-horizon' approach, maintaining counterterrorism partnerships with coastal West African states like Ivory Coast, Ghana, and Benin to prevent jihadist expansion southward.

Meanwhile, clashes have intensified in northern Malian towns between the Malian Army and the Azawad Liberation Front, and drone strikes have killed 15 in Sudan. Reports also indicate that Al-Qaeda extremists in Mali are receiving training and drones from Ukraine.

articles.headline: Cuba Experiences Second Power Grid Collapse Amidst Political Tensions
body: Cuba's entire power grid has collapsed for the second time in less than a week, amidst reports of the Cuban grid collapsing and the grandson of Fidel Castro seeking talks with the Trump administration. This widespread outage follows a period of heightened political tensions, including Cuba disrupting the U.S. Ambassador's speech at the UN.

The repeated grid failures highlight significant infrastructure challenges within Cuba, which are further exacerbated by ongoing economic and political pressures. The situation underscores the fragility of the nation's energy systems and the potential for widespread disruption.

articles.headline: France Pushes Syria Strategic Energy Corridor Vision Amidst Damascus Bombing
body: France is actively promoting a vision for a strategic energy corridor in Syria, a development that comes amidst a bombing in Damascus near French President Macron's hotel. This initiative suggests a renewed focus on energy infrastructure and regional influence in the war-torn country.

The bombing incident underscores the persistent instability in Syria, even as international actors like France seek to shape its future energy landscape. The strategic energy corridor could have significant geopolitical implications for the wider Middle East.

articles.headline: China Bans Helium Exports Amid Supply Squeeze and Tests SLBM
body: China has implemented a ban on helium exports, a move that deepens the ongoing global supply squeeze. This action follows a Qatar outage that has significantly impacted the international helium market.

In a separate development, China successfully tested a Submarine-Launched Ballistic Missile (SLBM) that landed in the Pacific's Nuclear-Weapon Free Zone. This test raises concerns about regional security and adherence to international agreements.
These actions highlight China's growing influence in global resource markets and its continued advancements in military technology, both of which have significant geopolitical implications.

articles.headline: Clashes Intensify in Northern Malian Town of Anefis
body: Clashes have intensified in the northern Malian town of Anefis between the Malian Army and the Azawad Liberation Front. This renewed fighting signals a deterioration of the security situation in the region.

The conflict in northern Mali has been ongoing for years, involving various armed groups and government forces. The recent escalation in Anefis underscores the persistent challenges to stability and peace in the Sahel.
International observers are closely monitoring the situation, as continued instability in Mali has broader implications for regional security and humanitarian efforts.

articles.headline: Gaza Ceasefire Strained as Israeli Military Activity Persists
body: Eight months after the adoption of UN Resolution 2803, which endorsed a U.S.-brokered 'Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict,' the ceasefire remains strained, with Israeli military activity persisting despite a nominal truce.

Israel has expanded its footprint beyond the demarcated Yellow Line, controlling an estimated 70-80% of the Gaza Strip as of early July. The Gaza Health Ministry, corroborated by Anadolu Agency, reported over 1,092 Palestinian deaths and 3,507 wounded since the truce began on October 10, 2025.

Hamas has reportedly rejected disarmament proposals, citing Israel's continued hostilities and restrictions on humanitarian aid as breaches of its ceasefire obligations. Humanitarian conditions have deteriorated even during the nominal ceasefire, with over 90% of the Strip reportedly destroyed.

articles.headline: Japan Bankruptcies Surge to All-Time High Amidst Falling Yen
body: Japan is experiencing a surge in bankruptcies, reaching an all-time high, primarily attributed to the falling value of the yen.
This economic challenge highlights the pressures on Japanese businesses in the current global financial climate, impacting their ability to manage costs and maintain profitability.

articles.headline: U.S. Trade Deficit Widens as AI Investment Drives Import Boom
body: The U.S. trade deficit widened by 42.2% in May to $77.6 billion, as imports reached a 14-month high and capital-goods imports hit a record $128 billion.
This increase was significantly driven by heavy investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure, leading to a surge in imports of semiconductors and computer accessories.
Companies also imported goods in anticipation of potential tariffs and shortages related to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, further contributing to the widening deficit.

articles.headline: Russia Bans Diesel Exports Amid Global Energy Market Volatility
body: Russia has announced a ban on diesel exports, a decision that is likely to further impact global energy markets already experiencing significant volatility.

This move by a major energy producer could lead to increased prices and supply concerns for countries reliant on Russian diesel. The ban comes amidst ongoing geopolitical tensions and efforts by various nations to secure their energy supplies.

articles.headline: U.S. and Iran Trade Strikes, Escalating Regional Conflict
body: The United States and Iran have engaged in their largest exchange of attacks since the June 17 memorandum, with Iran striking U.S.-aligned Gulf states and Washington hitting numerous Iranian targets.
This renewed exchange of strikes is widening the conflict from a maritime contest into a regional infrastructure crisis, with Iran also alleging damage near the Bushehr nuclear complex.

Despite President Trump's declaration that the ceasefire was 'over' after attacks on shipping, technical negotiations and mediation efforts have not entirely ceased, indicating a complex interplay of political rhetoric, operational escalation, and diplomatic engagement.

articles.headline: Oil Tanker Traffic Near Standstill in Strait of Hormuz Amid Escalated Tensions
body: Oil tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz was near a standstill by July 9, with only two tankers observed transiting and some vessels operating without normal tracking signals.
Insurers have paused or reconsidered coverage after recent attacks, demonstrating how quickly market actors can impose a de facto closure even when belligerents stop short of declaring one.

This collapse in tanker traffic highlights that legal access to Hormuz is meaningless without commercial confidence, as Iran has restored coercive leverage by proving that commercial shipping can be selectively punished.

articles.headline: Philippines Rejects Chinese Territorial Claims Over Batanes Province
body: The Philippine defense secretary has rejected assertions by Chinese scholars that the northern Philippine province of Batanes belongs to China.
This comes as China extends its gray-zone enforcement to Taiwan's eastern approaches, launching a new coast-guard patrol east of Taiwan, the second such operation in roughly a month.
Taipei has tracked the vessels and rejected Beijing's claim to law-enforcement authority, indicating growing tensions over territorial claims in the region.

articles.headline: Russia Launches Massed Strikes on Kyiv Ahead of NATO Summit
body: Russia launched a major missile-and-drone attack on Kyiv and other targets on the eve of the NATO summit in Ankara, demonstrating that Western political coordination has not reduced its offensive capacity.
This renewed aggression comes as the EU continues to impose sanctions on Russia, with recent measures targeting its military-industrial complex in response to deadly drone attacks on Ukraine.
The ongoing conflict and Russia's ability to conduct massed strikes underscore the persistent security challenges in Eastern Europe and the need for continued international support for Ukraine.

articles.headline: Clashes Intensify in Northern Mali as Russia Deepens Military Role
body: Clashes have intensified in the northern Malian town of Anefis between the Malian Army and the Azawad Liberation Front, even as Russia deepens its military role in the Sahel region.

Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso have pledged stronger military and military-technical cooperation with Moscow, including support from Russia's Africa Corps, after breaking with France and other Western partners.
The ongoing conflict and the increased Russian presence are seen as a test of Moscow's security model in the region, with jihadist groups continuing to gain ground despite efforts to suppress them.

articles.headline: U.S. to License Ukraine for Patriot System Production, Shifting Wartime Strategy
body: President Trump has announced that the United States will license Ukraine to produce Patriot air-defense systems, a significant reversal of longstanding resistance to foreign manufacturing of the system.

This decision marks a strategic shift from emergency aid toward indigenous wartime production, addressing Ukraine's recurring Russian missile and drone attacks and the constraints of allied inventories and U.S. manufacturing capacity.
The move is considered strategically more important than another finite transfer of interceptors, as it tackles the underlying production problem faced by Ukraine in its conflict with Russia.

body: OFAC published a new action on July 10, 2026: "Iran-related and Counter Terrorism Designations; Issuance of Iran-related General License". Full details are available at the official OFAC website.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related and Counter-Terrorism Designations, Issues General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related and counter-terrorism designations on July 10, 2026. These actions are part of the U.S. government's ongoing strategy to disrupt Iran's ability to fund and support terrorist organizations and its nuclear proliferation activities.

Alongside these designations, OFAC issued a new Iran-related General License. This license typically authorizes specific transactions or activities that would otherwise be prohibited under the sanctions regime, often to facilitate humanitarian aid or other permissible engagements.

The designations aim to further isolate individuals and entities that contribute to Iran's destabilizing actions, while the General License seeks to ensure that legitimate activities are not unduly hampered by the broad scope of the sanctions.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New General License for Democratic Republic of the Congo
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a new General License related to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) on July 10, 2026. This action aims to facilitate certain transactions or activities that would otherwise be prohibited under existing sanctions programs targeting the DRC.

General Licenses are often issued to allow for humanitarian aid, specific commercial activities, or other transactions deemed to be in the U.S. national interest, without undermining the broader sanctions objectives. This new license is expected to provide clarity and flexibility for certain operations in the DRC.

Entities and individuals involved in activities within the DRC should thoroughly review the terms and conditions of this new General License to ensure their operations align with U.S. sanctions policy and to avoid potential violations.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Key Iranian Financier and Network, Issues Iran-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related and counter-terrorism designations on July 10, 2026, targeting a key Iranian financier and his global network of assets. This action aims to disrupt financial infrastructure used to enrich Iranian regime elites and conceal illicit financial activity.

OFAC sanctioned Ali Ansari, who is alleged to oversee a sprawling global network of assets benefiting Iran's leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, and other regime elites through large-scale embezzlement. Ansari's Saint Kitts and Nevis-based holding company, Smart Global Limited, was also designated for its role in these activities.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued Iran General License Y, authorizing the wind down of transactions involving Smart Global Limited. This action follows renewed attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and the Trump administration's decision to revoke a temporary license authorizing the sale of Iranian oil.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Steptoe / ABA Banking Journal / Ceasefire Collapse Restores U.S. Leverage as Sanctions, Strikes Weaken Iran's Hand

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Democratic Republic of the Congo-related General License
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued a new General License related to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). While specific details of the license were not immediately available in the announcement, such general licenses typically authorize certain transactions or activities that would otherwise be prohibited under existing sanctions programs.

This action follows previous OFAC measures concerning the DRC, which have included sanctions against individuals and entities involved in human rights abuses and corruption. The issuance of a general license often aims to facilitate legitimate humanitarian aid, trade, or other activities while maintaining pressure on sanctioned actors.
The UK also recently added eight new designations under the Democratic Republic of the Congo sanctions regime on July 17, 2026, indicating continued international focus on the region.

articles.headline: Treasury Targets Key Supreme Leader Financier and Iran's Shadow Exchange Houses
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced sanctions on July 10, 2026, targeting Iranian financier Ali Ansari and his global network of assets. Ansari is accused of enriching Iranian regime elites, including individuals connected to the Supreme Leader's office, through large-scale embezzlement and overseas investments.

OFAC also targeted key Iranian exchange houses and related shell companies in Hong Kong and the United Arab Emirates, which were used to move billions of dollars on behalf of sanctioned Iranian banks and conceal the regime's illicit financial activity. This action, taken under Executive Orders 13902, 13876, and 13224, builds on previous efforts to disrupt Iran's shadow banking and sanctions-evasion networks.
In connection with these designations, OFAC issued Iran General License Y, authorizing the wind down of transactions involving Smart Global Limited.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.region: Democratic Republic of the Congo, Rwanda
articles.headline: OFAC Issues General License for Humanitarian Aid to DRC and Rwanda
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued Democratic Republic of the Congo-related General License 2, titled 'Authorizing Transactions Related to Agricultural Commodities, Medicine, Medical Devices, Replacement Parts and Components, Software Updates, or Clinical Trials.' This license aims to address significant humanitarian challenges in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), including an Ebola outbreak.

General License 2 expands upon existing authorizations by permitting U.S. persons to engage in transactions and activities ordinarily incident and necessary to the export or reexport of agricultural commodities, medicine, medical devices, and related items to the DRC or Rwanda. It also covers activities for the prevention, diagnosis, or treatment of diseases and the conduct of clinical trials and medical research in these countries.

The license has no expiration date and may authorize certain transactions involving Specially Designated Nationals (SDNs) designated under the DRC Sanctions Regulations, provided those SDNs are not also designated under other sanctions programs. This initiative supports humanitarian and healthcare-related trade in the region.

body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced additional Iran-related and counter-terrorism designations on July 10, 2026. These actions are part of the ongoing U.S. effort to target networks supporting Iran's illicit activities and its proxies.

articles.headline: Crude Oil Prices Decline in June, Outlook Clouded by Hormuz Escalation
body: Benchmark crude oil prices continued their downward slide in June, with North Sea Dated prices plunging by $31/bbl to $68/bbl by early July, their lowest since January.
This decline was attributed to an interim ceasefire agreement between the United States and Iran, which underpinned a strong recovery in oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz.
However, an escalation in hostilities on July 7-8 has clouded the outlook, with North Sea Dated last trading at $77/bbl, potentially upending forecasts of a market surplus next year.

articles.headline: China Expands Anti-Sanctions Toolkit, Raising Risks for Foreign Firms
body: China is actively expanding its counter-sanctions toolkit through new regulations and enforcement actions, increasing the compliance risks for multinational companies operating in the country.

Since March 2026, Beijing has enacted two new regulations: the 'Counter-Extraterritorial Jurisdiction Regulation' and the 'Supply Chain Regulation.' These measures broaden restrictions on foreign legal actions with extraterritorial effect in China and limit information gathering on Chinese supply chains.

In May 2026, the Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) issued its first-ever blocking order under the 2021 Blocking Rules, prohibiting the implementation of U.S. Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) designations against five Chinese 'teapot refineries' by any parties in China. This creates a compliance dilemma for foreign firms caught between conflicting legal obligations.

articles.headline: Global Oil Supply Rebounds Amid Hormuz Recovery, But Escalation Clouds Outlook
body: Global oil supply rebounded sharply by 4.1 million barrels per day (mb/d) in June, reaching 98.8 mb/d, driven by a recovery in oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz following an interim ceasefire agreement between the United States and Iran. This led to benchmark crude oil prices, such as North Sea Dated, plunging to $68/bbl by early July.

However, an escalation in hostilities between the U.S. and Iran on July 7-8, including renewed attacks and the U.S. reimposing a naval blockade, has clouded the market outlook. North Sea Dated prices subsequently rose to $77/bbl, and the International Energy Agency (IEA) warns that this escalation could upend the forecast of a market surplus next year.

Despite the June rebound, world oil output remains approximately 9.4 mb/d below pre-war levels. While a recovery in world oil demand is underway, with consumption expected to rise seasonally, the ongoing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East pose a significant risk to supply stability and price forecasts for 2026 and 2027.

articles.headline: Federal Reserve Maintains Benchmark Interest Rate, Signals Hawkish Stance
body: The Federal Reserve kept its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 3.50%–3.75% following the June Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting. This decision reflects the central bank's continued efforts to manage inflation while navigating complex economic conditions.

New Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, who took office in May 2026, signaled a shift in monetary policy by removing traditional forward guidance and emphasizing a stronger data-dependent framework. Half of the FOMC committee members reportedly expect a rate hike later this year, indicating a hawkish outlook.

This shift has led to a selloff in U.S. equities, a boost to the U.S. dollar, and increased pressure on gold prices, reinforcing expectations for potentially higher interest rates before the end of 2026.

articles.headline: Global Oil Supply Rebounds in June, But Hormuz Tensions Cloud Outlook
body: Global oil supply saw a significant rebound of 4.1 million barrels per day (mb/d) in June, reaching 98.8 mb/d, driven by a recovery in Gulf production and the resumption of flows through the Strait of Hormuz.
Benchmark crude oil prices, such as North Sea Dated, had plunged to $68/bbl by early July, their lowest since January, due to an interim ceasefire agreement between the U.S. and Iran.

However, an escalation in hostilities between the U.S. and Iran on July 7-8 has clouded the outlook, with North Sea Dated prices subsequently trading at $77/bbl. This renewed tension could upend forecasts of a market surplus next year.

articles.headline: China Expands Counter-Sanctions Toolkit Amidst Rising Geopolitical Tensions
body: China is actively expanding its counter-sanctions toolkit, introducing new regulations and enforcement actions to retaliate against foreign sanctions and export controls. This development comes as Beijing, Washington, and Brussels engage in tit-for-tat punitive measures, creating a complex environment for multinational companies.

Since March, China has passed two new regulations aimed at broadening restrictions on foreign legal actions with extraterritorial effect in China and limiting information gathering on Chinese supply chains. These measures are designed to enhance China's ability to hit back at perceived threats to its supply chain security or the enforcement of sanctions with 'improper extraterritorial jurisdiction.'

In May 2026, the Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) issued its first-ever blocking order under the 2021 Blocking Rules, prohibiting the implementation of U.S. Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) designations against five Chinese 'teapot refineries.' This tailored approach indicates China's focus on high-stakes international concerns and its willingness to use regulatory scrutiny as a lever to control strategically important sectors.

articles.headline: China Imposes Temporary Helium Export Ban Amid Supply Disruptions
body: China temporarily halted helium exports on July 10, a move reportedly triggered by disruptions to supplies from Qatar, which accounts for approximately one-third of global production.
The disruption is linked to the ongoing conflict in Iran, which has impacted shipping and resource availability in the region.
Helium is a critical component for several strategic industries, including semiconductor fabrication and medical imaging, raising concerns about potential impacts on these sectors.

Helium is a critical component for semiconductor fabrication, medical imaging, and other strategic industries. This ban highlights how regional conflicts can trigger defensive resource nationalism in unrelated strategic sectors.

articles.headline: U.S. Tariffs and Middle East Conflict Impact Global Economic Activity
body: Global economic activity experienced subdued growth in the first half of 2026, largely due to headwinds from the ongoing Middle East conflict and U.S. tariffs. These factors have contributed to increased foreign headline inflation, particularly in response to the sharp rise in energy and other commodity prices.

The conflict in the Middle East has severely constrained shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical oil passageway, leading to volatile oil prices. While AI-related investment has partially offset these headwinds, the broader impact on international trade and economic stability remains a concern.

The Federal Reserve's Monetary Policy Report for July 2026 highlights that core goods price inflation has notably increased over 2025 and continued into early 2026, with tariffs contributing to this upturn in consumer goods prices.

articles.headline: US Senators and Administration Agree to Advance Tougher Russia Sanctions Bill
body: A bipartisan group of U.S. senators announced on July 10, 2026, that they have reached an agreement with the Trump administration to advance long-delayed legislation aimed at imposing tougher economic penalties on Russia and countries supporting Moscow's war economy.

The 'Sanctioning Russia Act' is intended to give President Donald Trump a powerful new tool to pressure Russian President Vladimir Putin and punish countries helping Russia evade Western sanctions. The bill specifically targets five countries that have been circumventing sanctions by purchasing Russian energy for resale.

While the legislation aims to cut revenues from Russian energy sales, concerns have been raised by Democratic lawmakers regarding potential tariffs in the bill, which could grant President Trump new powers to impose trade measures on countries like India, Japan, and some EU nations. The bill also seeks to expand individual and sectoral restrictions, including a ban on U.S. investment in Russia's energy industry and restrictions on exports of U.S. energy resources to Russia.
