body: A bipartisan group of U.S. senators announced on July 10, 2026, that they have reached an agreement with the Trump administration to advance long-delayed legislation aimed at imposing tougher economic penalties on Russia and countries supporting Moscow's war economy.

The legislation, known as the Sanctioning Russia Act, is expected to provide the United States with a powerful new tool to pressure the Kremlin. It aims to punish countries helping Russia evade Western sanctions and create leverage for negotiations.

Concerns have been raised by Democratic lawmakers regarding potential tariffs within the bill, which they fear could grant President Trump new powers to impose trade measures on countries like India, Japan, and some EU members.

articles.headline: War in Ukraine Persists Amid Renewed Military Activity and Drone Strikes
body: The war frontlines in Ukraine continue to shift, with Kyiv making modest territorial gains driven by increased drone strikes targeting Russian supply lines and a rapid expansion in domestic defense production.
Ukraine is expected to continue conducting long-range drone strikes against critical infrastructure deeper inside Russian territory, signaling an expansion of the operational theater.
Near-term scenarios for the conflict are anticipated to oscillate between a managed low-intensity conflict and a persistent high-intensity conflict.

articles.headline: China Expands Anti-Sanctions Toolkit, Raising Risks for Foreign Firms
body: China is actively expanding its legal framework to counter foreign sanctions and export controls, increasing risks for multinational companies operating in the region. Since March, Beijing has enacted two new regulations that enhance its ability to retaliate against foreign entities perceived to have threatened its supply chain security or enforced sanctions with 'improper extraterritorial jurisdiction'.

A third law, currently in draft form, would allow Chinese prosecutors to pursue cases against foreign organizations and individuals whose 'unlawful acts harm the country's national interests or social public interest'. This move is part of a broader effort to strengthen China's public interest litigation law.

Firms are expressing concern about navigating conflicting legal obligations, as complying with U.S. or EU sanctions could expose them to fines, visa cancellations, asset freezes, investment restrictions, and curbs on imports or exports from China under Beijing's countermeasures.

articles.headline: Federal Regulators Propose New BSA/Sanctions Standards for Payment Stablecoin Issuers
body: Federal banking regulators, including the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), and FinCEN have jointly proposed new customer identification and BSA/sanctions compliance standards for permitted payment stablecoin issuers (PPSIs). These proposals aim to build out the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and sanctions compliance framework for this emerging financial sector.

The proposed rules, under the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins Act (GENIUS Act), would treat PPSIs as financial institutions under the BSA and require them to maintain effective customer identification programs (CIPs). This includes procedures for checking customers against government lists of known or suspected terrorists and terrorist organizations.

The OCC, in coordination with FinCEN and OFAC, also announced a proposed rulemaking to amend its March 2, 2026, proposed rule, implementing the GENIUS Act's requirement for the OCC to issue BSA and sanctions compliance standards for PPSIs under its jurisdiction.

articles.headline: OCC Proposes BSA/Sanctions Compliance Standards for Payment Stablecoin Issuers
body: The OCC, in coordination with FinCEN and OFAC, announced a proposed rulemaking on July 10, 2026, to amend its March 2, 2026, proposed rule.
This proposal aims to implement the GENIUS Act's requirement for the OCC to issue BSA and sanctions compliance standards for permitted payment stablecoin issuers (PPSIs) under its jurisdiction.
Comments on the OCC Compliance Standards Proposal are due by July 24, 2026, with the OCC specifically seeking input on its interaction with existing BSA and sanctions regimes.

articles.headline: Federal Regulators Propose New AML/CFT Standards for Payment Stablecoin Issuers
body: Federal banking regulators and FinCEN released two additional notices of proposed rulemaking on June 22, 2026, which would further build out Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and anti-money laundering/countering the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) compliance standards for payment stablecoin issuers (PPSIs).

The proposed rule would amend the Board's regulations prescribing AML/CFT program requirements for banks supervised by the Board, aligning them with the rules proposed by FinCEN and other agencies under the BSA on April 10, 2026.

A new subpart R to 12 C.F.R. Part 19 would establish a supervision and enforcement framework for PPSI AML/CFT programs, including a FinCEN–OCC consultation process for enforcement or significant supervisory actions. This initiative aims to address the growing complexity of international AML compliance in the digital asset space.

articles.headline: OCC Proposes BSA and Sanctions Compliance Standards for Payment Stablecoin Issuers
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), in coordination with FinCEN and Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), announced a proposed rulemaking on July 10, 2026. This proposal aims to amend its March 2, 2026, proposed rule to implement the GENIUS Act's requirement for the OCC to issue Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and sanctions compliance standards for permitted payment stablecoin issuers (PPSIs) under its jurisdiction.

The OCC Compliance Standards Proposal would add a new paragraph to proposed Part 15, cross-referencing obligations set out in the broader Stablecoin Proposal announced on April 8, and making corresponding changes to 12 C.F.R. Part 4 and Part 19.

A new subpart R to 12 C.F.R. Part 19 would establish a supervision and enforcement framework for PPSI AML/CFT programs, including a FinCEN–OCC consultation process for enforcement or significant supervisory actions. Comments on the OCC Compliance Standards Proposal are due by July 24, 2026.

articles.headline: Federal Regulators Propose New BSA/Sanctions Compliance Standards for Payment Stablecoin Issuers
body: Federal banking regulators, including the OCC, in coordination with FinCEN and OFAC, announced proposed rulemakings on June 22, 2026, to establish new Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and sanctions compliance standards for permitted payment stablecoin issuers (PPSIs).

These proposals aim to integrate PPSIs into the existing BSA and sanctions compliance framework, requiring them to maintain effective customer identification programs (CIP) and adhere to robust AML/CFT and sanctions compliance standards. This move reflects the increasing regulatory focus on digital assets and their potential for illicit finance.

articles.headline: OCC Appoints Receiver for Kentland Federal Savings and Loan Association
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced on July 10, 2026, that it has appointed a receiver for Kentland Federal Savings and Loan Association, located in Kentland, Indiana. This action typically occurs when a financial institution is deemed to be in an unsafe or unsound condition, or has violated laws or regulations.

The appointment of a receiver signifies a significant regulatory intervention aimed at resolving the institution's issues and protecting depositors. Further details regarding the specific reasons for the receivership were not immediately available in the initial announcement.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

articles.headline: OCC Seeks Comments on Proposed Stablecoin Compliance Standards
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) is seeking comments on its proposed compliance standards for payment stablecoin issuers, with comments due by July 24, 2026. This proposal amends the OCC's March 2, 2026, proposed rule by adding a new paragraph to proposed Part 15, cross-referencing obligations from the Stablecoin Proposal announced on April 8.

The OCC has specifically requested feedback on how proposed Part 15 would interact with its existing BSA and sanctions regimes, additional reserve-asset safeguards against fraud, and redemption protections for stablecoin holders.

The proposal also outlines a supervision and enforcement framework for payment stablecoin issuer AML/CFT programs, including a FinCEN–OCC consultation process for enforcement or significant supervisory actions.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency / Freshfields

articles.headline: OCC Proposes New BSA/Sanctions Compliance Standards for Payment Stablecoin Issuers
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), in coordination with FinCEN and OFAC, has announced a proposed rulemaking to amend its March 2, 2026, proposed rule. This amendment aims to implement the GENIUS Act's requirement for the OCC to issue BSA and sanctions compliance standards for Payment Stablecoin Issuers (PPSIs) under its jurisdiction.

The OCC Compliance Standards Proposal would establish a supervision and enforcement framework for PPSI AML/CFT programs, including a FinCEN–OCC consultation process for enforcement actions. Comments on this proposal are due by July 24, 2026.

The OCC has specifically requested feedback on how the proposed Part 15 would interact with existing BSA and sanctions regimes, additional reserve-asset safeguards, redemption protections for stablecoin holders, and alignment with parallel FDIC rules.

articles.headline: OCC Seeks Comments on Proposed AML/CFT Compliance Standards for Payment Stablecoin Issuers
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) is seeking comments on its proposed compliance standards for payment stablecoin issuers (PPSIs), which would amend the OCC's March 2, 2026 proposed rule. These new standards aim to establish a supervision and enforcement framework for PPSI anti-money laundering/countering the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) programs.

The proposal includes a FinCEN–OCC consultation process for AML/CFT enforcement or significant supervisory actions. An issuer with an effective AML/CFT program would generally not be subject to enforcement unless there is a 'significant or systemic failure to implement' that program.

Comments on the OCC Compliance Standards Proposal are due by July 24, 2026. The OCC has specifically requested feedback on how the proposed Part 15 would interact with existing BSA and sanctions regimes, additional reserve-asset safeguards, redemption protections, and alignment with parallel rules from the FDIC.

articles.headline: BIS Amends EAR to Provide Enhanced Favorable Treatment for UAE
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has issued a final rule amending the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Effective July 10, 2026, the UAE has been removed from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and added to Country Group A:5, which offers the most favorable license exception treatment under the EAR.

This change expands the availability of license exceptions, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA), for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities. This will facilitate the export, reexport, or transfer of military items, certain commercial satellites and spacecraft, and dual-use items relevant to sectors like oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. Additionally, the UAE Government and approved commercial entities will have license-free access to advanced computing items, including artificial intelligence chips and servers.

The move is consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework and acknowledges the UAE's role in advancing U.S. strategic interests, particularly in countering malign activities of Iran and its proxies.
articles.source: Federal Register / Sandler, Travis & Rosenberg, P.A.

articles.headline: BIS Upgrades UAE to Country Group A, Easing Export Controls
body: On July 10, 2026, the U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued a final rule amending the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to upgrade the United Arab Emirates (UAE) from Country Group D to Country Group A:5.

This change significantly eases export controls for the UAE, particularly for advanced computing and defense items. Exporters no longer need a license to ship items to the UAE with knowledge that they will be used in certain missile, rocket, or unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) projects, removing a diligence trigger that previously restricted aerospace transactions.

Additionally, U.S. persons may now provide certain support, such as servicing, financing, and shipping, to covered missile and UAV activities in the UAE without the specific authorization previously required. This move reflects a strategic shift in U.S. export policy towards the UAE.
articles.source: Akin Gump / The National Law Review

articles.headline: BIS Eases Export Controls for UAE, Including for Advanced Chips
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced on July 10, 2026, a significant upgrade to the status of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). This change recognizes the UAE's status as a U.S. Major Defense Partner and its support in advancing U.S. national security interests, including Operation Epic Fury.

The final rule removes the UAE from EAR Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adds it to Country Group A:5, making the country eligible for license-free exports under License Exception Strategic Trade Authorization (STA). This will eliminate restrictions on support for the UAE's unmanned aerial vehicle programs and ease requirements for certain commercial satellites, spacecraft, and dual-use items.

Crucially, the rule also allows the UAE government and certain Emirati companies to buy advanced American chips license-free, including AI chips and servers. This change is intended to help implement the U.S.-UAE AI chip deal signed in May 2025 and is seen as a recognition of the UAE's role in advancing U.S. national security interests.
articles.source: Bureau of Industry and Security / Export Compliance Daily / Sandler, Travis & Rosenberg, P.A.

This move recognizes the UAE's status as a U.S. Major Defense Partner and its support in advancing U.S. national security interests.

This change reclassifies the UAE to EAR Country Group A:5 and removes it from Country Groups D:3 and D:4.

This upgrade provides the UAE government and approved commercial entities with eligibility for license-free exports, reexports, and in-country transfers under License Exception STA (Strategic Trade Authorization) for BIS-controlled military items, certain commercial satellites and spacecraft, and dual-use items. It also eliminates restrictions on support for the UAE's unmanned aerial vehicle programs.

Furthermore, the UAE government and certain companies are now approved to receive advanced computing items, including artificial intelligence chips and servers, license-free. This move aims to facilitate increased trade in advanced computing and defense items with the UAE.

This includes BIS-controlled military items, certain commercial satellites and spacecraft, and dual-use items relevant to semiconductor packaging, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation.

articles.source: U.S. Department of Commerce BIS / Steptoe

articles.headline: BIS Grants UAE Enhanced Favorable Treatment Under Export Administration Regulations
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued a final rule on July 10, 2026, significantly upgrading the status of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). This change removes the UAE from Country Groups D:3 (Chemical & Biological) and D:4 (Missile Technology) and adds it to Country Group A:5, a designation typically reserved for close U.S. allies.

This enhanced favorable treatment expands the availability of several EAR license exceptions for exports, reexports, and transfers to eligible UAE recipients, including License Exception Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for certain military and dual-use items. The move recognizes the UAE's status as a Major Defense Partner and its commitment to effective export controls.

BIS also stated a favorable licensing review policy for applications to export semiconductors and servers to UAE-headquartered companies. However, some benefits for private-sector companies in advanced technology sectors may still depend on obtaining BIS approval through a newly established advisory opinion process.

articles.headline: BIS Closes Export Controls Loophole for Foreign-Owned Semiconductor Fabs in China
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced on July 10, 2026, that it has closed a loophole that previously allowed some foreign companies to export semiconductor manufacturing equipment and technology to China without a license.

This action puts these foreign-owned semiconductor fabrication facilities in China on par with their competitors, requiring them to obtain licenses for such exports. The move is part of a broader strategy to strengthen national security and control the flow of critical technologies.

The loophole, which was a Biden-era policy, had allowed a handful of foreign companies to operate with fewer restrictions, and its closure reflects the Trump administration's focus on tightening export controls related to semiconductors and China.

articles.headline: BIS Grants UAE Enhanced Favorable Treatment Under EAR
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has issued a final rule providing enhanced favorable treatment to the United Arab Emirates (UAE) under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). This change recognizes the UAE's status as a U.S. Major Defense Partner and its commitment to effective export controls.

The Final Rule removes the UAE from Country Groups D:3 (Chemical & Biological) and D:4 (Missile Technology) and adds it to Country Group A:5. This effectively expands the license exceptions available for exports, reexports, and in-country transfers to or within the UAE, including License Exceptions TMP, GOV, TSU, AVS, and APR.

The addition of the UAE to Country Group A:5 also makes License Exception STA available for eligible items, provided the ultimate consignee and all end users are approved entities listed in the newly added Supplement No. 8 to Part 740 of the EAR. This move aims to strengthen commercial ties and advance U.S. national security interests with the UAE.

articles.headline: Department of Commerce Eases Export Controls for UAE
body: The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced on July 10, 2026, that it will significantly upgrade the status of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Under the new rule, the UAE will be removed from EAR Country Groups D:3 and D:4. This change will eliminate restrictions on support for the UAE's unmanned aerial systems, among other things, streamlining export processes for certain items to the country.

Under Secretary for Industry and Security Jeffrey Kessler stated that export controls should evolve with changes in technology while protecting national security. This deregulatory action aims to alleviate compliance burdens while maintaining national security interests.

articles.headline: BIS Expands Entity List to Cover Affiliates of Listed Entities
body: The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued a new rule on July 10, 2026, that significantly strengthens the export control regime by closing a loophole in restricted party lists. This rule expands the Entity List to automatically cover any entity that is at least 50 percent owned by one or more entities already on the Entity List or the Military End-User (MEU) List.

Previously, the Entity List and MEU List only included specifically named entities, even if they were majority-owned by a listed company. This new 'Affiliates Rule' aims to prevent evasion of export controls through corporate structures and requires exporters to conduct additional due diligence for significant minority ownership by a listed company.

This change underscores BIS's commitment to preventing sensitive U.S. technologies from reaching unauthorized end-users and highlights the increasing scrutiny on complex ownership structures in export compliance.

articles.headline: Department of Commerce Eases Export Controls for United Arab Emirates
body: The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced on July 10, 2026, a significant upgrade to the status of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). This deregulatory action recognizes the UAE's status as a U.S. Major Defense Partner and its support in advancing U.S. national security interests.

BIS will remove the UAE from EAR Country Groups D:3 and D:4, which will eliminate restrictions on support for the UAE's unmanned aerial systems, among other things. This change makes additional provisions of several license exceptions available for items controlled for Chemical/Biological (CB) and Missile Technology (MT) reasons.

The final rule, published on July 14, 2026, opens new paths for UAE-related exports, eases some export licensing requirements, and reduces certain mandatory Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS) filing obligations.
articles.source: Bureau of Industry and Security / Export Compliance Daily

articles.headline: Department of Commerce Eases Export Controls for UAE, Designates as Major Defense Partner

articles.headline: OFAC and OFSI Publish Joint Comparative Guidance on U.S. and UK Sanctions Regimes
body: On June 23, 2026, the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) and His Majesty's Treasury's Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation (OFSI) jointly published 'U.S. and UK Economic Sanctions Authorities: A Comparative Overview.' This guidance aims to help companies better understand their respective sanctions obligations under both regimes.

The document consolidates key similarities and differences between the U.S. and UK sanctions frameworks, covering topics such as types of sanctions lists, licensing approaches, recordkeeping and reporting responsibilities, the standard for determining ownership or control by a sanctions target, and enforcement.

This joint publication underscores the increasing cross-border and multijurisdictional nature of sanctions enforcement and highlights the need for global companies to implement appropriate compliance controls to address obligations under multiple regulatory regimes.

articles.headline: Trump Administration Opts Against USMCA Renewal, Initiating Decade-Long Wind-Down
body: The Trump Administration has decided not to renew its trilateral trade pact with Canada and Mexico, the USMCA, opting instead for annual reviews of the treaty. This decision initiates a decade-long process to wind down the 32-year-old North American free trade zone.
The move comes as the three countries are expected to negotiate over proposed changes to the agreement.
The U.S. Trade Representative, Jamieson Greer, had previously indicated that due to the complexity of unresolved disputes, negotiations were likely to extend beyond the July 1 deadline.

articles.headline: OCC Encourages Participation in FinCEN's 314(b) Information Sharing Program
body: On July 9, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), along with the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), issued guidance encouraging financial institutions to participate in the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network's (FinCEN) Section 314(b) program. This program allows financial institutions to share information with one another in the fight against money laundering, fraud, and financial crime.

The agencies underscored the program's role in strengthening institutions' ability to identify criminal activity and protect clients in real time, especially in light of FinCEN's landmark update to the operational guidance on Section 314(b) issued on June 12, 2026.

This encouragement highlights the OCC's commitment to fostering collaboration among financial institutions to enhance anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing efforts, recognizing the growing complexity of international AML compliance.

articles.headline: White House Initiates Section 232 Review of Commercial Aircraft and Jet Engine Imports
body: The White House has initiated a Section 232 review of commercial aircraft, jet engines, and related parts, citing concerns about risks from foreign supply chain dependence, counterfeit components, and insufficient domestic manufacturing capacity. This investigation, under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, aims to determine the effects of these imports on national security.

This action follows a similar Section 232 invocation in January 2026 concerning imports of semiconductors and semiconductor manufacturing equipment. The reviews highlight the administration's focus on securing critical supply chains and reducing reliance on foreign sources for strategically important industries.

Interested parties are invited to submit written comments, data, and analyses to the Department of Commerce as part of this investigation, which could lead to recommendations for tariffs or other trade restrictions.

articles.headline: DOJ Declines to Prosecute Bosch Under New Self-Disclosure Policy, BIS Imposes Civil Penalty
body: On June 17, 2026, the Department of Justice's National Security Division (NSD) announced its first declination to prosecute Bosch under its 2026 Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy, imposing disgorgement of $11,430,098.00.
Concurrently, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced a parallel civil administrative settlement with Bosch, imposing $36,184,680 in penalties.

The resolution stems from two Bosch German subsidiaries exporting approximately $72.4 million worth of foreign-produced sensors and automotive software to Huawei Technologies and its affiliates between 2020 and 2024 without required U.S. export licenses under the Foreign Direct Product Rule (FDPR).

articles.headline: UN Security Council Updates ISIL (Da'esh) & Al-Qaida Sanctions List
body: On July 8, 2026, the United Nations Security Council Committee established pursuant to resolution 1533 (2004) updated its ISIL (Da'esh) & Al-Qaida Sanctions List. This list, which currently contains the names of 249 individuals and 88 entities, is subject to individual targeted sanctions including asset freezes, travel bans, and arms embargoes.

The updates to the sanctions list are a continuous effort by the Security Council to counter the global threat posed by ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaida and their affiliates. These revisions ensure that the list remains current and reflects the evolving landscape of terrorist organizations.
Member States are obligated to implement these sanctions against designated individuals, groups, undertakings, and entities to disrupt their ability to plan, finance, and carry out terrorist acts.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Russia-Related General License and Issues FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Russia-related General License and updated Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on July 8, 2026. This amendment and guidance are part of the ongoing U.S. response to Russia's actions in Ukraine and its broader destabilizing activities.

The amended General License likely modifies existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Russia, potentially adjusting the scope of permissible activities or clarifying compliance requirements. The accompanying FAQs provide crucial interpretive guidance for businesses and individuals navigating the complex Russian sanctions regime.
These updates reflect the dynamic nature of sanctions policy, where adjustments are made to address evolving geopolitical circumstances and to ensure the effectiveness and clarity of the measures.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Russia-Related General License and FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Russia-related General License and updated Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs). This action reflects ongoing adjustments to the U.S. sanctions regime targeting Russia, likely in response to evolving geopolitical circumstances and practical implementation challenges.

Amended General Licenses often modify the scope of previously authorized activities, either expanding or narrowing them, to better align with policy goals. The updated FAQs provide crucial clarifications and interpretations for businesses and individuals navigating the complexities of Russia sanctions.

These changes are important for ensuring that U.S. persons and entities remain compliant with the dynamic sanctions landscape related to Russia, particularly in light of the ongoing conflict in Ukraine.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Russia-Related General License 13R and FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued Russia-related General License 13R on July 8, 2026, authorizing certain administrative transactions prohibited by Directive 4 under Executive Order 14024.

This amended General License effectively extends the authorization of Russia-related GL 13 by three months, from its previous expiration date of July 9, 2026, to October 9, 2026. Additionally, OFAC amended two associated Russia-related Frequently Asked Questions, FAQs 999 and 1118, clarifying that U.S. persons whose divestment of assets in the Russian Federation involves an 'exit tax' should still seek a specific license.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

body: On July 8, 2026, the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued Russia-related General License 13R, 'Authorizing Certain Administrative Transactions Prohibited by Directive 4 under Executive Order 14024.'

This amended general license effectively extends the authorization for certain administrative transactions, such as payments of taxes, fees, or import duties to, and purchase or receipt of permits, licenses, registrations, certifications, or tax refunds from the Russian Central Bank, National Wealth Fund, or Ministry of Finance.

articles.headline: UN Security Council Amends ISIL (Da'esh) & Al-Qaida Sanctions List
body: The United Nations Security Council Committee pursuant to resolutions 1267 (1999), 1989 (2011) and 2253 (2015) concerning ISIL (Da'esh), Al-Qaida and associated individuals, groups, undertakings and entities, today enacted amendments to one entry on its ISIL (Da'esh) & Al-Qaida Sanctions List.

These amendments involve specific changes to an existing listing, which is subject to an assets freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo as set out in Security Council resolution 2734 (2024). The Sanctions List currently includes 249 individuals and 88 entities.

The Committee regularly reviews and updates its sanctions lists to ensure they remain accurate and effective in targeting individuals and entities associated with these terrorist organizations. Further details on the specific amendment are available on the UN website.

articles.headline: UN Security Council Committee Amends One Entry on ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions List
body: The Security Council Committee pursuant to resolutions 1267 (1999), 1989 (2011), and 2253 (2015) concerning ISIL (Da'esh), Al-Qaida, and associated individuals, groups, undertakings, and entities today enacted amendments to one entry on its ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions List.

The amendments, specified with strikethrough and underline, apply to an individual subject to the assets freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo set out in paragraph 1 of Security Council resolution 2734 (2024). The individual is noted for working as a mediator in financing channels for ISIL in Central Africa and for being charged with financing a bombing in Kampala, Uganda, in 2021.
An updated list is accessible on the ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions Committee's website, and the United Nations Security Council Consolidated List is also updated following these changes.

articles.headline: U.S. Small-Cap Stocks Outperform Giants in First Half of 2026 Amid AI Boom
body: The first half of 2026 saw U.S. small-company stocks significantly outperform their larger counterparts, with the Russell 2000 index surging approximately 22%, while the S&P 500 gained 9.6% (10.2% including dividends). International stocks also returned about 15%.

This market performance was largely driven by strong earnings, particularly fueled by the artificial intelligence (AI) build-out. The 2026 AI boom has broadened beyond a few mega-caps to include memory-chip makers, equipment suppliers, and power providers.

Energy was also a strong sector, with oil prices sharply higher due to the June conflict involving the U.S., Israel, and Iran. Despite an oil shock and inflation scare, the economy grew at a 2.1% annualized pace in the first quarter, with unemployment at 4.2% in June.

articles.headline: IMF Projects Uneven Global Growth Amidst War and Technology Crosscurrents
body: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) projects global growth at 3.0 percent for 2026 and 3.4 percent for 2027, remaining broadly unchanged cumulatively from its April 2026 World Economic Outlook. The outlook is characterized by unevenness, with the impact of war weighing on energy importers and vulnerable economies, while AI-driven demand is boosting countries integrated into the global technology value chain.

Global disinflation has stalled, and while risks are more balanced than in April, downside risks from renewed conflict and financial market repricing persist. Policymakers are advised to prioritize preserving price stability, rebuilding fiscal space, and strengthening adaptability.

The IMF's assessment highlights the complex interplay of geopolitical events and technological advancements shaping the global economic landscape, necessitating careful policy responses to navigate these crosscurrents.

articles.headline: IMF Maintains Global Growth Forecast Amidst Geopolitical Crosscurrents
body: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) released its July 2026 World Economic Outlook Update, projecting global GDP growth at 3.0 percent for 2026 and 3.4 percent for 2027. These figures remain broadly unchanged from the April 2026 projections, despite ongoing geopolitical uncertainties.

The IMF highlights two major, opposing forces shaping the global economy: the lingering effects of the Middle East war and a technology-driven investment boom. While the conflict weighs on energy importers and vulnerable economies, AI-driven demand is lifting countries integrated into the global technology value chain.

Global disinflation has stalled, with inflation forecast at 4.7 percent in 2026, a reversal from the previous disinflationary path. Risks to the outlook are now considered more balanced than in April, though downside risks from renewed conflict and financial market repricing persist.
articles.source: International Monetary Fund / CNBC Africa / Quasa Media / EFG International / SABC News

articles.headline: IMF July 2026 World Economic Outlook Update: Global Growth at 3.0%, Inflation Stalls
body: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) released its July 2026 World Economic Outlook Update, projecting global growth at 3.0 percent for 2026 and 3.4 percent for 2027, largely unchanged from the April 2026 outlook.

The report highlights an uneven outlook, with the war in the Middle East weighing on energy importers and vulnerable economies, while AI-driven demand is boosting countries integrated into the global technology value chain. Global disinflation has stalled, with headline inflation projected to rise from 4.1 percent in 2025 to 4.7 percent in 2026 before easing to 3.9 percent in 2027, primarily due to higher energy and food prices.

Risks are more balanced than in April, but downside risks from renewed conflict and financial market repricing persist. Policymakers are advised to prioritize price stability, rebuild fiscal space, and strengthen adaptability.

articles.headline: IMF Maintains Global Growth Forecast at 3.0% for 2026, Citing War and Technology Crosscurrents
body: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) released its July 2026 World Economic Outlook Update, maintaining its global growth forecast at 3.0 percent for 2026 and 3.4 percent for 2027. These figures remain broadly unchanged from the April projections, despite ongoing geopolitical uncertainties.

The IMF highlights two dominant and opposing forces shaping the global economy: the lingering effects of the Middle East war and a technology-driven investment boom, particularly in artificial intelligence. The war shock is weighing on energy importers and vulnerable economies, while AI-driven demand is lifting countries integrated into the global technology value chain.

Global inflation is now projected to rise from 4.1 percent in 2025 to 4.7 percent in 2026 before easing to 3.9 percent in 2027, primarily driven by higher energy and food prices. This upward revision for 2026 suggests a stall in the steady decline of headline inflation.

articles.headline: U.S. Markets See Strong First Half Driven by AI and Small-Cap Outperformance
body: The first half of 2026 saw the S&P 500 gain 9.6% (10.2% including dividends), crossing 7,600 for the first time. However, the significant headline was the Russell 2000 index of smaller companies, which surged approximately 22%, with international stocks returning about 15%. This marks a period where small-company stocks are outperforming larger counterparts.

This market performance was primarily driven by strong earnings, particularly those linked to artificial intelligence. First-quarter S&P 500 profits grew roughly 28% year-over-year on revenue growth near 12%, with about 85% of companies beating estimates. The AI build-out has broadened its impact, benefiting memory-chip makers, equipment suppliers, and power providers beyond just a few mega-cap companies.

Energy was also a strong sector due to sharply higher oil prices following a June conflict involving the U.S., Israel, and Iran. Despite market gains, market valuation data as of June 30, 2026, continues to show U.S. markets as strongly overvalued, though some have dropped slightly due to strong earnings data offsetting market gains.

articles.headline: ADB Lowers Growth Forecast for Developing Asia and the Pacific Amid Energy Crisis
body: The Asian Development Bank (ADB) has lowered its growth forecast for developing Asia and the Pacific economies to 4.9% for 2026, down from 5.5% in 2025. This reduction of 0.2 percentage points from April projections is primarily attributed to prolonged disruptions to energy markets caused by the Middle East conflict.

The ADB's July 2026 outlook warns that renewed conflict escalation and prolonged geopolitical uncertainty remain key risks to the region, potentially tightening energy markets, raising risk premia, and intensifying inflationary and external pressures. Tighter global financial conditions and rising borrowing costs also pose additional risks.

articles.headline: U.S. Market Sees Strong First Half Driven by Earnings and AI
body: The U.S. market experienced a robust first half of 2026, with the S&P 500 gaining 9.6% (10.2% including dividends) and crossing 7,600 for the first time. Notably, the Russell 2000 index of smaller companies surged approximately 22%, outperforming larger counterparts.

This strong performance was primarily driven by corporate earnings, with first-quarter S&P 500 profits growing roughly 28% year-over-year on revenue growth near 12%. Approximately 85% of companies exceeded estimates, well above the five-year average.

Artificial intelligence continued to be the economy's largest growth engine, with the 2026 version showing broader participation from memory-chip makers, equipment suppliers, and power providers, rather than just a few mega-cap companies. The energy sector also performed strongly following a June conflict involving the U.S., Israel, and Iran, which sent oil prices sharply higher.

articles.headline: IMF Projects Steady but Uneven Global Growth Amid War and Technology Crosscurrents
body: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) released its July 2026 World Economic Outlook Update, projecting global growth at 3.0 percent for 2026 and 3.4 percent for 2027, broadly unchanged cumulatively from the April 2026 outlook.

The outlook remains uneven, with the war in the Middle East weighing on energy importers and vulnerable economies, while AI-driven demand is boosting countries integrated into the global technology value chain. Global disinflation has stalled, with headline inflation projected to rise to 4.7 percent in 2026 before declining to 3.9 percent in 2027, primarily due to persistent energy price pressures.

Risks are more balanced than in April, but downside risks from renewed conflict and financial market repricing persist. Policymakers are advised to preserve price stability, rebuild fiscal space, and strengthen adaptability.

articles.headline: IMF Reports Steady but Uneven Global Growth Amid War and Technology Crosscurrents
body: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) released its July 2026 World Economic Outlook Update, projecting global growth at 3.0 percent for 2026 and 3.4 percent for 2027, broadly unchanged cumulatively from the April 2026 outlook. The outlook remains uneven, with the war shock weighing on energy importers and vulnerable economies, while AI-driven demand lifts countries integrated into the global technology value chain.

Global disinflation has stalled, and risks are more balanced than in April, though downside risks from renewed conflict and financial market repricing persist. The IMF advises policymakers to preserve price stability, rebuild fiscal space, and strengthen adaptability.

The outlook for energy-intensive economies and those dependent on fossil fuel imports is challenging, with headwinds from higher energy prices partly offset by tailwinds from increased defense spending. In the Middle East and Central Asia, growth is projected to drop sharply to 0.7 percent in 2026 before rebounding to 6.5 percent in 2027, consistent with a longer closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.headline: Wealthy AI workers send San Francisco house prices soaring
body: The median cost of a home in the city is now $1.7m, a record high, according to the latest figures.

articles.headline: US Initiates Process to Rescind Syria's State Sponsor of Terrorism Designation
body: On July 8, 2026, the U.S. Department of State announced that President Trump had notified Congress of his administration's intent to rescind Syria's designation as a State Sponsor of Terrorism (SST). This notification initiates a 45-day period before the rescission takes effect.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated that lifting sanctions on Syria would unlock international trade and investment, provide an opportunity for Syria to rebuild, and open a new chapter for the Syrian people.

This step follows Executive Order 14312 of June 30, 2025, counterterrorism measures undertaken by the Syrian government under President Ahmed al-Sharaa, and formal assurances from President al-Sharaa that Syria will refrain from supporting acts of international terrorism in the future.

articles.headline: Ebola Outbreak Worsens in DRC, Threatening Regional Economy and Livelihoods
body: The outbreak of the deadly Bundibugyo species of Ebola in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is expanding, with the death toll surpassing 500. The UN World Health Organization (WHO) has warned about the worsening situation, as efforts to accelerate testing and identify effective treatment options continue.
A new assessment from the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) indicates that the Ebola outbreak could cost Africa $3.6 billion, push 985,000 people into poverty, and put 300,000 jobs at risk.

This humanitarian crisis is compounded by other regional challenges, including rising debt payments for African countries, which have increased by 91% since 2020, diverting funds from essential services like education and health.
articles.source: Global Issues / UN World Health Organization

articles.headline: NSF to Prohibit Funding for Collaborations with Restricted Entities
body: The U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF) has announced a forthcoming policy that will prohibit the expenditure of NSF funds on collaborations with entities on U.S. restricted parties lists. This policy aims to safeguard NSF-funded research by preventing engagement with entities deemed contrary to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.

The NSF's decision aligns with the Department of War's approach to collaborations with restricted entities, seeking to promote consistency and reduce administrative burden across government agencies. The policy is intended to be implemented in Fiscal Year 2027.

Appendix A of the announcement lists various U.S. proscribed party lists, including the Department of Commerce's Entity List and Military End-User Entities, and the Department of the Treasury's Non-SDN Chinese Military-Industrial Complex Companies.

articles.headline: CBP Issues Updated Forced Labor Enforcement Guidance, Including UFLPA
body: U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) published its Forced Labor Enforcement Operational Guidance for Importers (2026 Guidance) on June 9, 2026, replacing its previous Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA)-only guidance. This consolidated guidance addresses enforcement under the UFLPA, Section 321A of the Countering America's Adversaries Through Sanctions Act (CAATSA), and 19 U.S.C. § 1307, which covers Withhold Release Orders (WROs) and Findings.

The 2026 Guidance clarifies the procedures for detention, exclusion, seizure, review, and protest, emphasizing that importers must be prepared to quickly provide complete supply-chain evidence to prove admissibility. It introduces process maps and a comparison table to help importers identify the governing authority and response options for different forced labor actions.

CBP's UFLPA enforcement statistics for fiscal year 2026 are generally in line with FY 2025, with 17,651 shipments detained and 10,959 denied entry under the UFLPA alone from FY 2025 through April of FY 2026. Compliance with UFLPA continues to be challenged by increased transshipment of Chinese goods and a lack of supply chain transparency.
articles.source: Clark Hill / Diaz Trade Law / Clark Hill

articles.headline: NSF to Prohibit Collaborations with Restricted Entities on Funded Projects
body: The U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF) is implementing a new policy prohibiting the expenditure of NSF funds on collaborations with entities on U.S. restricted parties lists. This forthcoming policy, detailed in publication number NSF 26-022, aims to mitigate research security risks.

Appendix A of the supporting document lists various U.S. Proscribed Party Lists, including those from the Departments of War, Commerce (BIS Entity List, Military End-User Entities, Denied Persons), Treasury (OFAC Annex of Executive Order 14032, Non-SDN Chinese Military-Industrial Complex Companies), and State.

The NSF intends to implement this prohibition in Fiscal Year 2027, aligning with the Department of War's approach to collaborations with entities on U.S. restricted party lists to safeguard NSF-funded research and promote consistency.

articles.headline: President Trump Moves to Revoke Syria's State Sponsor of Terrorism Designation
body: President Donald Trump announced on July 8, 2026, his intention to remove Syria from the U.S. list of state sponsors of terrorism, a designation held for nearly five decades. This decision followed a meeting with Syria's interim President Ahmed al-Sharaa at the NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed that Trump had informed Congress of the administration's intent, citing 'positive changes and counterterrorism actions' taken under al-Sharaa. Rubio stated that lifting sanctions would unlock international trade and investment, allowing Syria to rebuild and open a new chapter for its people. Congress now has a 45-day window to potentially block the request.

articles.headline: OCC Enforcement Activity Declines at Slower Rate Compared to Other Agencies
body: A recent analysis indicates that the decline in enforcement activity at the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) is at a substantially slower rate than the Federal Reserve and FDIC.
Annual enforcement numbers have gradually fallen from their mid-2010 levels into the early 2020s, with a downward trend in their rolling average.
However, the OCC has shown more variability year by year, with a substantial spike in enforcement in 2024 that appears to have been short-lived.

articles.headline: Trump Administration Initiates Process to Rescind Syria's State Sponsor of Terrorism Status
body: Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced on July 8 that President Trump has informed Congress of the administration's intention to rescind Syria's State Sponsor of Terrorism status. This initiates a 45-day pre-notification process.

The eventual rescission of this designation, which has been in place since 1979, will result in Syria's removal from the highly restricted Country Group E:1 under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR).
This move is expected to open the way for a broader range of license-free exports and significantly improve Syria's trade relations with the United States.

articles.headline: NSF to Prohibit Funding for Collaborations with U.S. Restricted Entities
body: The U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF) has announced a forthcoming policy that will prohibit the expenditure of NSF funds on collaborations with entities on U.S. restricted parties lists. This policy aims to mitigate research security risks associated with entities whose behavior is deemed contrary to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.

The prohibition will extend to senior/key personnel, preventing them from collaborating with or holding appointments/receiving research support from these restricted entities for the duration of an NSF award. Appendix A of the policy lists various U.S. proscribed party lists, including those from the Departments of Commerce (BIS Entity List, Military End-User Entities), Treasury (OFAC Annex of EO 14032, Non-SDN Chinese Military-Industrial Complex Companies), and others.

The NSF intends to implement this prohibition in Fiscal Year 2027, aligning with the Department of War's approach to collaborations with restricted entities to safeguard NSF-funded research and promote consistency across government agencies.

articles.headline: NSF Prohibits Funding for Collaborations with Restricted Entities
body: The U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF) issued a new policy on July 8, 2026, prohibiting the expenditure of NSF funds on collaborations with entities on U.S. restricted parties lists. This policy aims to mitigate research security risks associated with entities deemed contrary to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.

Appendix A of the policy outlines the U.S. Proscribed Party Lists, which include entities from the Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) Entity List, Military End-User Entities, and Denied Persons List, among others. This broad prohibition underscores the government's comprehensive approach to safeguarding federally funded research.

Organizations receiving NSF funds will be responsible for ensuring that senior and key personnel are aware of and comply with this prohibition, and for identifying and addressing any prohibited activities before funds are expended. The NSF's move aligns with efforts by other U.S. government agencies to prevent sensitive research and technology from falling into the wrong hands.

articles.headline: NSF to Prohibit Collaborations with Restricted Entities on U.S. Proscribed Party Lists
body: The U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF) is implementing a new policy that will prohibit NSF funds from being expended on collaborations with entities on U.S. restricted party lists. This forthcoming policy, detailed in NSF 26-022, aims to safeguard NSF-funded research by preventing engagement with entities deemed contrary to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.

Appendix A of the policy outlines the U.S. Proscribed Party Lists, which include the Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) Entity List and Military End-User Entities, as well as OFAC's Non-SDN Chinese Military-Industrial Complex Companies, among others.

The NSF intends to implement this prohibition in Fiscal Year 2027, meaning senior/key personnel will be barred from collaborating with these restricted entities on NSF-funded projects and from holding appointments or receiving research support from them for the duration of an NSF award.

articles.headline: NSF to Prohibit Collaborations with Restricted Entities on Funded Projects
body: The U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF) is implementing a new policy that will prohibit the expenditure of NSF funds on collaborations with entities on U.S. restricted parties lists.

This forthcoming policy, set to be implemented in Fiscal Year 2027, aims to safeguard NSF-funded research by aligning with the Department of War's approach to collaborations with entities on U.S. restricted party lists.

The NSF has determined that research security risk mitigation for projects involving these restricted entities is insufficient, emphasizing the U.S. government's focus on national security and foreign policy interests.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Iran-Related General License, Reinstating Oil Sanctions
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued Iran General License X1, which supersedes and effectively terminates the earlier General License X. This action reinstates sanctions on Iranian-origin crude oil, petroleum products, and petrochemical products.

General License X1 authorizes the wind-down of activities previously permitted under GL X, with a deadline of 12:01 AM EST on July 17, 2026. This move follows renewed Iranian attacks against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and President Trump's declaration that the June ceasefire with Iran was over.

The re-imposition of these sanctions marks a significant shift in U.S. policy towards Iran, aiming to cut off a major source of income for the Iranian regime. The previous GL X had provided temporary sanctions relief in the aftermath of a June ceasefire between the United States and Iran.

articles.headline: Issuance of Amended Iran-related General License
body: OFAC published a new action on July 07, 2026: "Issuance of Amended Iran-related General License". Full details are available at the official OFAC website.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today issued an amended Iran-related General License. This amendment modifies existing authorizations for certain transactions or activities involving Iran, aiming to refine the scope of permissible engagements under the sanctions program.

Amended General Licenses often reflect a recalibration of sanctions policy, either to tighten restrictions on specific sectors or to ease burdens on certain legitimate activities. Entities engaged in Iran-related transactions must carefully review the updated terms to ensure continued compliance.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License, Reinstating Oil Sanctions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Iran-related General License on July 7, 2026. This action revoked the temporary license that previously authorized the sale of Iranian oil (General License X) and replaced it with General License XI, effectively reinstating sanctions on the sale of crude oil, petrochemical products, and petroleum products of Iranian origin.

The revocation of General License X and the issuance of General License XI signify a tightening of U.S. sanctions on Iran's energy sector. This move is part of the U.S. government's strategy to increase economic pressure on Iran.

The amended general license allows for a wind-down period for transactions made pursuant to the revoked General License X through July 17, 2026. This provides a limited timeframe for entities to conclude any ongoing activities that were previously authorized.

articles.headline: OFAC Revokes Iran General License X, Reinstates Oil Sanctions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) revoked Iran General License X (GL X) on July 7, 2026, and replaced it with Iran General License X1 (GL X1). This action reinstates sanctions on the sale of crude oil, petrochemical, and petroleum products of Iranian origin.

GL X, issued on June 22, 2026, had temporarily authorized transactions involving Iranian-origin crude oil and related products, including importation into the United States and U.S. dollar payments. The revocation follows renewed hostilities in the Strait of Hormuz and Iran's continued assertion of control over the waterway.

GL X1 provides a narrow wind-down authorization for transactions previously permitted under GL X, effective through July 17, 2026. It explicitly states that no new transactions, including purchases or loading of products, are authorized on or after July 7.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Iran-Related General License, Reversing Previous Sanctions Relaxation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Iran-related General License on July 7, 2026, effectively revoking Iran General License X and replacing it with a narrower wind-down authorization, GL X1. This action reverses a previous relaxation of U.S. sanctions related to a U.S.-Iran Memorandum of Understanding.

General License X, issued in June, had authorized the production, delivery, and sale of Iranian crude, petrochemical products, and petroleum products. The new GL X1 authorizes activities ordinarily incident and necessary to the wind down of transactions previously permitted by GL X, with a deadline of July 17, 2026.

Crucially, GL X1 explicitly states that it does not authorize any new transactions, including purchases or loading of products on or after July 7. Furthermore, any payments to blocked persons must now be deposited into an interest-bearing account in the United States.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / OFAC Reverses US Sanctions Relaxation Related to US-Iran Memorandum of Understanding

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Iran-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Iran-related General License. This action follows the revocation of the temporary license authorizing the sale of Iranian oil (General License X) and its replacement with General License XI, which reinstated sanctions on the sale of Iranian crude oil and petrochemical products.

The amended General License X1 authorizes the wind-down of transactions made pursuant to the previously issued GL X through July 17, 2026. This provides a limited period for parties to conclude activities that were previously permitted under the temporary authorization.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal / Steptoe

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Iran-Related General License, Reinstating Sanctions on Oil Exports
body: On July 7, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued General License X1, which amends and effectively revokes General License X. This action reinstates U.S. sanctions against Iranian crude oil, petrochemical products, and petroleum products.
General License X, issued on June 22, 2026, had temporarily authorized transactions related to Iranian-origin oil and petroleum products, including importation into the U.S. and U.S. dollar payments.

Companies now have until July 17, 2026, to wind down transactions previously authorized by General License X, with General License X1 explicitly prohibiting new transactions unrelated to this wind-down.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Iran-Related General License, Reinstating Broad Sanctions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Iran-related General License on July 7, 2026, effectively revoking General License X and reinstating a comprehensive ban on most U.S. trade with Iran. This action follows a brief period where General License X had temporarily authorized certain transactions involving Iranian-origin oil and petroleum products.

The new General License, designated as X1, provides a ten-day wind-down period for transactions previously authorized under General License X, which was issued on June 22, 2026. This rapid reversal of policy comes amid renewed hostilities and a declaration by President Trump that the ceasefire agreement between the U.S. and Iran was 'over.'

Companies involved in the oil, logistics, and energy sectors are urged to immediately cease new Iranian oil transactions and re-evaluate their approaches to Iranian oil, as GL X1 explicitly prohibits new transactions unrelated to the completion or termination of previously authorized activities by July 17, 2026.

articles.headline: OFAC Revokes Iran General License X, Reinstates Sanctions on Oil Trade
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) revoked Iran-related General License X and issued General License X1 on July 7, 2026.

General License X1 effectively reinstates all U.S. sanctions against Iranian crude oil, petrochemical products, and petroleum products, revoking the temporary authorization for such transactions that was issued on June 21, 2026.

This action follows reported attacks by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) on commercial tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and subsequent U.S. retaliatory strikes. Parties have until July 17, 2026, to wind down transactions previously authorized by General License X.

articles.headline: OFAC Revokes Iran General License X, Issues Narrow Wind-Down Authorization GL X1
body: On July 7, 2026, the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) revoked Iran-related General License X and replaced it with General License X1.

General License X, issued in June, had temporarily authorized transactions involving Iranian-origin crude oil, petrochemical products, and petroleum products. Its revocation came abruptly, reportedly following renewed hostilities in the Strait of Hormuz.

GL X1 provides a narrow wind-down authorization, permitting only activities ordinarily incident and necessary to conclude transactions previously authorized by GL X, with a strict deadline of 12:01 a.m. EDT on July 17, 2026. No new transactions, including purchases or loading of products, are permitted on or after July 7.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Global Sanctions and Export Controls Blog

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Iran-Related General License, Revoking Previous Authorization
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Iran-related General License on July 7, 2026, which effectively revoked Iran General License X (GL X).

GL X had previously authorized the production, delivery, and sale of Iranian crude, petrochemical products, and petroleum products. The new authorization, Iran General License X1 (GL X1), provides a narrow wind-down period for transactions previously permitted under GL X, expiring at 12:01 am EDT on July 17, 2026.

GL X1 explicitly prohibits any new transactions, including purchases or loading of products, on or after July 7, 2026, and requires payments to blocked persons to be deposited into an interest-bearing account in the United States.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Iran-Related General License, Reinstates Oil Sanctions

This amendment revoked the temporary license authorizing the sale of Iranian oil, General License X, and replaced it with General License XI, effectively reinstating sanctions on the sale of crude oil, petrochemical, and petroleum products of Iranian origin.

This action signifies a tightening of sanctions against Iran's energy sector, a core objective of U.S. sanctions targeting Iran across successive administrations. The move is likely to impact Iran's ability to export oil and generate revenue, further increasing economic pressure on the country.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Iran-Related General License Amidst Renewed Sanctions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Iran-related General License on July 7, 2026. This action follows the Trump Administration's reinstatement of sanctions on Iranian oil, effectively terminating an earlier general license.

articles.headline: UN General Assembly Debates US Sanctions Against Cuba Amid Humanitarian Concerns
body: The United Nations General Assembly overwhelmingly voted on July 7, 2026, to debate United States sanctions against Cuba, at Havana's request. The debate focused on the decades-long embargo and warnings of increasing suffering on the Caribbean island.

Cuba accused the United States of intensifying extraterritorial measures, which it claims are worsening humanitarian conditions and economic damage. Conversely, the United States attributed the crisis to Cuba's repression, financial mismanagement, and human rights violations.

Member States largely opposed the embargo, calling on both parties to engage in dialogue to resolve the situation. The Non-Aligned Movement described the strengthening of the embargo as a 'serious setback' to normalizing bilateral relations, noting new measures obstructing Cuba's oil supply and imposing secondary sanctions on foreign entities.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Iran-Related General License Amid Renewed Tensions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today issued an amended Iran-related General License. This action follows the Trump Administration's reinstatement of sanctions on Iranian oil and the termination of a previous ceasefire agreement with Iran.

The amendment to the General License is a direct consequence of the escalating tensions in the Middle East, particularly after renewed Iranian attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. This move further tightens restrictions on transactions involving Iran, signaling a more aggressive stance from the U.S. government.

articles.headline: OFAC Revokes Iran Oil Sanctions Rollback, Reinstates Restrictions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has revoked Iran-related General License X and issued General License X1, effectively reinstating sanctions on the sale of Iranian crude oil, petrochemical products, and petroleum products.

General License X1, titled 'Revocation and Wind Down of June 21, 2026 Authorization for the Production, Delivery and Sale of Crude Oil, Petrochemical Products, and Petroleum Products of Iranian Origin,' replaces and supersedes GL X in its entirety, effective July 7, 2026.

This action follows reported attacks by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) on commercial tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and subsequent U.S. retaliatory strikes. articles.headline: OFAC Revokes Iran General License X, Issues Wind-Down General License X1
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has revoked Iran-related General License X and issued Iran-related General License X1, titled "Revocation and Wind Down of June 21, 2026 Authorization for the Production, Delivery and Sale of Crude Oil, Petrochemical Products, and Petroleum Products of Iranian Origin."

Effective July 7, 2026, General License X, which had temporarily authorized broad commercial activity involving Iranian-origin crude oil, petrochemical products, and petroleum products, is replaced and superseded in its entirety by General License X1.

General License X1 prohibits all new transactions involving Iranian crude oil, petroleum products, or petrochemical products after July 7, 2026, absent a specific license from OFAC, and provides a narrow wind-down authorization through July 17, 2026.
