articles.headline: OCC Enters Consent Order with FinTech Partner Bank for BSA/AML Violations
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) entered into a consent order with a fintech partner bank due to deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act and Anti-Money Laundering (BSA/AML) compliance program. The bank, despite its single branch, had significantly expanded its payment processing business, including a large volume of wire and ACH transfers and cross-border activity.

The OCC found that the bank failed to develop a BSA/AML program proportionate to its growth and risk. Issues included deficient criteria for its automated suspicious activity alerting system, insufficient customer due diligence, and a weak internal auditing program.

The consent order mandates the creation of a compliance committee, a corrective action plan, a comprehensive third-party review of its BSA/AML program, and the implementation of new internal controls and a risk-based program for identifying and reporting suspicious activity. No monetary penalty was assessed in this action.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

articles.headline: OCC Enters Consent Order with FinTech Bank for BSA/AML Program Deficiencies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has entered into a consent order with a fintech partner bank due to significant deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act and Anti-Money Laundering (BSA/AML) compliance program. The bank, despite its single branch, had rapidly expanded its payment processing business, including a large volume of wire and ACH transfers and cross-border activity.

The OCC found that the bank failed to develop a BSA/AML program commensurate with its growth and risk. Issues included deficient criteria for its automated suspicious activity alerting system, insufficient customer due diligence, and a failure to determine if it had correspondent accounts with foreign financial institutions.

The consent order mandates the creation of a compliance committee, a corrective action plan, a comprehensive third-party review of its BSA/AML program, and the implementation of new internal controls and a risk-based program for suspicious activity. No monetary penalty was assessed in this action.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

articles.headline: OFAC Designates 9 Hizballah-Aligned Officials in Lebanon — Iran's Ambassador, MPs, Security Officers Targeted
body: OFAC designated nine individuals in Lebanon on May 21, 2026 for obstructing the peace process and impeding Hizballah's disarmament. Those designated include Ibrahim al-Moussawi (Hizballah MP), Iran's designated ambassador to Lebanon, and senior Lebanese security officials. Mohamed Abdel-Mottaleb Fanich, who leads Hizballah's executive council, was also designated.

Secretary Bessent stated: 'Hizballah is a terrorist organization and must be fully disarmed.' The action forms part of a broader U.S. push to support Lebanese state authority following Hizballah's military setbacks in 2024-25.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates 9 Hizballah-Aligned Lebanese Officials Including Sitting MP Ibrahim al-Moussawi
body: OFAC designated nine Hizballah-aligned officials on May 21, 2026, including Ibrahim al-Moussawi — a sitting Lebanese member of parliament — and Iran's ambassador to Lebanon. The designations target Hizballah's political infrastructure and its financial support network in Lebanon, including entities that funnel Iranian funds to Hizballah through charitable fronts.

The action is coordinated with the State Department's listing of Hizballah as a Foreign Terrorist Organization. All property and interests in property of designated individuals subject to U.S. jurisdiction are blocked. U.S. persons are prohibited from transacting with or providing services to any entity owned 50% or more by a Hizballah-designated party.

articles.headline: OCC Releases May 2026 Enforcement Actions, Including Consent Order for BSA/AML Deficiencies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) released its enforcement actions for May 2026, which included a consent order against Community Federal Savings Bank in Woodhaven, New York. The order addresses deficiencies in the bank's Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and Anti-Money Laundering (AML) compliance program, leading to violations of law or regulation.

The OCC found that the bank had significantly expanded its payment processing capabilities without commensurately scaling its compliance infrastructure, resulting in systemic breakdowns in internal controls and weak independent testing. These deficiencies included inadequate suspicious activity monitoring and ineffective customer due diligence.

Additionally, the OCC issued an order of prohibition against Dyemond Williams, a former Associate at JP Morgan Chase Bank, N.A., for making or assisting in unauthorized withdrawals from customer accounts, resulting in a loss of at least $38,500 to the bank.

articles.headline: OCC Issues Consent Order to Community Federal Savings Bank for BSA/AML Program Failures
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced enforcement actions for May 2026, including a Consent Order against Community Federal Savings Bank, Woodhaven, New York. The order cites deficiencies in the bank's Bank Secrecy Act/Anti-Money Laundering (BSA/AML) compliance program, resulting in violations of law and regulation, including 12 CFR 21.21 (BSA/AML program violation) and 12 CFR 163.180(d) (suspicious activity reporting violation).

The OCC found that the bank had significantly expanded its payment processing business relative to its size, including a large volume of wire and ACH transfers and cross-border activity, without commensurately scaling its BSA/AML program. This led to issues such as deficient criteria for its automated suspicious activity alerting system and insufficient customer due diligence.

In a separate action, the OCC issued an Order of Prohibition against Dyemond Williams, a former Associate at JP Morgan Chase Bank, N.A., for making or assisting in unauthorized withdrawals from customer accounts, resulting in a loss of at least $38,500 to the bank.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency / Weiner Brodsky Kider PC

articles.headline: OCC Issues Consent Order Against Community Federal Savings Bank for BSA/AML Failures
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) made public an April 2026 consent order against Community Federal Savings Bank, Woodhaven, New York, for significant deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act/Anti-Money Laundering (BSA/AML) compliance program. The order cites violations of 12 CFR 21.21 (BSA/AML program violation), 12 CFR 163.180(d) (suspicious activity reporting violation), and 31 CFR 1010.520(b)(3) (information sharing requirement under the USA PATRIOT Act).

The OCC found that the bank had rapidly expanded its payment processing business, including a large volume of wire and ACH transfers and cross-border activity, without commensurately scaling its BSA/AML program. Deficiencies included inadequate criteria for its automated suspicious activity alerting system, insufficient customer due diligence, and a failure to determine if it had correspondent accounts with foreign financial institutions.

The consent order mandates the bank to create a compliance committee, develop a corrective action plan, obtain a comprehensive third-party review of its BSA/AML program, and implement new internal controls and a risk-based program for suspicious activity. This action underscores regulators' heightened scrutiny of smaller institutions, especially those with rapid growth in fintech partnerships and payment services.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

articles.headline: OCC Releases May 2026 Enforcement Actions, Including BSA/AML Consent Order
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) released its enforcement actions for May 2026, which included a Consent Order against Community Federal Savings Bank, Woodhaven, New York. The order addresses deficiencies in the bank's Bank Secrecy Act/Anti-Money Laundering (BSA/AML) compliance program, leading to violations of law and regulation.

The OCC found that the bank's BSA/AML program failures included systemic internal control breakdowns, weak independent testing, and inadequate BSA staffing. Specifically, the bank's suspicious activity monitoring processes were deficient, with an automated alert triage system auto-closing a high percentage of alerts that should have been escalated.

In a separate action, the OCC also issued an Order of Prohibition against Dyemond Williams, a former Associate at JP Morgan Chase Bank, N.A., for making or assisting in unauthorized withdrawals from customer accounts, resulting in a loss of at least $38,500 to the bank.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

articles.headline: OCC Issues Consent Order Against Community Federal Savings Bank for BSA/AML Program Failures
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) made public a May 2026 consent order against Community Federal Savings Bank, a federal savings association in Woodhaven, New York. The order addresses deficiencies in the bank's Bank Secrecy Act/Anti-Money Laundering (BSA/AML) compliance program, which resulted in violations of law or regulation, including 12 CFR 21.21 (BSA/AML program violation) and 12 CFR 163.180(d) (suspicious activity reporting violation), and 31 CFR 1010.520(b)(3) (information sharing requirement under the USA PATRIOT Act).

The OCC found that since 2020, the bank had significantly expanded its payment processing capabilities, leading to substantial annual wire and ACH activity, including cross-border transactions involving foreign financial institutions. Despite this rapid growth in transaction volume and associated risk, the bank failed to develop and maintain commensurate controls and risk management processes.

The findings detailed a cascade of interconnected failures, including deficient suspicious activity monitoring processes, an inadequately tuned automated alerting system, and an ineffective customer due diligence program. These shortcomings meant the bank did not adequately understand the nature of certain customers' businesses or the purpose of their transactions.

articles.headline: OCC Issues Consent Order to Community Federal Savings Bank for BSA/AML Deficiencies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) made public a consent order on May 21, 2026, against Community Federal Savings Bank (CFSB) in Woodhaven, New York, citing deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act/Anti-Money Laundering (BSA/AML) compliance program. The order, dated April 2026, highlights systemic internal control breakdowns, weak independent testing, and inadequate BSA staffing at the institution.

The OCC found that CFSB's suspicious activity monitoring processes were deficient, including an automated alert triage system that auto-closed a high percentage of alerts that should have been escalated for review. Furthermore, the bank's customer due diligence program was deemed ineffective, failing to adequately understand the nature of certain customer businesses and transaction purposes.

This action serves as a warning to community banks, particularly those expanding into payment processing and fintech partnerships, that regulators are closely scrutinizing compliance infrastructure. The OCC has ordered CFSB to appoint a Compliance Committee and a third-party Program Consultant to assess and remediate the identified deficiencies.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

articles.headline: OCC Issues Consent Order to Community Federal Savings Bank for BSA/AML Failures
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced enforcement actions for May 2026, including a Consent Order against Community Federal Savings Bank, Woodhaven, New York. The order addresses significant deficiencies in the bank's Bank Secrecy Act/Anti-Money Laundering (BSA/AML) compliance program.

The OCC found that the bank's BSA/AML program failures resulted in violations of law and regulation, including issues with its BSA/AML program, suspicious activity reporting, and information sharing requirements under the USA PATRIOT Act. These deficiencies were particularly notable given the bank's rapid growth in payment processing, including cross-border activity, without a commensurate scaling of its compliance infrastructure.

The Consent Order mandates corrective measures, such as establishing a compliance committee, developing a corrective action plan, and undergoing a comprehensive third-party review of its BSA/AML program. The OCC also issued an Order of Prohibition against Dyemond Williams, a former Associate at JP Morgan Chase Bank, N.A., for making unauthorized withdrawals from customer accounts, resulting in a loss of at least $38,500.

articles.headline: OCC Issues Consent Order Against Community Federal Savings Bank for BSA/AML Deficiencies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced an enforcement action against Community Federal Savings Bank (CFSB) of Woodhaven, New York, on May 21, 2026, citing deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act/Anti-Money Laundering (BSA/AML) compliance program. The consent order addresses violations of law or regulation, including 12 CFR 21.21 (BSA/AML program violation) and 12 CFR 163.180(d) (suspicious activity reporting violation), and 31 CFR 1010.520(b)(3) (information sharing requirement under the USA PATRIOT Act).

The OCC found that while CFSB's size and payment processing activity, including cross-border activities, had significantly increased since 2020, the bank's controls and risk management processes were not commensurate with the heightened risk and growth. Deficiencies included systemic internal control breakdowns, weak independent testing, and insufficient BSA staffing. The bank's suspicious activity monitoring processes were also found to be deficient, with an automated alert triage system auto-closing a high percentage of alerts that should have been escalated.

As a result, the OCC ordered CFSB to appoint a Compliance Committee to ensure adherence to the order and a third-party Program Consultant to prepare a written BSA program assessment. The bank is also required to develop an action plan to remediate the identified deficiencies.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency / Investment Executive

articles.headline: OCC Issues Prohibition Order Against Former JP Morgan Chase Associate for Unauthorized Withdrawals
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced a prohibition order against Dyemond Williams, a former Associate at JP Morgan Chase Bank, N.A., Columbus, Ohio, on May 21, 2026. The order was issued due to Williams making or assisting others in making unauthorized withdrawals from customer accounts, resulting in a loss of at least $38,500 for the bank.

Prohibition orders are issued by the OCC against institution-affiliated parties (IAPs) to deter, encourage correction of, or prevent violations, unsafe or unsound practices, or breaches of fiduciary duty. Such actions reinforce the accountability of individuals for their conduct regarding the affairs of a bank.
This enforcement action underscores the OCC's commitment to maintaining integrity within the banking system and holding individuals accountable for fraudulent activities.

body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced the termination of several enforcement actions, including formal agreements with Axiom Bank, National Association, Maitland, Florida, and The First National Bank of Waverly, Waverly, Ohio.
Additionally, the OCC terminated consent orders against Cenlar Federal Savings Bank, Ewing, New Jersey, and a formal agreement with Lincoln FSB of Nebraska, Lincoln, Nebraska.

These terminations signify that the respective banks have demonstrated compliance with the articles of their enforcement actions, or the OCC has determined that the articles are no longer necessary for the institutions' safety and soundness or legal compliance.

articles.headline: OCC Announces Enforcement Actions for May 2026, Including BSA/AML Consent Order
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) released its enforcement actions for May 2026, which included a Consent Order against Community Federal Savings Bank, Woodhaven, New York. The order addresses deficiencies in the bank's Bank Secrecy Act/Anti-Money Laundering (BSA/AML) compliance program, leading to violations of law or regulation, including 12 CFR 21.21 (BSA/AML program violation) and 12 CFR 163.180(d) (suspicious activity reporting violation).

The OCC's findings detailed a cascade of interconnected failures, noting that the bank had significantly expanded its payment processing capabilities since 2020 without commensurately scaling its compliance infrastructure. This resulted in inadequate controls and risk management processes for its substantial annual wire and ACH activity, including cross-border transactions.

Furthermore, the OCC issued an Order of Prohibition against Dyemond Williams, a former Associate at JP Morgan Chase Bank, N.A., Columbus, Ohio, for making or assisting in unauthorized withdrawals from customer accounts, resulting in a loss of at least $38,500 for the bank. The OCC also terminated a Formal Agreement with Axiom Bank, National Association, Maitland, Florida.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

articles.headline: OCC Announces May 2026 Enforcement Actions, Including BSA/AML Violations
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) released its enforcement actions for May 2026, featuring a Consent Order against Community Federal Savings Bank, Woodhaven, New York. The order addresses significant deficiencies in the bank's Bank Secrecy Act/Anti-Money Laundering (BSA/AML) compliance program.

These deficiencies resulted in violations of law or regulation, including 12 CFR 21.21 (BSA/AML program violation), 12 CFR 163.180(d) (suspicious activity reporting violation), and 31 CFR 1010.520(b)(3) (information sharing requirement under the USA PATRIOT Act).

Additionally, the OCC issued an Order of Prohibition against Dyemond Williams, a former Associate at JP Morgan Chase Bank, N.A., Columbus, Ohio, for making or assisting others in making unauthorized withdrawals from customer accounts, resulting in a loss of at least $38,500 for the bank.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

articles.headline: OCC Issues Consent Order to Community Federal Savings Bank for BSA/AML Program Deficiencies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) issued a Consent Order against Community Federal Savings Bank, Woodhaven, New York, for deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act/Anti-Money Laundering (BSA/AML) compliance program. These deficiencies resulted in violations of law or regulation, including BSA/AML program violations and suspicious activity reporting violations.

The OCC found that the bank had significantly expanded its payment processing business relative to its size, including a large volume of wire and ACH transfers and cross-border activity, without commensurately scaling its compliance infrastructure. This led to deficient criteria in its automated suspicious activity alerting system and insufficient customer due diligence.

The consent order requires the bank to develop a corrective action plan, obtain a comprehensive third-party review of its BSA/AML program, and implement a new risk-based program to identify and report suspicious activity.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

articles.headline: OCC Enters Consent Order with Community Federal Savings Bank for BSA/AML Program Failures
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) publicly announced an April 2026 consent order against Community Federal Savings Bank (CFSB) in Woodhaven, New York, for deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act/Anti-Money Laundering (BSA/AML) compliance program. The OCC's findings indicated that the bank's controls and risk management processes were insufficient given its significant growth in payment processing and cross-border activities since 2020.

The consent order cited systemic internal control breakdowns, weak independent testing, and inadequate BSA staffing within CFSB's compliance program. Specifically, the bank's automated suspicious activity alerting system was found to have deficient criteria, leading to a high percentage of alerts being auto-closed without proper review.

Furthermore, the OCC identified failures in the bank's customer due diligence program, including an inability to understand the nature of certain customers' businesses and the purpose of their transactions. CFSB was ordered to appoint a Compliance Committee and a third-party Program Consultant to address these deficiencies.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

articles.headline: OCC Prohibits Former JP Morgan Chase Associate for Unauthorized Customer Withdrawals
body: In its May 2026 enforcement actions, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) issued an Order of Prohibition against Dyemond Williams, a former Associate at JP Morgan Chase Bank, N.A., Columbus, Ohio.

Williams was prohibited from any participation in the affairs of a bank or other institution for making or assisting others in making unauthorized withdrawals from customer accounts, which resulted in a loss of at least $38,500 for the bank. This action reinforces the OCC's commitment to holding individuals accountable for their conduct within financial institutions.

articles.headline: OCC Releases May 2026 Enforcement Actions, Citing BSA/AML Failures at Community Federal Savings Bank
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced its enforcement actions for May 2026, which included a Consent Order against Community Federal Savings Bank, Woodhaven, New York. The order cited significant deficiencies in the bank's Bank Secrecy Act/Anti-Money Laundering (BSA/AML) compliance program, leading to violations of law and regulation.

The OCC found that the bank, despite its rapid growth in payment processing and cross-border activity, failed to develop a BSA/AML program commensurate with its increased risk. This included issues with its automated suspicious activity alerting system, insufficient customer due diligence, and a weak internal auditing program.

The enforcement action underscores the OCC's focus on smaller institutions, particularly those expanding into fintech partnerships and payments services without adequately scaling their compliance infrastructure. The bank did not admit or deny the allegations but is required to implement a comprehensive corrective action plan.

articles.headline: OFAC Sanctions Sinaloa Cartel Fentanyl Networks — 6 Ethereum Addresses Blacklisted, Cash-to-Crypto Pipeline from US Streets to Mexico
body: OFAC sanctioned more than a dozen individuals comprising two Sinaloa Cartel networks on May 20, 2026. Armando de Jesus Ojeda Aviles leads a Los Chapitos-affiliated money laundering network converting fentanyl proceeds from U.S. streets into cryptocurrency for transfer to Mexico — six Ethereum wallet addresses were added to the SDN list. Jesus Gonzalez Penuelas heads a separate trafficking and laundering organisation.

Since February 2025, OFAC has sanctioned over 600 Sinaloa Cartel-linked persons. TRM Labs notes five of the six blacklisted Ethereum addresses are attributed to a single individual using multi-wallet fragmentation for layering — a pattern now subject to immediate blocking by all U.S.-regulated crypto exchanges.

articles.headline: OFAC Cuba Sanctions — 8 Entities Supporting Cuban Security Forces and Internet Disruption Tools Designated
body: OFAC designated 8 Cuban entities and individuals in May 2026 for providing material support to Cuba's Ministry of the Interior (MININT) and the Brigadas de Respuesta Rápida (BRR) — paramilitary groups that violently suppressed the 2021 pro-democracy protests and continued crackdowns in 2025-2026. Three of the designated entities supplied surveillance software and internet disruption tools used against Cuban civil society.

The Cuba sanctions programme prohibits U.S. persons from engaging in virtually all transactions with Cuba without an OFAC general or specific licence. The Cuban Assets Control Regulations (CACR) apply extraterritorially to U.S.-owned or controlled foreign entities. Travel-related transactions, certain exports, and academic exchanges may qualify under general licences — companies should review the 12 categories of general licences before transacting.

articles.headline: OFAC Penalizes Adani Enterprises Limited $275,000,000 for Sanctions Violations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) assessed a civil monetary penalty of $275,000,000 against Adani Enterprises Limited for apparent violations of OFAC-administered sanctions programs.
The settlement agreement is available at: https://ofac.treasury.gov/media/935631/download?inline

articles.headline: OFAC $275M Settlement with Adani Enterprises — 32 Iran LPG Violations, Shadow Fleet, USD Payments Through US Banks
body: OFAC announced a $275 million settlement with Adani Enterprises Limited (AEL) on May 18, 2026 — one of the largest Iran sanctions penalties ever imposed on a non-U.S. company. AEL settled potential civil liability for 32 apparent violations of Iran sanctions arising from LPG purchases made between November 2023 and June 2025 from a Dubai-based trader who supplied what was purported to be Omani and Iraqi gas. OFAC determined the LPG actually originated from Iran.

AEL caused U.S. financial institutions to process approximately $192 million in dollar-denominated payments for the shipments — bringing the transactions within OFAC's jurisdiction. OFAC classified the violations as egregious and non-voluntarily self-disclosed, with a statutory maximum penalty of $384 million. The penalty was reduced to $275 million based on AEL's cooperation, remedial measures, and the implementation of maritime intelligence technology. Notably, OFAC did not allege AEL knowingly purchased Iranian LPG — the egregious finding was based on recklessness and failure to investigate clear red flags including suspicious vessel activity, implausible shipping logistics, and unusually discounted pricing.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / GRC Report / Corruption Crime & Compliance

articles.headline: OFAC GL 134C Extends Russian Crude Oil Wind-Down to June 17 — Shadow Fleet Vessels Explicitly Covered
body: OFAC issued General License 134C on May 18, 2026, replacing expiring GL 134B and extending operational authorisation through June 17, 2026 for vessels that loaded Russian crude on or before April 17, 2026.

GL 134C explicitly covers designated shadow fleet vessels — allowing qualifying cargoes to complete their voyage without triggering new violations. The June 17 expiry creates the next key compliance decision point for affected counterparties.

articles.headline: FinCEN Beneficial Ownership Reporting — Enforcement Phase Begins May 2026, Willful Violations Up to $591/Day
body: FinCEN's beneficial ownership information (BOI) reporting requirements under the Corporate Transparency Act moved into active enforcement in May 2026. Companies formed before January 1, 2024 that have not filed are now subject to civil penalties of up to $591 per day per violation and criminal fines up to $10,000 with potential imprisonment.

FinCEN estimates over 32 million small businesses are covered reporting companies. The most common exemptions are large operating companies (20+ full-time employees, $5M+ US-source revenue, physical office in the US), SEC-registered companies, and regulated entities. FinCEN has stated it will prioritise egregious willful violations particularly those involving known bad actors attempting to conceal beneficial ownership.

articles.headline: Emerging Technology Technical Advisory Committee
body: The Emerging Technology Technical Advisory Committee (ETTAC) advises and assists the Department of Commerce on matters related to export control policies. The ETTAC will meet on June 2, 2026, to review and discuss these matters. This meeting will be partially closed to the public pursuant to the exemptions under the Federal Advisory Committee Act (FACA) and the Government in the Sunshine Act. The meeting will be held in person, with no option for virtual attendance.

articles.headline: Economic Fury — OFAC Targets Iran IRGC Oil Operations, Designates 12 Entities Selling Iranian Oil to China
body: OFAC designated 12 individuals and entities enabling the IRGC's sale and shipment of Iranian oil to China. The IRGC relies on front companies in permissive jurisdictions to obfuscate its role in oil sales and funnel revenue to the Iranian regime.

Since February 2025, OFAC has sanctioned approximately 1,000 Iran-related persons, vessels, and aircraft as part of the Economic Fury maximum pressure campaign. The revenue is directed toward weapons development, backing terrorist proxies, and funding security forces that suppress citizens.

Updated model risk management guidance was issued jointly with the Federal Reserve and FDIC on April 17, 2026. The guidance aims to tailor the supervisory framework to reduce unnecessary burden while promoting risk-based examination across institutions of all sizes.

articles.headline: U.S. CPI Reaccelerates to 3.3% in March as Gasoline Surges 21.2% — Fed Under New Leadership
body: U.S. CPI came in at 3.3% year-over-year in March 2026, up from 2.4% in February, driven by a 21.2% monthly surge in gasoline prices linked to Strait of Hormuz supply disruption. Two Fed governors dissented from the April FOMC majority.

Kevin Warsh has been confirmed to succeed Jerome Powell as Fed Chair, whose term as chair expired May 15, 2026. Markets are watching for any shift in rate policy under new leadership as energy-driven inflation complicates the inflation outlook.

articles.headline: Treasury Sanctions Russia's Two Largest Oil Companies — Rosneft and Gazprom Neft Targeted as Putin Refuses Ceasefire
body: The U.S. Department of Treasury's OFAC sanctioned Russia's two largest oil companies — funding the Kremlin's war machine — as a direct consequence of Russia's lack of serious commitment to a peace process to end the war in Ukraine. Secretary Bessent stated: 'Now is the time to stop the killing and for an immediate ceasefire. Given President Putin's refusal to end this senseless war, Treasury is sanctioning Russia's two largest oil companies that fund the Kremlin's war machine.'

The action increases pressure on Russia's energy sector and degrades the Kremlin's ability to raise revenue for its war machine and support its weakened economy. Treasury stated it will continue to use its authorities in support of a peace process and that a permanent peace depends entirely on Russia's willingness to negotiate in good faith.

articles.headline: BIS Settles with Coastal PVA Technology for Illegal Semiconductor Equipment Exports to China
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) entered into a settlement agreement with Coastal PVA Technology, Inc. on April 13, 2026, for selling EAR99 items to Chinese parties on BIS's Entity List. The settlement, publicly reported on April 23, 2026, resolves allegations that Coastal violated the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by exporting semiconductor manufacturing equipment without authorization.

Coastal PVA Technology, a California-based company, manufactured and exported polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) brushes used in semiconductor manufacturing. Between May 2021 and May 2024, Coastal allegedly sold these brushes, valued at $400,088, to Semiconductor Manufacturing International (Beijing) Corporation (SMIC Beijing) and Semiconductor Manufacturing North China (Beijing) Corporation (SMIC North) through third-party distributors.

This enforcement action is the latest example of the U.S. government's focus on semiconductor and semiconductor manufacturing equipment, and BIS's policy to enforce licensing requirements for Entity List transactions, even for EAR99 items. It highlights the critical need for manufacturers to implement robust compliance programs to avoid penalties.

articles.headline: BIS Settles with Coastal PVA Technology for Entity List Violations
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry & Security (BIS) entered into a settlement agreement with Coastal PVA Technology, Inc. on April 13, 2026, for selling EAR99 items to Chinese parties on BIS' Entity List.

The settlement resolves allegations that Coastal violated the EAR by exporting, reexporting, or transferring controlled semiconductor manufacturing equipment to restricted Chinese entities, including Semiconductor Manufacturing International (Beijing) Corporation (SMIC Beijing), without authorization.

BIS imposed a $1,700,000 civil penalty, suspended for one year due to Coastal's limited ability to pay, underscoring the agency's focus on semiconductor-related trade and enforcement of Entity List restrictions even for low-level technology products.

articles.headline: OCC Consent Order Against Federal Savings Bank Chicago — $10.8B in VA Loans, Deceptive Marketing, Restitution Required
body: The OCC issued a consent order against The Federal Savings Bank of Chicago for deceptive marketing of VA-backed cash-out refinance loans to military service members between 2022 and 2024. The bank originated $10.8 billion in loans covering 30,361 transactions.

This is the bank's second consent order in five years. The board must engage an independent restitution consultant within 90 days. Former CEO Stephen Calk's 2021 conviction for bribery related to Paul Manafort loans preceded the bank's first enforcement action.

articles.headline: BIS Settles with Coastal PVA Technology for Exporting EAR99 Items to Entity List Companies
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry & Security (BIS) reached a settlement agreement with Coastal PVA Technology, Inc. on April 13, 2026, for exporting EAR99 items to Chinese entities on BIS's Entity List. Coastal, a California-based manufacturer of polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) brushes used in semiconductor manufacturing, allegedly sold products valued at $400,088 to Semiconductor Manufacturing International (Beijing) Corporation (SMIC Beijing) and Semiconductor Manufacturing North China (SMIC North) between May 2021 and May 2024 without authorization.

This enforcement action highlights BIS's continued focus on semiconductor and semiconductor manufacturing equipment, and its policy to enforce licensing requirements for Entity List transactions, even for EAR99 items, which are the least restrictive U.S. export classification. SMIC Beijing and SMIC North have been on the Entity List since late 2020, triggering increased scrutiny and licensing requirements for any shipments.

The settlement underscores the critical need for manufacturers to implement robust compliance programs, particularly in industries related to critical technologies. This case is part of an ongoing enforcement surge by BIS targeting chip exports to China, with several high-price penalties issued in early 2026 against companies dealing with SMIC.

articles.headline: Extension of Authorized Integrated Circuit (IC) Designer Status and Application Deadline To Become an Approved IC Designer
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by extending by about eight months the triggering date for authorized integrated circuit designer status and submission date for applications to become an approved integrated circuit (IC) designer. The new date is December 31, 2026.

articles.headline: BIS Enforcement Focuses on China Semiconductor and Entity List Compliance
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has initiated 2026 with several significant administrative enforcement actions, underscoring its aggressive policing of export controls related to China, Entity List parties, and semiconductor trade. These cases highlight BIS's focus on not only obvious diversion or evasion risks but also flawed legal interpretations and compliance-process failures.

One notable case involved Exyte Management GmbH, a Germany-based engineering company, which agreed to pay a $1.5 million civil penalty for 13 violations. BIS alleged Exyte Shanghai caused the in-country transfer of over 800 EAR99 items to Semiconductor Manufacturing International (Beijing) Corporation (SMIC Beijing), an Entity-listed party, without authorization.

These actions serve as a reminder that Entity List restrictions are not limited to exports from the United States and apply to any item subject to the EAR transferred to an Entity-listed party. Companies in the semiconductor supply chain are urged to understand beneficial end-users and implement robust compliance programs.

articles.headline: UK OFSI £30M Monetary Penalty — UK Bank Fined for Processing Russia-Linked Transactions Through Turkish Correspondent
body: OFSI imposed a £30 million monetary penalty on a UK-authorised bank for processing approximately £420 million in transactions linked to Russian designated persons through a Turkish correspondent banking relationship between March 2022 and September 2023. OFSI found the bank failed to conduct adequate due diligence on beneficial owners and ignored multiple internal compliance red flags.

The penalty reflects OFSI's use of enhanced enforcement powers under the Economic Crime Act 2022, which raised the maximum civil penalty to the greater of £1 million or 50% of the transaction value. OFSI directed the bank to appoint an independent skilled person to review its Russia sanctions compliance programme.

articles.headline: FinCEN Assesses Historic $80 Million Penalty Against Canaccord Genuity LLC for BSA Violations
body: The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) assessed an $80 million civil money penalty against Canaccord Genuity LLC on March 6, 2026, marking the largest Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) penalty ever imposed against a broker-dealer. FinCEN alleged that Canaccord, despite its position as a market maker, failed to detect red flags in securities trading due to an under-resourced Anti-Money Laundering (AML) program that was not proportional to its business model's risks.

This enforcement action highlighted systemic deficiencies in both supervisory and AML frameworks, including the firm's failure to surveil trillions of shares in low-priced over-the-counter (OTC) transactions over nearly a decade. Parallel to FinCEN's action, FINRA imposed a separate $20 million fine for similar AML program failures.

The case also involved the alleged backdating of nearly 400 documents in response to regulator inquiries, which transformed long-standing compliance weaknesses into an aggravated enforcement case, signaling zero tolerance for misleading regulators. This action underscores the critical need for robust and adequately resourced AML programs in the financial sector.

articles.headline: FinCEN Assesses Record $80 Million Penalty Against Broker-Dealer for BSA Violations
body: The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) imposed a historic $80 million civil money penalty against Canaccord Genuity LLC, marking the largest Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) penalty ever levied against a broker-dealer. The penalty stems from the firm's alleged willful failure to implement an effective anti-money laundering (AML) program from approximately March 2018 through June 2024.

According to FinCEN, Canaccord, despite its position as a market maker, failed to detect red flags in securities for which it provided trading services due to an under-resourced AML program that was not proportional to its business model's risks. This action highlights systemic deficiencies in both supervisory and AML frameworks, including a failure to surveil trillions of shares in low-priced over-the-counter (OTC) transactions.

The FinCEN action was coordinated with parallel enforcement actions by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA), each imposing a $20 million fine. Of the $80 million FinCEN penalty, $5 million is suspended pending a compliance lookback review, with an immediate $35 million owed to the Treasury Department after crediting the SEC and FINRA penalties.

articles.headline: FinCEN Imposes $80 Million Penalty on Canaccord Genuity LLC for BSA Violations
body: The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) imposed an $80 million civil money penalty against Canaccord Genuity LLC on March 6, 2026, for willful Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) violations. This was the largest BSA enforcement action against a broker-dealer at the time.

FinCEN alleged that Canaccord Genuity LLC failed to implement an effective anti-money laundering (AML) program from approximately March 2018 through June 2024, despite being well-positioned to detect red flags in securities trading.

The firm's under-resourced AML program allegedly led to a failure to timely detect and report suspicious activity by numerous high-risk customers, including those involved in moving money for Russian oligarchs and implicated in OFAC investigations.

articles.headline: FinCEN Imposes $80 Million Penalty on Broker-Dealer for AML Failures
body: The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) imposed an $80 million civil money penalty against a global broker-dealer on March 6, 2026, for systemic anti-money laundering (AML) failures. This marks the largest Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) enforcement action ever brought against a broker-dealer.

The action arose from the broker-dealer's alleged willful failure to implement an effective AML program over several years, including inadequate controls relative to the risks of its over-the-counter (OTC) business. Key surveillance reports were not reviewed, and those that were, relied on arbitrary filters and unreasonable thresholds, rendering them ineffective.

Parallel enforcement actions were also taken by the SEC and FINRA, with FinCEN's penalty including credits of $20 million each to these agencies. The case highlights the severe consequences for underinvesting in AML surveillance and the importance of meaningful analysis and timely follow-up on flagged activity.

articles.headline: FinCEN Imposes Record $80 Million Penalty on Broker-Dealer for AML Failures
body: The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) imposed an $80 million civil money penalty against a global broker-dealer on March 6, 2026, marking the largest Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) enforcement action ever against such an entity. This action was taken due to the broker-dealer's alleged willful failure to implement an effective anti-money laundering (AML) program from approximately March 2018 through June 2024.

The FinCEN action was coordinated with parallel enforcement actions by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA), which each imposed $20 million fines. The alleged deficiencies included systemic failures in supervisory and AML frameworks, such as the failure to surveil trillions of shares in low-priced over-the-counter (OTC) transactions and chronic underinvestment in compliance.

Of the $80 million penalty, $5 million is suspended pending a compliance lookback review, and after crediting the SEC and FINRA penalties, the broker-dealer owes an immediate $35 million to the Treasury Department. articles.headline: FinCEN Imposes Record $80 Million Penalty on Broker-Dealer for BSA Violations
body: The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) assessed a historic $80 million civil money penalty against Canaccord Genuity LLC on March 6, 2026, marking the largest Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) penalty ever imposed against a broker-dealer. The penalty stems from Canaccord's willful failure to implement an effective anti-money laundering (AML) program from approximately March 2018 through June 2024.

According to FinCEN, Canaccord, despite its position as a market maker, failed to detect red flags in securities for which it provided trading services due to an under-resourced AML program that was not proportional to its business model's risks. This included systemic deficiencies in supervisory and AML frameworks, such as failing to surveil trillions of shares in low-priced over-the-counter (OTC) transactions.

The FinCEN action was coordinated with parallel enforcement actions by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA), each imposing $20 million fines. After crediting these penalties, Canaccord owes an immediate $35 million to the Treasury Department.

articles.headline: Applied Materials to Pay $252 Million Penalty for Illegally Exporting Semiconductor Equipment to China
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced a settlement agreement with Applied Materials Inc. (AMAT) and Applied Materials Korea, Ltd. (AMK) for illegal exports of U.S. semiconductor manufacturing equipment to China. The companies agreed to pay a penalty of approximately $252 million, the second-highest penalty ever imposed by BIS.

In 2021 and 2022, AMAT violated BIS's licensing requirements by shipping ion implanters, a type of semiconductor manufacturing equipment, first to AMK in Korea for assembly and then onward to a company on the Entity List in China, without obtaining the necessary export licenses. The value of the illegally shipped merchandise was approximately $126 million.

This enforcement action highlights BIS's aggressive stance on safeguarding sensitive American technologies and deterring violations of export controls, particularly concerning critical industries like semiconductors and designated Chinese military end-users. As part of the settlement, AMAT also agreed to conduct multiple audits of its export compliance program.
articles.source: Bureau of Industry and Security / Wiggin and Dana LLP

articles.headline: BIS Penalizes Applied Materials $252 Million for Offshoring to Evade China Export Controls
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced a settlement agreement on February 11, 2026, with Applied Materials Inc. and its South Korean subsidiary, Applied Materials Korea, Ltd. (AMK), imposing a $252 million penalty. This is the second-highest penalty ever imposed by BIS in a stand-alone enforcement action.

The settlement addresses 56 violations of the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) stemming from AMK's unauthorized reexport and attempted reexport of semiconductor manufacturing equipment to China-incorporated Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation (SMIC) and its subsidiaries.

Applied Materials allegedly attempted to circumvent EAR license requirements by moving final production and testing to AMK in South Korea, believing the substantial transformation would render the equipment foreign-produced and not subject to the EAR. BIS rejected this argument, asserting that the equipment remained 'U.S.-origin' under the specific circumstances, including the use of U.S.-origin parts and the sole purpose of avoiding U.S. licensing requirements for sales to SMIC.

articles.headline: Applied Materials Settles with BIS for $252.5 Million Over Semiconductor Equipment Exports to China
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced a civil settlement with Applied Materials, Inc. and its Korean subsidiary, Applied Materials Korea, resolving allegations that the companies reexported controlled semiconductor manufacturing equipment to a restricted Chinese entity without the required Export Administration Regulations (EAR) authorization. The settlement includes a $252.5 million penalty, representing the statutory maximum.

The violations occurred between November 8, 2020, and July 18, 2022, involving 56 occasions where ion implanters, critical semiconductor materials, were reexported or attempted to be reexported to SMIC Subsidiaries despite BIS informing them of the licensing requirement.

Beyond the substantial fine, the settlement mandates that Applied Materials complete two internal compliance audits with findings reported to BIS and imposes a three-year denial of export privileges, suspended contingent on timely payment and audit completion. This case highlights BIS's aggressive enforcement in the semiconductor sector.

articles.headline: BIS Revises Semiconductor Export Licensing Rule for China, Shifts to Case-by-Case Review
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has issued a significant final rule, effective January 15, 2026, revising export licensing requirements for advanced semiconductor chips destined for China.

The updated rule shifts the review process for high-performance chips, such as the Nvidia H200 and AMD MI325X, from a presumption of denial to a case-by-case evaluation of export license applications.

This policy change, following President Trump's December 8, 2025 announcement, allows for shipments to approved customers in China under controlled circumstances, provided exporters meet new security and compliance conditions.

articles.headline: BIS Revises Export Review Policy for Advanced AI Chips to China and Macau
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) published a final rule effective January 15, 2026, altering the export license review policy for certain advanced computing semiconductors destined for the People's Republic of China (PRC) and Macau. This marks a shift from a presumption of denial to a case-by-case licensing approach with strict conditions.

The new policy applies to a narrow category of advanced computing chips that fall below defined performance thresholds, specifically those with a total processing performance (TPP) of less than 21,000 and a total DRAM bandwidth below 6,500 GB/s. This includes chips at the level of NVIDIA's H200 GPU and AMD's MI325X accelerator.

This calibrated approach aims to balance support for U.S. AI-related technology exports with national security interests. For exporters, this means a more dynamic and documentation-heavy process, requiring robust compliance programs to manage evidence-driven workflows and audit-ready records.

articles.headline: BIS Revises License Review Policy for Advanced Computing Exports to China
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revised its license review policy for exports of certain semiconductors to China and Macau, shifting from a presumption of denial to a case-by-case review. This change, effective January 15, 2026, applies to semiconductors such as the Nvidia H200 and its equivalents, as well as less advanced chips, provided specific conditions are met.

To qualify for the case-by-case review, exporters must certify that there is sufficient supply of the product in the United States, that production for exports to China will not divert global foundry capacity for similar or more advanced products for U.S. customers, and that the Chinese purchaser has adopted export compliance procedures.

This rule follows President Trump's December 8, 2025, announcement to allow the shipment of H200 and similar products to approved customers in China, aiming to strengthen national security by maintaining U.S. leadership in artificial intelligence.

articles.headline: BIS Revises License Review Policy for Advanced Computing Commodities, Introduces Third-Party Testing Requirement
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced revisions to its license review policy for advanced computing commodities, specifically impacting 'supercomputer,' 'advanced-node integrated circuits,' and semiconductor manufacturing equipment end-use controls.

This final rule introduces a case-by-case license review policy and, notably, requires exporters to confirm as part of the license application process that AI commodities will be reviewed by a qualified third-party testing lab.

This third-party testing aims to confirm the technical capabilities and functions of the AI commodities described in the exporter's license application, with reviews potentially performed by representative sampling of a batch of semiconductors.

articles.headline: Global Export Control Convergence — Wassenaar, EU Dual-Use, UK Strategic Controls Align Against Russia and China Technology Transfer
body: The Wassenaar Arrangement's 42 participating states have aligned export controls to prevent technology transfer to Russia and restrict sensitive dual-use technology flows to China. The EU's Dual-Use Regulation (2021/821) and UK Strategic Export Controls provide the primary frameworks for European enforcement, with the UK maintaining its own independent strategic export licensing regime post-Brexit.

Key developments: The EU revised its Common High Priority Items list to restrict 38 categories of goods critical for Russia's military-industrial complex. The UK's Export Control Joint Unit (ECJU) has increased enforcement activity against Russia-linked diversion through third-country hubs including UAE, Turkey, Kazakhstan, and Armenia. Companies operating dual-use supply chains must screen against all three regimes — U.S. EAR, EU Dual-Use Regulation, and UK Export Control Order — simultaneously.
articles.source: Wassenaar Arrangement / UK ECJU / EU Commission

articles.headline: BIS Fines Exyte Management $1.5 Million for Subsidiary's Dealings with SMIC
body: In January 2026, the U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) fined Germany's Exyte Management $1.5 million for its Chinese subsidiary's dealings with Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation (SMIC). SMIC has been on the BIS Entity List since 2020 and designated as a Chinese military company in 2021.

The enforcement action stemmed from Exyte China's failure to recognize that licensing requirements under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) applied to in-country transfers of EAR-controlled goods by China-based distributors to SMIC. This case underscores the extraterritorial reach of U.S. export controls and the importance for foreign companies to understand and comply with these regulations when dealing with listed entities.

articles.headline: BIS Fines Germany's Exyte Management $1.5 Million for SMIC Dealings
body: The U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) fined Germany's Exyte Management $1.5 million in January 2026 for its Chinese subsidiary's dealings with Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation (SMIC).

This enforcement action is part of BIS's broader surge in targeting chip exports to China, particularly to SMIC, which was added to the BIS Entity List in 2020 and designated a Chinese military company in 2021.

The penalty underscores the U.S. government's continued focus on enforcing export controls related to semiconductor technology and entities on the Entity List, even for foreign subsidiaries of international companies.

articles.headline: OFAC Sanctions Four Venezuela Oil Sector Companies — Four Shadow Fleet Tankers Designated as Blocked Property
body: OFAC sanctioned four companies operating in Venezuela's oil sector and identified four associated oil tankers as blocked property. The vessels, some of which are part of the shadow fleet serving Venezuela, continue to provide financial resources that fuel Maduro's illegitimate narco-terrorist regime.

Maduro's regime increasingly depends on a shadow fleet of worldwide vessels to facilitate sanctionable activity, including sanctions evasion, and to generate revenue for its destabilising operations. The action signals that those involved in the Venezuelan oil trade continue to face significant sanctions risks.

articles.headline: OFAC, Australia and UK Coordinate Sanctions Against Russian Bulletproof Hosting — Media Land and Hypercore Designated
body: OFAC, Australia's Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, and the UK's FCDO announced coordinated sanctions targeting Media Land — a Russia-based bulletproof hosting service provider — for its role in supporting ransomware operations and other cybercrime. OFAC also designated three members of Media Land's leadership and three sister companies.

OFAC and the UK additionally designated Hypercore Ltd., a front company of Aeza Group LLC, another bulletproof hosting provider. Bulletproof hosting service providers sell access to specialised servers designed to evade detection and defy law enforcement efforts to disrupt malicious cyber activities.

articles.headline: BIS Adds 29 Entities to Entity List for Diversion to Iran
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amended the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by adding 29 entries (26 entities and 3 addresses) to the Entity List, effective October 8, 2025. These entities are located in the People's Republic of China (19), Turkey (9), and the United Arab Emirates (1).

These additions were made based on information indicating that these companies are diverting U.S.-origin items to Iran, including to parties already on the BIS Entity List and OFAC's Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List.

Iran has been subject to comprehensive U.S. sanctions and export controls for decades, requiring licenses for most items on the Commerce Control List and certain EAR99 items for export, reexport, or in-country transfer to or within Iran.

articles.headline: BIS Expands Entity List Controls to Cover Affiliates of Listed Entities
body: The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued an Interim Final Rule that expands the export control restrictions of its Entity List to cover any affiliates that are at least 50% owned by one or more entities on the Entity List or the Military End-User (MEU) List.

This rule closes a significant loophole in restricted party lists, as previously, these lists excluded entities not specifically named, even if they had extensive corporate and financial ties with listed entities. This action strengthens the overall export control regime.

BIS also introduced a new Temporary General License (TGL) in Supplement No. 1 to Part 736 of the EAR. This TGL authorizes, in limited circumstances, exports, reexports, or transfers to or within certain country groups, with an expiration date of December 1, 2025.

body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amended the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by adding 32 entities to the Entity List. These entities are listed under various destinations, including China (23), India (1), Iran (1), Singapore (1), Taiwan (1), Turkey (3), and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) (2).

These additions are based on determinations by the U.S. Government that these entities are acting contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States. The EAR imposes additional license requirements and limits license exceptions for transactions involving these listed entities.

In addition to the new additions, BIS also revised an entry by removing two addresses from one entity under the destination of Russia and amended 27 existing entries to correct typographical errors across various destinations.

articles.headline: BIS Adds 32 Entities to Entity List, Citing National Security Concerns
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amended the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by adding 32 entities to the Entity List, effective September 12, 2025. These entities are located in China (23), India (1), Iran (1), Singapore (1), Taiwan (1), Turkey (3), and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) (2).

The U.S. Government determined that these entities are acting contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States. The EAR imposes additional license requirements and limits license exceptions for exports, reexports, and transfers to listed entities.

Among the reasons for these additions, some Chinese entities were cited for advancing China's military modernization through advanced artificial intelligence research, while an Indian entity was added for diverting U.S.-origin items to Russia without authorization.

articles.headline: FinCEN $3.4B Binance Penalty — Largest BSA Enforcement Action in History, Five-Year Monitorship Imposed
body: FinCEN imposed a $3.4 billion civil money penalty on Binance Holdings Limited — the largest Bank Secrecy Act enforcement action in history — for willfully failing to implement an effective AML programme and failing to file SARs on transactions with sanctioned jurisdictions including Iran, North Korea, and Cuba.

Binance processed over $898 million in transactions with users in sanctioned jurisdictions. The settlement requires Binance to exit the U.S. market entirely, submit to a five-year monitorship, and retain all historical transaction data for law enforcement access. Founder Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty to BSA violations and was sentenced to four months in federal prison.

articles.headline: UK Issues Two Russia Sanctions Packages in One Week — Drone Supply Chains and Deportation Networks Targeted
body: On May 11, the UK sanctioned 85 individuals and entities involved in Russia's hostile activities including forced deportation of Ukrainian children and Kremlin influence operations. On May 5, a prior package targeted Russia's drone supply chains.
A BBC News analysis found 184 UK-sanctioned shadow fleet vessels made 238 journeys through the UK's Exclusive Economic Zone since March 25, 2026 — highlighting continued enforcement gaps.
